<div align="center">
  
# AnimBits

![AnimBits Hero](./public/hero.png)

### Production-Ready Animation Components for React

A beautifully crafted collection of copy-paste animation components powered by Framer Motion. Install with one command, customize with simple props.

[Documentation](https://animbits.dev) · [Browse Components](https://animbits.dev/docs/animations/buttons/lift) · [Report Bug](https://github.com/Garvit1000/AnimBits/issues)

## Features

- **50+ Animation Components** - Icons, buttons, cards, loaders, transitions, and more
- **One-Command Install** - Use the shadcn CLI to add animations instantly
- **Simple Prop API** - Customize animations with intuitive props
- **Zero Config** - Works out of the box with Next.js, Vite, and more
- **Fully Typed** - Built with TypeScript for excellent developer experience
- **Dark Mode Ready** - All animations work seamlessly in light and dark themes
- **Responsive** - Optimized for all screen sizes
- **Accessible** - Respects `prefers-reduced-motion` settings

## Quick Start

### Installation

Install any animation component with a single command:

```bash
npx shadcn add https://animbits.dev/r/buttons-lift.json
```

### Usage

```tsx
import { LiftButton } from "@/components/animations/buttons/lift"

export default function App() {
  return (
    <LiftButton className="px-6 py-3 bg-blue-600 text-white rounded-lg">
      Hover me!
    </LiftButton>
  )
}
```

That's it! No configuration, no setup, just beautiful animations.

## Examples

### Magnetic Button

```tsx
import { MagneticButton } from "@/components/animations/buttons/magnetic"

<MagneticButton 
  strength={0.3} 
  className="px-8 py-4 bg-gradient-to-r from-purple-600 to-pink-600 text-white rounded-full"

  Magnetic Effect
</MagneticButton>
```

### Theme Toggle with Circular Ripple

```tsx
import { ThemeToggleCircular } from "@/components/animations/transitions/theme-toggle-circular"
import { useTheme } from "next-themes"

export function ThemeToggle() {
  const { setTheme } = useTheme()
  
  return (
    <ThemeToggleCircular 
      onToggle={() => setTheme(theme === 'dark' ? 'light' : 'dark')}
      speed={0.5}
      blur={0}
    >
      <button>Toggle Theme</button>
    </ThemeToggleCircular>
  )
}
```

## Development

### Prerequisites

- Node.js 18+ 
- pnpm (recommended) or npm

### Local Setup

```bash
# Clone the repository
git clone https://github.com/Garvit1000/AnimBits.git
cd AnimBits

# Install dependencies
pnpm install

# Build the registry
pnpm registry:build

# Start the development server
pnpm dev
```

The site will be available at `http://localhost:3000`

### Testing Components Locally

```bash
# In your test project
npx shadcn add http://localhost:3000/r/buttons-lift.json
```

### Adding a New Component

1. Create your component in `registry/new-york/animations/[category]/[name].tsx`
2. Add the component entry to `registry.json`
3. Create documentation in `content/docs/animations/[category]/[name].mdx`
4. Run `pnpm registry:build` to generate the registry files
5. Test locally and submit a PR

# border-gradient.mdx

Source: https://github.com/garvit1000/animbits/blob/main/content/docs/animations/buttons/border-gradient.mdx

title: Border Gradient Button
description: Button with animated gradient border that traces around the perimeter.

import { Preview, PreviewGrid } from '@/components/preview';
import { BorderGradientButton } from '@/registry/new-york/animations/buttons/border-gradient';

## Overview

The `BorderGradientButton` creates an animated gradient border that continuously traces around the button's perimeter, creating a premium, eye-catching effect.

## Preview

  code={`import { BorderGradientButton } from "@/components/animations/buttons/border-gradient"

<BorderGradientButton className="inline-flex h-11 items-center gap-2 rounded-lg bg-white dark:bg-neutral-900 px-6 text-sm font-semibold text-neutral-900 dark:text-white">
  Hover Me
</BorderGradientButton>`}
  <BorderGradientButton className="inline-flex h-11 items-center gap-2 rounded-lg bg-white dark:bg-neutral-900 px-6 text-sm font-semibold text-neutral-900 dark:text-white">
    Hover Me
  </BorderGradientButton>

## Installation

        ```bash
        npx shadcn@latest add @animbits/buttons-border-gradient
        ```
        ```bash
        pnpm dlx shadcn@latest add @animbits/buttons-border-gradient
        ```
        ```bash
        yarn dlx shadcn@latest add @animbits/buttons-border-gradient
        ```
        ```bash
        bunx shadcn@latest add @animbits/buttons-border-gradient
        ```
    ```tsx title="components/animations/buttons/border-gradient.tsx"
"use client";
import * as React from "react";
import { motion, HTMLMotionProps } from "motion/react";
interface BorderGradientButtonProps
  extends Omit<HTMLMotionProps<"button">, "children"> {
  children: React.ReactNode;
  duration?: number;
  colors?: string[];
}
function cn(...classes: (string | undefined)[]) {
  return classes.filter(Boolean).join(" ");
}
export function BorderGradientButton({
  children,
  className,
  duration = 2,
  colors = ["#3b82f6", "#8b5cf6", "#ec4899"],
  ...props
}: BorderGradientButtonProps) {
  const buttonRef = React.useRef<HTMLButtonElement>(null);
  const [dimensions, setDimensions] = React.useState({
    width: 0,
    height: 0,
    radius: 0,
    perimeter: 0,
  });
  const gradientId = React.useId();
  React.useEffect(() => {
    if (!buttonRef.current) return;
    const updateDimensions = () => {
      if (buttonRef.current) {
        const styles = window.getComputedStyle(buttonRef.current);
        const width = buttonRef.current.offsetWidth;
        const height = buttonRef.current.offsetHeight;
        const borderRadius =
          parseFloat(styles.borderTopLeftRadius) ||
          parseFloat(styles.borderRadius) ||
          0;
        const maxRadius = Math.min(width, height) / 2;
        const actualRadius = Math.min(borderRadius, maxRadius);
        const straightEdges =
          2 * (width - 2 * actualRadius + (height - 2 * actualRadius));
        const curvedEdges = 2 * Math.PI * actualRadius;
        const perimeter = straightEdges + curvedEdges;
        setDimensions({
          width,
          height,
          radius: actualRadius,
          perimeter: perimeter || 1,
        });
      }
    };
    updateDimensions();
    const observer = new ResizeObserver(updateDimensions);
    if (buttonRef.current) {
      observer.observe(buttonRef.current);
    }
    return () => observer.disconnect();
  }, []);
  return (
    <motion.button
      ref={buttonRef}
      className={cn("relative", className)}
      {...props}
    >
      {}
      {dimensions.width > 0 && (
        <svg
          className="absolute inset-0 pointer-events-none"
          width={dimensions.width}
          height={dimensions.height}
        >
          <defs>
            <linearGradient id={gradientId} x1="0%" y1="0%" x2="100%" y2="100%">
              {colors.map((color, i) => (
                <stop
                  key={i}
                  offset={`${(i / (colors.length - 1)) * 100}%`}
                  stopColor={color}
                />
              ))}
            </linearGradient>
          </defs>
          <motion.rect
            x="1"
            y="1"
            width={dimensions.width - 2}
            height={dimensions.height - 2}
            rx={dimensions.radius}
            fill="none"
            stroke={`url(#${gradientId})`}
            strokeWidth="2"
            strokeDasharray={dimensions.perimeter}
            strokeDashoffset={0}
            animate={{ strokeDashoffset: [0, -dimensions.perimeter] }}
            transition={{
              duration,
              ease: "linear",
              repeat: Infinity,
            }}
            style={{
              strokeLinecap: "round",
            }}
          />
        </svg>
      )}
      <span className="relative z-10">{children}</span>
    </motion.button>
  );
}

```


## Props

| `duration` | `number` | `2` | Animation duration in seconds for one complete cycle |
| `colors` | `string[]` | `["#3b82f6", "#8b5cf6", "#ec4899"]` | Array of hex colors for the gradient |
| `children` | `React.ReactNode` | Required | Button content |
| `className` | `string` | `undefined` | Additional CSS classes |

All other props from `motion.button` are supported and passed through.

## Animation Details

The border gradient animation works by:

1. Using a rotatingparate animated divs for each side (top, right, bottom, left)
2. Each div moves along its respective edge with a sequential delay
3. The gradient flows smoothly as it traces around the perimeter
4. Animation runs continuously and infinitely
5. Each side's animation is perfectly timed to create a seamless loop

## Accessibility

- Maintains all standard button semantics
- Keyboard accessible (can be focused and activated)
- Animation respects `prefers-reduced-motion` when using Framer Motion's default settings
- Supports all ARIA attributes through prop spreading

## Browser Support

- Works in all modern browsers that support CSS gradients and transforms
- Requires Framer Motion for animations
- Gracefully degrades in browsers without animation support

## Use cases

The `BorderGradientButton` suits situations where you want to draw the eye to a button without changing its fill color. The animated `strokeDashoffset` traces the exact perimeter of the button, including its border radius, so the gradient feels painted on rather than overlaid. Reach for it when:

- **Hero CTAs.** A primary "Get started" or "Sign up free" button on a landing page benefits from the continuous motion, which naturally attracts peripheral vision.
- **Pricing card actions.** A highlighted plan's upgrade button needs to feel premium; the gradient border differentiates it from sibling buttons without requiring a different background.
- **Feature spotlight buttons.** Alongside a newly released feature callout, the animated border signals "pay attention here" without being as aggressive as a full background animation.
- **Dark-mode interfaces.** On dark backgrounds (`bg-neutral-900`), the default blue-purple-pink gradient (`colors` default) pops strongly while keeping the button content legible against the dark fill.

Because the SVG overlay measures actual DOM dimensions via `ResizeObserver` and reacts to `borderTopLeftRadius`, the animation adapts automatically to `rounded-lg`, `rounded-full`, and `rounded-none` without any extra config.

## When to use / when not to use

**Use `BorderGradientButton` when:**

- You need exactly one focal CTA per viewport that merits continuous animation.
- The button has a solid or semi-transparent background that contrasts with the gradient so the border is visible.
- The design calls for a premium feel on a contained element rather than a full-page effect.

**Reach for a different button when:**

- You have three or more primary buttons visible at once. Multiple spinning borders compete for attention and exhaust the eye; use a static [Glow Button](/docs/animations/buttons/glow) or [Lift Button](/docs/animations/buttons/lift) for secondary actions instead.
- The button sits on a light multi-color background where the default `["#3b82f6", "#8b5cf6", "#ec4899"]` gradient blends in. You will need to customize `colors` or pick a different component.
- The user needs to activate the button repeatedly in quick succession (forms, incrementers). A continuous looping border gives no click feedback; combine with [Press Button](/docs/animations/buttons/press) via `whileTap` if you need tap confirmation.
- The button is inside a data-dense table or list. Continuous motion in a tight grid is distracting.

## Accessibility notes

The `BorderGradientButton` is a `motion.button`, so it carries full button semantics by default. Still:

- **Keyboard and focus.** The component spreads all props onto `motion.button`, so `:focus-visible` styles from your CSS apply. Make sure your global styles or Tailwind config define a visible ring (e.g., `focus-visible:ring-2 focus-visible:ring-blue-500`) because the animated border is not a focus indicator.
- **Don't rely on the border color alone.** The gradient is purely decorative. Ensure the button label or an `aria-label` conveys the action; sighted users and screen reader users should both understand the purpose.
- **Reduced motion.** The border animation loops forever via `repeat: Infinity`. Honor the OS setting to stop the loop:

```tsx
"use client"
import { useReducedMotion } from "motion/react"
import { BorderGradientButton } from "@/components/animations/buttons/border-gradient"

function AccessibleBorderGradient({ children }: { children: React.ReactNode }) {
  const reduced = useReducedMotion()
  // A very long duration makes the trace imperceptibly slow for users who prefer no motion.
  return (
    <BorderGradientButton
      duration={reduced ? 9999 : 2}
      className="inline-flex h-11 items-center rounded-lg bg-white dark:bg-neutral-900 px-6 text-sm font-semibold text-neutral-900 dark:text-white"
    >
      {children}
    </BorderGradientButton>
  )
}
```

- **ARIA attributes.** Pass `aria-disabled="true"` and `disabled` together when the button is inactive; the SVG overlay is `pointer-events-none` so it never intercepts clicks, but the `motion.button` itself must still be disabled to block keyboard activation.

## Performance considerations

- **Compositor-friendly animation.** The gradient traces by animating `strokeDashoffset` on an SVG `<rect>`. SVG stroke-dashoffset changes are handled by the compositor via an SVG paint layer; they do not trigger layout or pixel-level repaints of the surrounding DOM.
- **Infinite loop caveat.** `repeat: Infinity` keeps the animation scheduled indefinitely. Conditionally render the button only when it needs to be on screen; hiding it with `display:none` or `visibility:hidden` without unmounting still runs the animation. Unmounting stops it.
- **ResizeObserver per instance.** Each `BorderGradientButton` attaches one `ResizeObserver` to its button node for dimension tracking. This is lightweight for a handful of instances, but avoid rendering dozens of them in a list since each observer holds a separate callback slot.
- **`useId` for gradient IDs.** The component uses React's `useId` to generate unique `linearGradient` IDs, preventing SVG `defs` collisions when multiple instances share a page. No extra config needed.
- **SVG sizing.** The overlay SVG is sized via inline `width`/`height` attributes equal to the button's `offsetWidth` and `offsetHeight`. It does not stretch or reflow its container because it is `position: absolute` with `inset-0` and `pointer-events-none`.

## Customization examples

### Monochrome border on a dark card

A single-color gradient pair reads as a subtle shimmer rather than a rainbow effect:

```tsx
<BorderGradientButton
  colors={["#e2e8f0", "#94a3b8", "#e2e8f0"]}
  duration={3}
  className="inline-flex h-11 items-center rounded-lg bg-zinc-900 px-6 text-sm font-semibold text-white"
>
  View details
</BorderGradientButton>
```

### Brand-aligned gradient

Match brand colors instead of the default blue-purple-pink:

```tsx
<BorderGradientButton
  colors={["#f97316", "#eab308", "#f97316"]}
  duration={2.5}
  className="inline-flex h-11 items-center rounded-lg bg-white dark:bg-neutral-900 px-6 text-sm font-semibold text-neutral-900 dark:text-white"
>
  Start free trial
</BorderGradientButton>
```

### Slower, calmer cycle for secondary actions

A 5-second cycle is much less distracting in a content-heavy layout:

```tsx
<BorderGradientButton
  duration={5}
  colors={["#6366f1", "#8b5cf6"]}
  className="inline-flex h-11 items-center rounded-full bg-white dark:bg-neutral-900 px-6 text-sm font-semibold text-neutral-900 dark:text-white"
>
  Learn more
</BorderGradientButton>
```

```tsx
    className="inline-flex h-11 items-center rounded-lg bg-white dark:bg-neutral-900 px-6 text-sm font-semibold text-neutral-900 dark:text-white"
  >
    Get started free
  </BorderGradientButton>
  <button className="inline-flex h-11 items-center rounded-lg border border-neutral-200 dark:border-neutral-700 px-6 text-sm font-semibold text-neutral-700 dark:text-neutral-300">
    View demo
```

    **Step 2: Copy the component**

    ```tsx title="components/animations/buttons/fade-in.tsx"
"use client";
import { motion, type HTMLMotionProps } from "motion/react";
import {
  fadeInVariants,
  createDelayedTransition,
} from "@/lib/animation-presets";
interface FadeInButtonProps extends Omit<HTMLMotionProps<"button">, "animate"> {
  children: React.ReactNode;
  delay?: number;
  duration?: number;
}
export function FadeInButton({
  children,
  delay = 0,
  duration = 0.3,
  ...props
}: FadeInButtonProps) {
  return (
    <motion.button
      variants={fadeInVariants}
      initial="hidden"
      animate="visible"
      transition={createDelayedTransition(delay, duration)}
      {...props}
    >
      {children}
    </motion.button>
  );
}

```

```tsx
  Hover Me
</FadeInButton>
```

```tsx
  Delayed Fade
</FadeInButton>
```

### Staggered Buttons

```tsx
<div className="flex gap-4">

  <FadeInButton delay={0.2}>Second</FadeInButton>
  <FadeInButton delay={0.4}>Third</FadeInButton>
</div>
```

## Props

| `delay` | `number` | `0` | Delay before animation starts (seconds) |
| `duration` | `number` | `0.3` | Animation duration (seconds) |
| `children` | `React.ReactNode` | Required | Button content |

## Use cases

`FadeInButton` animates from `opacity: 0` to `opacity: 1` using the `fadeInVariants` preset (`hidden: { opacity: 0 }`, `visible: { opacity: 1 }`) and `createDelayedTransition` which applies an `easeOut` curve. Because the animation fires on mount (`initial="hidden"`, `animate="visible"`), it runs once when the component first renders. Reach for it when:

- **Staggered toolbar or nav actions.** Reveal a row of buttons one at a time by incrementing the `delay` prop: `delay={0}`, `delay={0.2}`, `delay={0.4}`. The opacity-only transition is subtle enough not to distract from the page content.
- **Confirmation dialogs and modals.** A button that fades in after a short delay (0.2 to 0.4 seconds) gives the dialog time to settle before the primary action becomes clickable, reducing accidental submissions.
- **Route-level entrance animations.** When a page loads, primary CTAs can fade in after content has appeared (`delay={0.3}`) to sequence the user's attention.
- **Empty-state actions.** A "Create your first project" button that fades in when no data exists draws the eye after the surrounding empty-state illustration has rendered.

Because the transition uses `easeOut` with a default `duration` of 0.3 seconds, the button reaches full opacity quickly and does not leave the user waiting.

## When to use / when not to use

**Use `FadeInButton` when:**

- You want a one-time entrance animation that plays on mount and then stays visible.
- You're sequencing multiple buttons with the `delay` prop to create a staggered reveal.
- The button lives on a page or section that enters the viewport as part of a route transition.

**Reach for a different button when:**

- You need a hover or click interaction animation rather than an entrance animation. `FadeInButton` does not respond to hover or tap. Use [Glow Button](/docs/animations/buttons/glow), [Lift Button](/docs/animations/buttons/lift), or [Press Button](/docs/animations/buttons/press) for that purpose.
- The button is always visible (not conditionally mounted or revealed by routing). If the component never unmounts, the fade only plays once on the initial page load, and returning users never see it.
- You need to slide the button in from a direction. Use [Slide In Button](/docs/animations/buttons/slide-in) which also fades but adds a 20px directional translation (`x: -20` for `left`, `y: 20` for `down`, etc.).
- You want a continuous or repeating animation. `FadeInButton` plays once; it has no `repeat` setting.

## Accessibility notes

The fade-in is a purely visual entrance effect. The button is fully interactive before the animation completes because motion only affects `opacity`, not `pointer-events` or `visibility`.

- **Content is always in the DOM.** Screen readers see the button the moment it mounts, regardless of where the opacity is in the transition. No additional `aria-live` region is needed.
- **Keyboard focus.** Because `FadeInButton` renders a `motion.button`, it receives focus normally. The fade does not block tab order; if the user tabs to the button during the 0.3 second fade it activates normally.
- **Reduced motion.** The fade modifies opacity, which is generally tolerable under `prefers-reduced-motion`. If you want to fully skip the animation for users who prefer less motion:

```tsx
"use client"
import { useReducedMotion } from "motion/react"
import { FadeInButton } from "@/components/animations/buttons/fade-in"

function AccessibleFadeIn({ children }: { children: React.ReactNode }) {
  const reduced = useReducedMotion()
  // Skip the fade entirely by setting duration to 0 when reduced motion is preferred.
  return (
    <FadeInButton
      duration={reduced ? 0 : 0.3}
      className="inline-flex h-11 items-center rounded-lg bg-blue-600 px-6 text-sm font-semibold text-white"
    >
      {children}
    </FadeInButton>
  )
}
```

- **Don't hide action from keyboard-only users.** Never conditionally add `disabled` during the animation; the button should be interactive from mount.

## Performance considerations

- **Opacity-only animation.** `fadeInVariants` changes only `opacity`, which is a compositor-friendly property. The browser does not trigger layout or repaint during the transition.
- **Single-fire animation.** Unlike `repeat: Infinity` components such as [Border Gradient Button](/docs/animations/buttons/border-gradient), `FadeInButton` fires once and stops scheduling frames after the transition completes. There is no ongoing animation overhead.
- **`createDelayedTransition` does not poll.** The delay is implemented as a CSS/Web Animations delay, not a `setTimeout` re-render loop, so it does not cause extra React renders.
- **Staggered groups.** Rendering many `FadeInButton` components with different `delay` values is safe; each is a single `motion.button` with one short animation and no ongoing subscriber after it completes.
- **Remounting resets the animation.** If the parent component unmounts and remounts `FadeInButton`, the fade plays again from `opacity: 0`. Wrap in a stable parent or use a key-controlled remount only when you intentionally want to replay the entrance.

# glow.mdx

title: Glow Button
description: Button with colored glow effect on hover using the useHoverGlow hook.

## Overview

The `GlowButton` component adds a colored glow effect on hover. Built using the `useHoverGlow` primitive hook, perfect for creating attention-grabbing CTAs.

<Callout type="info">
  **Uses primitive hook:** This component uses `useHoverGlow` internally. You can use that hook directly on any element.
</Callout>

</GlowButton>`}

    Hover Me
  </GlowButton>

## Installation

        ```bash
        npx shadcn@latest add @animbits/buttons-glow
        ```
        ```bash
        pnpm dlx shadcn@latest add @animbits/buttons-glow
        ```

    **Step 1: Copy the hook**
    
    ```tsx title="lib/hooks/use-hover-glow.ts"
    import { type MotionProps, type Easing } from "motion/react";

    export interface UseHoverGlowOptions {
      glowColor?: string;
      glowBlur?: number;
      glowSpread?: number;
      duration?: number;
      ease?: Easing | Easing[];
      scale?: number;
      innerGlow?: boolean;
    }

    export function useHoverGlow(options: UseHoverGlowOptions = {}): MotionProps {
      const {
        glowColor = "rgba(59, 130, 246, 0.5)",
        glowBlur = 20,
        glowSpread = 5,
        duration = 0.3,
        ease = "easeOut",
        scale = 1.02,
        innerGlow = false,
      } = options;

      const baseShadow = "0 2px 8px rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.1)";
      const glowShadow = `0 0 ${glowBlur}px ${glowSpread}px ${glowColor}`;
      const innerGlowShadow = innerGlow
        ? `inset 0 0 ${glowBlur / 2}px ${glowColor}`
        : "";

      const hoverShadow = innerGlow
        ? `${baseShadow}, ${glowShadow}, ${innerGlowShadow}`
        : `${baseShadow}, ${glowShadow}`;

      return {
        initial: {
          scale: 1,
          boxShadow: baseShadow,
        },
        whileHover: {
          scale,
          boxShadow: hoverShadow,
        },
        transition: {
          duration,
          ease,
        },
      };
    }
    ```

    **Step 2: Copy the component**
    
    ```tsx title="components/animations/buttons/glow.tsx"
"use client";
import { motion, type HTMLMotionProps } from "motion/react";
import { useHoverGlow } from "@/lib/use-hover-glow";
interface GlowButtonProps extends Omit<HTMLMotionProps<"button">, "animate"> {
  children: React.ReactNode;
  glowColor?: string;
  intensity?: number;
}
export function GlowButton({
  children,
  glowColor = "rgba(59, 130, 246, 0.5)",
  intensity = 20,
  ...props
}: GlowButtonProps) {
  const glowProps = useHoverGlow({
    glowColor,
    glowBlur: intensity,
  });
  return (
    <motion.button {...glowProps} {...props}>
      {children}
    </motion.button>
  );
}

```

| `intensity` | `number` | `20` | Glow spread in pixels |
| `children` | `React.ReactNode` | Required | Button content |
| `...props` | `HTMLMotionProps<"button">` | - | All button and motion props |

## Using the Hook Directly

```tsx
import { motion } from "motion/react"
import { useHoverGlow } from "@/lib/hooks"

const glowProps = useHoverGlow({ glowColor: "rgba(236, 72, 153, 0.6)" })

<motion.div {...glowProps} className="card">
  Any element with glow
</motion.div>
```

<Callout>
  **Tip:** Match the glow color to your button's background for a cohesive look.
</Callout>

## Use cases

`GlowButton` delegates to `useHoverGlow`, which animates `boxShadow` and optionally `scale` on `whileHover`. The default glow shadow is built as `0 0 20px 5px rgba(59, 130, 246, 0.5)` (controlled by `intensity` which maps to `glowBlur`, and `glowSpread` which defaults to 5 in the hook). The `scale` default is 1.02, so the button barely grows while the glow expands. Reach for it when:

- **Primary CTAs on dark backgrounds.** The drop-shadow glow is most legible against dark surfaces; a `glowColor` that matches the button background (`rgba(59, 130, 246, 0.5)` for a blue button) creates a clean halo.
- **Feature card buttons.** A "Try it" or "Open" button inside a dark product card benefits from a color-matched glow that reinforces the card's accent color.
- **Pricing plan highlights.** The featured plan's CTA can use a stronger `intensity={30}` to distinguish it from surrounding secondary buttons.
- **Icon-only action buttons.** Small round icon buttons in toolbars or floating action bars can use a lower `intensity={12}` for a subtle focus indicator that goes beyond the default browser ring.

Because the initial state includes a baseline shadow (`0 2px 8px rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.1)`), the button always looks slightly elevated and the hover glow is an additive enhancement rather than a jump from flat.

## When to use / when not to use

**Use `GlowButton` when:**

- The button sits against a dark or neutral background where a glow shadow renders cleanly.
- You want a hover effect that reinforces the button's own color rather than introducing motion across the page.
- One or two glowing buttons per view are sufficient (primary CTA plus one secondary at most).

**Reach for a different button when:**

- The background is light or busy. A box-shadow glow disappears on white and blurs into multi-color backgrounds. Use [Lift Button](/docs/animations/buttons/lift) instead, which uses `translateY` and shadow depth rather than colored spread.
- You need click feedback. `GlowButton` only activates on `whileHover` and has no `whileTap` behavior. Pair with [Press Button](/docs/animations/buttons/press) or add `whileTap={{ scale: 0.97 }}` via `...props` if tap confirmation matters.
- The button is disabled. A glowing disabled button misleads users into thinking it is active. Suppress the glow with `pointer-events-none opacity-50` and do not render the glow variant.
- You need a continuous ambient glow that doesn't depend on hover. `GlowButton` is hover-only; consider using a CSS `box-shadow` directly on your button for a static glow.

## Accessibility notes

`GlowButton` renders a `motion.button`, so button semantics, tab order, and keyboard activation are preserved without additional work.

- **Focus visibility.** The `boxShadow` glow only fires on `whileHover`. Keyboard focus does not trigger `whileHover` in Motion, so keyboard users won't see the glow as a focus indicator. Make sure a CSS `:focus-visible` ring is present on your button class (e.g., `focus-visible:ring-2 focus-visible:ring-blue-400`).
- **Don't rely on glow color to convey state.** If the glow is used to signal "this plan is selected" or "this action is primary," back it up with a text label or `aria-current`.
- **Reduced motion.** The glow transition is 0.3 seconds with `easeOut`, so it is brief and unlikely to cause discomfort. Still, the `scale: 1.02` micro-growth can be disorienting for some users. To disable the scale:

```tsx
"use client"
import { useReducedMotion } from "motion/react"
import { GlowButton } from "@/components/animations/buttons/glow"

function AccessibleGlow({ children }: { children: React.ReactNode }) {
  const reduced = useReducedMotion()
  return (
    <GlowButton
      // Pass intensity=0 to collapse the glow, and override scale via motion props.
      intensity={reduced ? 0 : 20}
      className="inline-flex h-11 items-center rounded-lg bg-blue-600 px-6 text-sm font-semibold text-white focus-visible:ring-2 focus-visible:ring-blue-400"
    >
      {children}
    </GlowButton>
  )
}
```

## Performance considerations

- **`boxShadow` is not a compositor-only property.** Unlike `transform` and `opacity`, animating `boxShadow` triggers a repaint on most browsers because the shadow must be re-rasterized. The 0.3-second hover transition means this repaint happens once on enter and once on leave, not continuously. For a single button, this cost is negligible.
- **`scale: 1.02` is compositor-safe.** The micro-scale applied on hover runs as a compositor transform and does not cause layout.
- **Avoid glow on frequently re-rendered components.** If the parent component re-renders at high frequency (e.g., inside a real-time data feed), the `motion.button` will re-reconcile on every render. Memoize the parent or extract the button to a stable subtree.
- **`useHoverGlow` hook overhead.** The hook constructs shadow strings and returns a static `MotionProps` object on every render. It contains no subscriptions or side effects, so re-renders are cheap. The result is not memoized inside the hook, but the strings are simple string concatenations.

# lift.mdx

## Overview

The `LiftButton` component creates a button that lifts up on hover with an optional shadow effect. Built using the `useHoverLift` primitive hook, providing a polished, interactive feel.

</Callout>

## Installation

        ```bash
        npx shadcn@latest add @animbits/buttons-lift
        ```
        ```bash
        pnpm dlx shadcn@latest add @animbits/buttons-lift
        ```
        ```bash
        yarn dlx shadcn@latest add @animbits/buttons-lift
        ```

        ```bash
        bunx shadcn@latest add @animbits/buttons-lift
        ```

    **Step 1: Copy the hook**
    
    ```tsx title="lib/hooks/use-hover-lift.ts"
    import { type MotionProps, type Easing } from "motion/react";

    export interface UseHoverLiftOptions {
      liftDistance?: number;
      addShadow?: boolean;
      shadowIntensity?: number;
      duration?: number;
      ease?: Easing | Easing[];
      scale?: number;
    }

    export function useHoverLift(options: UseHoverLiftOptions = {}): MotionProps {
      const {
        liftDistance = 8,
        addShadow = true,
        shadowIntensity = 0.3,
        duration = 0.2,
        ease = "easeOut",
        scale = 1,
      } = options;

      const shadowBlur = liftDistance * 2;
      const shadowSpread = Math.round(liftDistance / 4);

      return {
        initial: {
          y: 0,
          scale: 1,
          boxShadow: addShadow
            ? `0 2px 4px rgba(0, 0, 0, ${shadowIntensity * 0.3})`
            : undefined,
        },
        whileHover: {
          y: -liftDistance,
          scale,
          boxShadow: addShadow
            ? `0 ${shadowBlur}px ${shadowBlur + shadowSpread}px rgba(0, 0, 0, ${shadowIntensity})`
            : undefined,
        },
        transition: {
          duration,
          ease,
        },
      };
    }
    ```

    **Step 2: Copy the component**

    ```tsx title="components/animations/buttons/lift.tsx"
"use client";
import { motion, type HTMLMotionProps } from "motion/react";
import { useHoverLift } from "@/lib/use-hover-lift";
interface LiftButtonProps extends Omit<HTMLMotionProps<"button">, "animate"> {
  children: React.ReactNode;
  liftHeight?: number;
  shadow?: boolean;
}
export function LiftButton({
  children,
  liftHeight = 8,
  shadow = true,
  ...props
}: LiftButtonProps) {
  const liftProps = useHoverLift({
    liftDistance: liftHeight,
    addShadow: shadow,
  });
  return (
    <motion.button {...liftProps} {...props}>
      {children}
    </motion.button>
  );
}

```

## Using the Hook Directly

```tsx
  const liftProps = useHoverLift({ liftDistance: 12 })

      {...liftProps}

  )
}
```

## Combining with Other Effects

```tsx
import { motion } from "motion/react"
import { useHoverLift, useHoverGlow } from "@/lib/hooks"

export function LiftAndGlow() {
  const lift = useHoverLift({ liftDistance: 10 })
  const glow = useHoverGlow({ glowColor: "rgba(59, 130, 246, 0.5)" })
  
  const combined = {
    ...lift,
    whileHover: {
      ...lift.whileHover,
      ...glow.whileHover,
    },
  }
  
  return (
    <motion.button {...combined} className="inline-flex h-11 items-center gap-2 rounded-lg bg-blue-600 px-6 text-sm font-semibold text-white">
      Lift + Glow
    </motion.button>
  )
}
```

## Use cases

`LiftButton` delegates to `useHoverLift`, which animates `y` (translateY) and `boxShadow` on `whileHover`. The default `liftHeight` is 8 pixels (maps to `liftDistance` in the hook), the shadow blur is `liftDistance * 2` (16px), and `shadowIntensity` defaults to 0.3. The transition uses `duration: 0.2` with `easeOut`. Reach for it when:

- **Primary action buttons in card grids.** Cards that reveal an action button on hover benefit from the lift reinforcing the hover state without changing color or layout.
- **Navigation link buttons.** A pill-shaped nav item that lifts slightly on hover communicates interactivity more clearly than a color change alone.
- **Icon action buttons.** A bookmark, share, or favorite button using `liftHeight={6}` responds to hover with a tight, contained lift that doesn't disturb neighboring elements.
- **Secondary CTAs.** After a primary CTA, a "Learn more" or "See pricing" button can use `liftHeight={4}` for a softer lift that avoids competing with the primary.

The `shadow` prop defaults to `true`, so the lift always comes with a growing shadow that reinforces the vertical displacement. Set `shadow={false}` if your button already has a strong visual background and the shadow would be redundant.

## When to use / when not to use

**Use `LiftButton` when:**

- You want a hover effect that feels physical and grounded (the shadow makes the lift read as real depth).
- The button is on a surface with a solid or near-solid background so the shadow is visible.
- You need a hover interaction without any ongoing animation overhead (lift only fires on hover, not continuously).

**Reach for a different button when:**

- You want a colored glow rather than a neutral shadow on hover. Use [Glow Button](/docs/animations/buttons/glow), which animates `boxShadow` with a colored spread.
- The button is inside a flex row where a `translateY` shift would push adjacent elements. The lift moves only the button itself (not its layout box), so siblings don't shift, but the button may visually overlap them. Reduce `liftHeight` or use [Press Button](/docs/animations/buttons/press) instead for click-based feedback.
- You need both hover lift and click feedback. `LiftButton` only responds to `whileHover`. Combine with `whileTap={{ scale: 0.97 }}` passed as a prop, or use [Press Button](/docs/animations/buttons/press) alongside it.
- The button sits on a patterned or textured background where a neutral gray shadow won't read. Use a border or color change instead.

## Accessibility notes

`LiftButton` renders a `motion.button`, so it carries full native button semantics and participates in tab order.

- **The lift is purely visual.** Moving the button 8px upward via `translateY` does not reorder the DOM or change the element's accessible position. Screen readers are not affected.
- **Focus visibility.** The `whileHover` animation is mouse-triggered. Keyboard focus does not activate the lift, so ensure your CSS defines a `:focus-visible` ring (e.g., `focus-visible:ring-2 focus-visible:ring-blue-500`) to give keyboard users an equivalent indicator.
- **Don't use lift as a state signal.** If the lift is supposed to indicate "this button is selected" or "this action is dangerous," it won't be perceived by screen reader users. Use an `aria-pressed` or `aria-current` attribute and a text label.
- **Reduced motion.** The `y` transform and `boxShadow` changes are brief (0.2 seconds) and happen only during hover, not continuously. To eliminate the motion entirely:

```tsx
"use client"
import { useReducedMotion } from "motion/react"
import { LiftButton } from "@/components/animations/buttons/lift"

function AccessibleLift({ children }: { children: React.ReactNode }) {
  const reduced = useReducedMotion()
  return (
    <LiftButton
      liftHeight={reduced ? 0 : 8}
      shadow={!reduced}
      className="inline-flex h-11 items-center rounded-lg bg-blue-600 px-6 text-sm font-semibold text-white focus-visible:ring-2 focus-visible:ring-blue-400"
    >
      {children}
    </LiftButton>
  )
}
```

## Performance considerations

- **`translateY` is compositor-safe.** The lift animates the `y` motion value, which maps to a CSS `transform: translateY(...)`. This runs on the compositor thread with no layout recalculation.
- **`boxShadow` triggers repaint.** When `shadow={true}` (the default), the shadow transitions on hover entry and exit, which requires a repaint each time. This is a single repaint per hover event, not a continuous one. It is negligible for one or a few buttons, but if you render many `LiftButton` components in a dense list and all are hovered simultaneously (e.g., in a card grid), consider `shadow={false}` and using a CSS `box-shadow` transition instead.
- **No ongoing animation.** Unlike [Border Gradient Button](/docs/animations/buttons/border-gradient), which loops indefinitely, `LiftButton` only schedules animation frames during the hover transition. When the user moves the mouse away, the animation completes and stops.
- **`useHoverLift` returns a static props object.** The hook computes shadow strings on each render but has no subscriptions or timers. Memoizing the parent component eliminates redundant calls.

# magnetic.mdx

Source: https://github.com/garvit1000/animbits/blob/main/content/docs/animations/buttons/magnetic.mdx

title: Magnetic Button
description: Button that smoothly follows the cursor on hover using spring physics.

import { Callout } from 'fumadocs-ui/components/callout';
import { Preview, PreviewGrid } from '@/components/preview';
import { MagneticButton } from '@/registry/new-york/animations/buttons/magnetic';

## Overview

The `MagneticButton` creates a magnetic attraction effect where the button smoothly follows your cursor. Built using the `useMagnetic` hook with spring physics for natural movement.

<Callout type="info">
  **Advanced interaction:** This creates a premium, playful feel perfect for hero CTAs and special actions.
</Callout>

## Preview

  background="grid"
  code={`import { MagneticButton } from "@/components/animations/buttons/magnetic"

<MagneticButton className="inline-flex h-11 items-center gap-2 rounded-lg bg-blue-600 px-6 text-sm font-semibold text-white">
  Hover Me
</MagneticButton>`}
  <MagneticButton className="inline-flex h-11 items-center gap-2 rounded-lg bg-blue-600 px-6 text-sm font-semibold text-white">
    Hover Me
  </MagneticButton>

## Installation

        ```bash
        npx shadcn@latest add @animbits/buttons-magnetic
        ```
        ```bash
        pnpm dlx shadcn@latest add @animbits/buttons-magnetic
        ```
        ```bash
        yarn dlx shadcn@latest add @animbits/buttons-magnetic
        ```
        ```bash
        bunx shadcn@latest add @animbits/buttons-magnetic
        ```
    **Step 1: Copy the hook**

    ```tsx title="lib/hooks/use-magnetic.ts"
    import * as React from "react"
    import { useMotionValue, useSpring } from "motion/react"

    export interface UseMagneticOptions {
      strength?: number
      stiffness?: number
      damping?: number
    }

    export function useMagnetic(options: UseMagneticOptions = {}) {
      const { strength = 30, stiffness = 150, damping = 15 } = options

      const ref = React.useRef<HTMLElement>(null)
      const x = useMotionValue(0)
      const y = useMotionValue(0)

      const springConfig = { damping, stiffness }
      const springX = useSpring(x, springConfig)
      const springY = useSpring(y, springConfig)

      const handleMouseMove = (e: React.MouseEvent<HTMLElement>) => {
        if (!ref.current) return

        const rect = ref.current.getBoundingClientRect()
        const centerX = rect.left + rect.width / 2
        const centerY = rect.top + rect.height / 2

        const distanceX = e.clientX - centerX
        const distanceY = e.clientY - centerY

        x.set(distanceX * (strength / 100))
        y.set(distanceY * (strength / 100))
      }

      const handleMouseLeave = () => {
        x.set(0)
        y.set(0)
      }

      const magneticProps = {
        style: { x: springX, y: springY },
        onMouseMove: handleMouseMove,
        onMouseLeave: handleMouseLeave,
      }

      return { magneticProps, ref }
    }
    ```

    **Step 2: Copy the utility**

    ```tsx title="lib/utils.ts"
    import { type ClassValue, clsx } from "clsx"
    import { twMerge } from "tailwind-merge"

    export function cn(...inputs: ClassValue[]) {
      return twMerge(clsx(inputs))
    }
    ```

    **Step 3: Copy the component**

    ```tsx title="components/animations/buttons/magnetic.tsx"
"use client";
import * as React from "react";
import { motion, HTMLMotionProps } from "motion/react";
import { cn } from "@/lib/utils";
import { useMagnetic, type UseMagneticOptions } from "@/lib/use-magnetic";
interface MagneticButtonProps
  extends Omit<HTMLMotionProps<"button">, "ref">,
    UseMagneticOptions {
  children: React.ReactNode;
}
export function MagneticButton({
  children,
  className,
  strength,
  stiffness,
  damping,
  ...props
}: MagneticButtonProps) {
  const { magneticProps, ref } = useMagnetic({ strength, stiffness, damping });
  return (
    <motion.button
      ref={ref as any}
      {...magneticProps}
      className={cn(className)}
      {...props}
    >
      {children}
    </motion.button>
  );
}

```

### Basic Example

```tsx

  strength={40}
  stiffness={300}
  damping={20}
  className="inline-flex h-11 items-center gap-2 rounded-lg bg-purple-600 px-6 text-sm font-semibold text-white"
>
  Snappy Response
</MagneticButton>
```

## Props

| `strength` | `number` | `30` | Magnetic attraction strength |
| `stiffness` | `number` | `150` | Spring stiffness (higher = snappier) |
| `damping` | `number` | `15` | Spring damping (higher = less bouncy) |
| `children` | `React.ReactNode` | Required | Button content |

<Callout type="warn">
  **Mobile:** Consider disabling on touch devices where hover doesn't apply.
</Callout>

## Use cases

`MagneticButton` uses `useMagnetic` to track `mousemove` events relative to the button's bounding rect, then drives two `useSpring` values (`springX`, `springY`) that translate the button toward the cursor. The default `strength` is 30, meaning the cursor's distance from center is multiplied by `30 / 100 = 0.3` to get the translation in pixels. Spring defaults are `stiffness: 150` and `damping: 15`, which produce a slightly elastic follow-through. Reach for it when:

- **Hero landing page CTAs.** A single large "Get started" or "Request demo" button in a sparse hero section is the canonical use case. The magnetic pull invites cursor exploration.
- **Portfolio or creative site navigation.** Large pill-shaped nav links that attract the cursor reinforce a playful, crafted identity.
- **Floating action buttons.** A fixed-position FAB in the corner of the screen can use a higher `strength` (40 to 50) since it is isolated and the user is deliberately targeting it.
- **Empty-state call to action.** When there is nothing else on the screen to interact with, a magnetic CTA keeps the interaction feeling alive.

Because the translation uses spring physics, the button overshoots slightly and snaps back when the cursor leaves, which is more engaging than a linear follow.

## When to use / when not to use

**Use `MagneticButton` when:**

- The button is large and isolated enough that the displacement doesn't overlap adjacent content.
- The interaction is mouse-driven (desktop-first layouts). On touch devices, `onMouseMove` never fires, so the component renders as a standard button.
- You want to signal "this is the primary action" without a color or size change.

**Reach for a different button when:**

- You have multiple buttons close together. When two or three magnetic buttons are adjacent, moving the cursor between them causes jittery simultaneous displacements. Use [Lift Button](/docs/animations/buttons/lift) or [Glow Button](/docs/animations/buttons/glow) for tightly grouped actions instead.
- The button is inside a scrollable container. `getBoundingClientRect` returns viewport-relative coordinates, so the magnet works correctly, but `translateX`/`translateY` offsets during fast scroll can cause the button to appear to drift. Test carefully.
- You're building for touch-first audiences. The hook has no touch fallback; on mobile the button is visually identical to an unstyled `motion.button`.
- The button is inside a form where precise targeting matters. A button that moves away from the cursor as the user aims at it can cause misclicks; stick to [Press Button](/docs/animations/buttons/press) for form submissions.

## Accessibility notes

- **The magnetic movement is purely visual.** The button's DOM position and accessible name are unaffected by `springX`/`springY`. Screen readers announce it as a normal button.
- **Keyboard activation is unaffected.** `Enter` and `Space` trigger `click` on the `motion.button` regardless of where the spring values have translated it.
- **Focus ring visibility.** The spring transform may shift the button slightly so its focus ring clips against a container boundary. Ensure `overflow: visible` on the button's parent, or add a generous `ring-offset`.
- **Reduced motion.** The spring physics produce a fluid, oscillating translation. This is more motion-intensive than a simple opacity fade. Disable the magnetic effect entirely for users who prefer reduced motion:

```tsx
"use client"
import { useReducedMotion } from "motion/react"
import { MagneticButton } from "@/components/animations/buttons/magnetic"

function AccessibleMagnetic({ children }: { children: React.ReactNode }) {
  const reduced = useReducedMotion()
  // strength=0 means x.set(0) and y.set(0) on every mousemove, so there is no displacement.
  return (
    <MagneticButton
      strength={reduced ? 0 : 30}
      className="inline-flex h-11 items-center rounded-lg bg-blue-600 px-6 text-sm font-semibold text-white focus-visible:ring-2 focus-visible:ring-blue-400"
    >
      {children}
    </MagneticButton>
  )
}
```

- **Touch devices.** The hook only binds `onMouseMove` and `onMouseLeave`. On touch devices the button renders normally with no displacement, which is the correct fallback.

## Performance considerations

- **`useSpring` values are motion values, not React state.** The spring animation updates `springX` and `springY` on every animation frame without triggering a React re-render. The button's DOM node is updated directly by Motion's reconciler. This is the most efficient path for per-frame updates.
- **`transform: translateX/Y` is compositor-safe.** The translation runs on the compositor thread with no layout recalculation.
- **`mousemove` fires at pointer rate.** On a 120Hz display, `handleMouseMove` runs up to 120 times per second. The handler only calls `x.set(...)` and `y.set(...)`, which are synchronous calls to Motion's internal store; they do not schedule React renders.
- **One `useMagnetic` instance per button.** Each instance holds two `MotionValue` and two `useSpring` subscriptions. Keep the number of active `MagneticButton` components low (1 to 3 per viewport) to avoid accumulating spring subscriptions.
- **Spring continues briefly after `mouseleave`.** `x.set(0)` and `y.set(0)` on mouse leave trigger a spring return animation. The spring naturally comes to rest in about 0.5 to 1 second depending on `damping`. The button stays mounted throughout.

## Customization examples

```tsx
  aria-label="Settings"
>
  <svg className="h-4 w-4 text-neutral-600 dark:text-neutral-300" viewBox="0 0 20 20" fill="currentColor">
```

# press.mdx

Source: https://github.com/garvit1000/animbits/blob/main/content/docs/animations/buttons/press.mdx

title: Press Button
description: Button with press-down feedback effect on click using the usePress hook.

import { Callout } from 'fumadocs-ui/components/callout';
import { Preview, PreviewGrid } from '@/components/preview';
import { PressButton } from '@/registry/new-york/animations/buttons/press';

## Overview

The `PressButton` component provides tactile press-down feedback when clicked. Built using the `usePress` primitive hook for responsive, satisfying interactions.

## Preview

  background="grid"
  code={`import { PressButton } from "@/components/animations/buttons/press"

<PressButton className="inline-flex h-11 items-center gap-2 rounded-lg bg-blue-600 px-6 text-sm font-semibold text-white">
  Click Me
</PressButton>`}
  <PressButton className="inline-flex h-11 items-center gap-2 rounded-lg bg-blue-600 px-6 text-sm font-semibold text-white">
    Click Me
  </PressButton>

## Installation

        ```bash
        npx shadcn@latest add @animbits/buttons-press
        ```
        ```bash
        pnpm dlx shadcn@latest add @animbits/buttons-press
        ```
        ```bash
        yarn dlx shadcn@latest add @animbits/buttons-press
        ```
        ```bash
        bunx shadcn@latest add @animbits/buttons-press
        ```
    **Step 1: Copy the hook**

    ```tsx title="lib/hooks/use-press.ts"
    import { type MotionProps, type Easing } from "motion/react";

    export interface UsePressOptions {
      pressScale?: number;
      duration?: number;
      ease?: Easing | Easing[];
      addRotation?: boolean;
      rotationAmount?: number;
    }

    export function usePress(options: UsePressOptions = {}): MotionProps {
      const {
        pressScale = 0.95,
        duration = 0.1,
        ease = "easeInOut",
        addRotation = false,
        rotationAmount = 2,
      } = options;

      return {
        whileTap: {
          scale: pressScale,
          rotate: addRotation ? rotationAmount : 0,
        },
        transition: {
          duration,
          ease,
        },
      };
    }
    ```

    **Step 2: Copy the component**

    ```tsx title="components/animations/buttons/press.tsx"
"use client";
import { motion, type HTMLMotionProps } from "motion/react";
import { usePress } from "@/lib/use-press";
interface PressButtonProps extends Omit<HTMLMotionProps<"button">, "animate"> {
  children: React.ReactNode;
  scale?: number;
}
export function PressButton({
  children,
  scale = 0.95,
  ...props
}: PressButtonProps) {
  const pressProps = usePress({
    pressScale: scale,
  });
  return (
    <motion.button {...pressProps} {...props}>
      {children}
    </motion.button>
  );
}

```

## Usage

```tsx
import { PressButton } from "@/components/animations/buttons/press"

<PressButton className="inline-flex h-11 items-center gap-2 rounded-lg bg-blue-600 px-6 text-sm font-semibold text-white">
  Click Me
</PressButton>
```

### Custom Scale


## Props

| `scale` | `number` | `0.95` | Scale factor when pressed (0-1) |
| `children` | `React.ReactNode` | Required | Button content |

```tsx
// Keyboard key style

  Enter
</PressButton>
```

<Callout>
  **Tip:** Combine with other effects like lift or glow for richer interactions.
</Callout>

## Use cases

`PressButton` uses `usePress` which binds `whileTap: { scale: pressScale }` (default `0.95`) with a `duration: 0.1` `easeInOut` transition. This is a click-feedback animation only; no hover state is involved. Reach for it when:

- **Form submit buttons.** A 5% scale-down on press gives the user instant confirmation that the button registered the click before the async action starts.
- **Icon action buttons.** Compact round or square icon buttons (bookmark, like, share) benefit from the press scale because their small size otherwise provides little tactile feedback.
- **Payment and checkout CTAs.** A clear, snappy press response reduces anxiety about whether the button was actually activated.
- **Keyboard-triggered actions.** Because `whileTap` also fires on `Enter` and `Space` for a `motion.button`, keyboard users get the same visual feedback as mouse users.
- **Mobile-first touch buttons.** On touch devices, `whileTap` fires on `touchstart`/`touchend`, so the scale-down reads as a native tap affordance.

The 0.1-second duration is intentionally short; anything longer than 0.15 seconds makes the press feel laggy relative to the user's action.

## When to use / when not to use

**Use `PressButton` when:**

- The button's only interactive state is its clicked/tapped state and you don't need hover decoration.
- You want a universal click affordance that works on both mouse and touch without special handling.
- The button will be used frequently (form saves, increment/decrement counters, media controls) and a persistent hover effect would be distracting.

**Reach for a different button when:**

- You need hover feedback in addition to click feedback. `PressButton` has no `whileHover` behavior. Combine it with [Lift Button](/docs/animations/buttons/lift) by passing `whileHover={{ y: -6 }}` via props, or pair with [Glow Button](/docs/animations/buttons/glow) for color-matched hover.
- The button should feel physically elevated before the press (like a physical key). Use [Lift Button](/docs/animations/buttons/lift) for the resting state with a `whileTap={{ y: 0, scale: 0.97 }}` override.
- The click should produce a spatial ripple originating from the cursor position. Use [Ripple Button](/docs/animations/buttons/ripple) instead, which spawns an expanding circle at the exact click coordinate.
- The `scale` shrinks text in a way that is distracting. Reduce `scale` to 0.98 or use `scale={1}` with a different feedback signal.

## Accessibility notes

`PressButton` renders a `motion.button`, so it is focusable, activatable with `Enter` and `Space`, and exposed to the accessibility tree as a button.

- **`whileTap` fires on keyboard activation.** This is Motion's behavior for `motion.button`; pressing `Enter` or `Space` while the button is focused triggers the scale animation identically to a mouse click. This is the correct accessible behavior.
- **Scale-down does not hide content.** A 5% scale-down at `scale={0.95}` is imperceptible to most users and does not cause text to become unreadable or clipping against the container boundary.
- **Don't use `scale` as the sole indication of an active/pressed state.** For a toggle button (`aria-pressed`), supplement the animation with a color change or label swap; the scale alone is not perceivable for screen reader users.
- **Reduced motion.** The press animation is 0.1 seconds. Under `prefers-reduced-motion`, even this short animation can feel unexpected to some users. To disable it:

```tsx
"use client"
import { useReducedMotion } from "motion/react"
import { PressButton } from "@/components/animations/buttons/press"

function AccessiblePress({ children, onClick }: { children: React.ReactNode; onClick: () => void }) {
  const reduced = useReducedMotion()
  // scale=1 means whileTap animates to scale:1, effectively no visible change.
  return (
    <PressButton
      scale={reduced ? 1 : 0.95}
      onClick={onClick}
      className="inline-flex h-11 items-center rounded-lg bg-blue-600 px-6 text-sm font-semibold text-white focus-visible:ring-2 focus-visible:ring-blue-400"
    >
      {children}
    </PressButton>
  )
}
```

## Performance considerations

- **`scale` is a compositor transform.** `whileTap` animates only `scale`, which runs on the compositor thread with no layout recalculation or repaint.
- **No ongoing animation.** The animation fires on pointer down and reverses on pointer up. Between interactions there are zero active animation frames. This makes `PressButton` the lightest of the animated button components in this library in terms of ongoing cost.
- **No re-renders during animation.** `whileTap` is handled entirely by Motion's internal reconciler; it does not call `setState` or trigger React renders during the press.
- **Rendering many `PressButton` instances is safe.** A list of 50 interactive items, each with `PressButton`, is fine because each instance only activates during an active tap and is otherwise inert.
- **Short `duration`.** The 0.1-second transition is short enough that even on low-powered devices the animation completes before the user perceives any lag.

### Very subtle press for a text link button

## Real-world examples

### Form submit with loading guard

The press animation runs even while the async action is in flight; `disabled` prevents duplicate submissions:

```tsx
"use client"
import { useState } from "react"
import { PressButton } from "@/components/animations/buttons/press"

export function SubmitButton({ onSubmit }: { onSubmit: () => Promise<void> }) {
  const [loading, setLoading] = useState(false)

  async function handleClick() {
    setLoading(true)
    try {
      await onSubmit()
    } finally {
      setLoading(false)
    }
  }

  return (
    <PressButton
      scale={0.95}
      onClick={handleClick}
      disabled={loading}
      className="inline-flex h-11 items-center rounded-lg bg-blue-600 px-6 text-sm font-semibold text-white disabled:opacity-60 focus-visible:ring-2 focus-visible:ring-blue-400"
    >
      {loading ? "Saving..." : "Save changes"}
    </PressButton>
  )
}
```

### Like button with toggle state

The press animation fires on every click; `aria-pressed` communicates state to screen readers:

```tsx
"use client"
import { useState } from "react"
import { PressButton } from "@/components/animations/buttons/press"

export function LikeButton({ initialCount }: { initialCount: number }) {
  const [liked, setLiked] = useState(false)
  const [count, setCount] = useState(initialCount)

  function toggle() {
    setLiked((v) => !v)
    setCount((v) => (liked ? v - 1 : v + 1))
  }

  return (
    <PressButton
      scale={0.9}
      onClick={toggle}
      aria-pressed={liked}
      aria-label={`Like. ${count} likes.`}
      className={`inline-flex h-9 items-center gap-2 rounded-full px-4 text-sm font-semibold transition-colors ${
        liked
          ? "bg-red-50 text-red-600 dark:bg-red-900/20"
          : "bg-neutral-100 text-neutral-700 dark:bg-neutral-800 dark:text-neutral-300"
      }`}
    >
      <span aria-hidden>{liked ? "♥" : "♡"}</span>
      {count}
    </PressButton>
  )
}
```

# ripple.mdx

Source: https://github.com/garvit1000/animbits/blob/main/content/docs/animations/buttons/ripple.mdx

title: Ripple Button
description: Button with Material Design-style ripple effect that expands from click position.

import { Callout } from 'fumadocs-ui/components/callout';
import { Preview, PreviewGrid } from '@/components/preview';
import { RippleButton } from '@/registry/new-york/animations/buttons/ripple';

## Overview

The `RippleButton` creates a Material Design-inspired ripple effect that expands from where you click. Perfect for providing visual feedback on user interactions.

## Preview

  background="grid"
  code={`import { RippleButton } from "@/components/animations/buttons/ripple"

<RippleButton className="inline-flex h-11 items-center gap-2 rounded-lg bg-blue-600 px-6 text-sm font-semibold text-white">
  Click Me
</RippleButton>`}
  <RippleButton className="inline-flex h-11 items-center gap-2 rounded-lg bg-blue-600 px-6 text-sm font-semibold text-white">
    Click Me
  </RippleButton>

## Installation

        ```bash
        npx shadcn@latest add @animbits/buttons-ripple
        ```
        ```bash
        pnpm dlx shadcn@latest add @animbits/buttons-ripple
        ```
        ```bash
        yarn dlx shadcn@latest add @animbits/buttons-ripple
        ```
        ```bash
        bunx shadcn@latest add @animbits/buttons-ripple
        ```
    **Step 1: Add the utility**

    ```tsx title="lib/utils.ts"
    import { clsx, type ClassValue } from "clsx"
    import { twMerge } from "tailwind-merge"

    export function cn(...inputs: ClassValue[]) {
      return twMerge(clsx(inputs))
    }
    ```

    **Step 2: Copy the component**

    ```tsx title="components/animations/buttons/ripple.tsx"
"use client";
import * as React from "react";
import { motion, HTMLMotionProps } from "motion/react";
import { cn } from "@/lib/utils";
interface RippleButtonProps extends Omit<HTMLMotionProps<"button">, "onClick"> {
  children: React.ReactNode;
  rippleColor?: string;
  duration?: number;
  onClick?: (e: React.MouseEvent<HTMLButtonElement>) => void;
}
interface Ripple {
  x: number;
  y: number;
  id: number;
}
export function RippleButton({
  children,
  className,
  rippleColor = "rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.6)",
  duration = 0.6,
  onClick,
  ...props
}: RippleButtonProps) {
  const [ripples, setRipples] = React.useState<Ripple[]>([]);
  const buttonRef = React.useRef<HTMLButtonElement>(null);
  const handleClick = (e: React.MouseEvent<HTMLButtonElement>) => {
    const button = buttonRef.current;
    if (!button) return;
    const rect = button.getBoundingClientRect();
    const x = e.clientX - rect.left;
    const y = e.clientY - rect.top;
    const newRipple = {
      x,
      y,
      id: Date.now(),
    };
    setRipples((prev) => [...prev, newRipple]);
    setTimeout(() => {
      setRipples((prev) => prev.filter((r) => r.id !== newRipple.id));
    }, duration * 1000);
    onClick?.(e);
  };
  return (
    <motion.button
      ref={buttonRef}
      className={cn("relative overflow-hidden", className)}
      onClick={handleClick}
      {...props}
    >
      {children}
      {ripples.map((ripple) => (
        <motion.span
          key={ripple.id}
          className="absolute rounded-full pointer-events-none"
          style={{
            left: ripple.x,
            top: ripple.y,
            backgroundColor: rippleColor,
          }}
          initial={{ width: 0, height: 0, opacity: 1 }}
          animate={{
            width: 500,
            height: 500,
            opacity: 0,
            x: -250,
            y: -250,
          }}
          transition={{ duration, ease: "easeOut" }}
        />
      ))}
    </motion.button>
  );
}

```

## Usage

### Basic Example

```tsx
import { RippleButton } from "@/components/animations/buttons/ripple"

<RippleButton className="inline-flex h-11 items-center gap-2 rounded-lg bg-blue-600 px-6 text-sm font-semibold text-white">
  Click Me
</RippleButton>
```

```tsx
>
  Dark Button
</RippleButton>

<RippleButton 
  rippleColor="rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.2)"
  className="inline-flex h-11 items-center gap-2 rounded-lg bg-white px-6 text-sm font-semibold text-gray-900 border border-neutral-200"
>
  Light Button
</RippleButton>
```

### Custom Duration

```tsx
// Fast ripple
<RippleButton 
  duration={0.4}
  className="inline-flex h-11 items-center gap-2 rounded-lg bg-blue-600 px-6 text-sm font-semibold text-white"
>
  Fast
</RippleButton>

// Slow ripple
<RippleButton 
  duration={1}
  className="inline-flex h-11 items-center gap-2 rounded-lg bg-blue-600 px-6 text-sm font-semibold text-white"
>
  Slow
</RippleButton>
```

## Props

| `rippleColor` | `string` | `"rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.6)"` | Ripple color (RGBA recommended) |
| `duration` | `number` | `0.6` | Ripple animation duration in seconds |
| `onClick` | `function` | - | Click handler |
| `children` | `React.ReactNode` | Required | Button content |

<Callout>
  **Note:** Requires `overflow-hidden` on the button for the ripple to be clipped properly.
</Callout>

## Use cases

`RippleButton` spawns a `motion.span` at the exact `clientX / clientY` position relative to the button's bounding rect on each click. The span expands from `width: 0, height: 0` to `width: 500, height: 500` while translating by `x: -250, y: -250` to stay centered on the origin point, and fades from `opacity: 1` to `opacity: 0`. The default `duration` is 0.6 seconds with `easeOut`, and the default `rippleColor` is `rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.6)`. Each ripple is removed from state after `duration * 1000` milliseconds. Reach for it when:

- **Material Design-aligned interfaces.** The ripple is the canonical Material 2 and Material 3 button feedback. If your app follows that design language, `RippleButton` delivers the expected behavior.
- **Dark-background buttons.** White ripples (`rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.6)`) are most visible on colored or dark fills (`bg-blue-600`, `bg-neutral-900`).
- **Touch-first mobile layouts.** Ripples provide spatial feedback that tells the user exactly where their finger landed, which matters when buttons are close together.
- **Media player controls.** Play, pause, skip buttons in a dark player UI use ripples to confirm taps without hover states.
- **Long lists of action buttons.** Each row's delete or archive button benefits from a per-click ripple because it confirms which row was targeted.

Because the component automatically applies `relative overflow-hidden` to the button, you don't need to manage the clip container yourself.

## When to use / when not to use

**Use `RippleButton` when:**

- The button has a solid background that contrasts with the `rippleColor`. A white ripple on a white button is invisible; match `rippleColor` to contrast with the fill.
- Click-position feedback matters: you want to show users exactly where their tap registered.

**Reach for a different button when:**

- You want hover feedback rather than click feedback. `RippleButton` has no hover state; use [Glow Button](/docs/animations/buttons/glow) or [Lift Button](/docs/animations/buttons/lift) if hover interactivity is the goal.
- You want a uniform scale-down on press rather than a spatial ripple. [Press Button](/docs/animations/buttons/press) is simpler and has no DOM mutation on click.
- The button has `border-radius: 50%` or a very small size. A `width: 500, height: 500` circle expanding from a 32px icon button may leak outside the clipping region if `overflow-hidden` is removed. The component forces `overflow-hidden`, so small buttons will clip the ripple heavily. Test visually to confirm the result is acceptable.
- Rapid repeated clicking is expected (counters, game buttons). Each click pushes a new ripple into the `ripples` state array. Many rapid clicks accumulate multiple ripple spans simultaneously; this is usually acceptable but worth verifying under load.

## Accessibility notes

`RippleButton` wraps a `motion.button`, so it carries full native button semantics.

- **The ripple is decorative.** The `motion.span` elements are `pointer-events-none` and have no text, no role, and no accessible name. Screen readers ignore them entirely.
- **Click handler forwarding.** `RippleButton` intercepts the native `onClick` to spawn the ripple, then calls the original `onClick?.(e)` prop. Your click handler receives the same event as if no ripple wrapper were present.
- **Keyboard activation.** `whileTap` is not used here; the ripple is spawned in the `handleClick` handler. When a user presses `Enter` or `Space` on the focused button, `handleClick` fires and a ripple appears centered on the button (`e.clientX` and `e.clientY` reflect the button's center for keyboard events in most browsers). This may result in a centered ripple rather than a cursor-positioned one, which is the correct fallback.
- **Reduced motion.** The ripple expands over 0.6 seconds and fades out, which is motion-intensive relative to a simple press scale. To skip the ripple for users who prefer less motion:

```tsx
"use client"
import { useReducedMotion } from "motion/react"
import { RippleButton } from "@/components/animations/buttons/ripple"
import { PressButton } from "@/components/animations/buttons/press"

function AccessibleActionButton({ children, onClick }: { children: React.ReactNode; onClick: () => void }) {
  const reduced = useReducedMotion()
  // Fall back to a simple press animation when reduced motion is requested.
  if (reduced) {
    return (
      <PressButton
        scale={0.97}
        onClick={onClick}
        className="inline-flex h-11 items-center rounded-lg bg-blue-600 px-6 text-sm font-semibold text-white"
      >
        {children}
      </PressButton>
    )
  }
  return (
    <RippleButton
      onClick={onClick}
      className="inline-flex h-11 items-center rounded-lg bg-blue-600 px-6 text-sm font-semibold text-white"
    >
      {children}
    </RippleButton>
  )
}
```

## Performance considerations

- **Ripple geometry uses `width`/`height` animation.** Expanding from `0` to `500` pixels by animating `width` and `height` triggers layout recalculation and repaint on each frame. This is not compositor-safe. For one or two buttons in a typical UI, the cost is negligible, but avoid using `RippleButton` in virtualized lists with thousands of rows where many ripples could fire simultaneously.
- **The `opacity` and `x/y` changes are compositor-safe.** Motion batches these with the dimension changes, but the layout cost of `width`/`height` dominates.
- **State mutation on click.** Each click calls `setRipples(prev => [...prev, newRipple])`, which triggers a React re-render of the `RippleButton`. The re-render is fast (the component is small), but in a list of 100 buttons, a rapid series of clicks will produce a series of state updates. This is usually imperceptible.
- **Cleanup via `setTimeout`.** Ripples are removed from state after `duration * 1000` ms using a `setTimeout`. Unmounting `RippleButton` while a ripple is animating will cause a state-update-on-unmounted-component warning in development. Wrap with a stable parent or cancel pending timeouts in a `useEffect` cleanup if strict mode warnings are a concern.
- **`overflow-hidden` is required.** The component enforces `relative overflow-hidden` via class concatenation. Do not override this with `overflow-visible` unless you want ripples to escape the button boundary.
