# shine.mdx

Source: https://github.com/garvit1000/animbits/blob/main/content/docs/animations/buttons/shine.mdx

title: Shine Button
description: Button with shine sweep effect that travels across on hover.

import { Preview, PreviewGrid } from '@/components/preview';
import { ShineButton } from '@/registry/new-york/animations/buttons/shine';

## Overview

The `ShineButton` creates a shine/shimmer effect that sweeps across the button on hover, adding a premium, polished feel.

## Preview

  background="default"
  code={`import { ShineButton } from "@/components/animations/buttons/shine"

<ShineButton className="inline-flex h-11 items-center gap-2 rounded-lg bg-blue-600 px-6 text-sm font-semibold text-white">
  Hover Me
</ShineButton>`}
  <ShineButton className="inline-flex h-11 items-center gap-2 rounded-lg bg-blue-600 px-6 text-sm font-semibold text-white">
    Hover Me
  </ShineButton>

## Installation

        ```bash
        npx shadcn@latest add @animbits/buttons-shine
        ```
        ```bash
        pnpm dlx shadcn@latest add @animbits/buttons-shine
        ```
        ```bash
        yarn dlx shadcn@latest add @animbits/buttons-shine
        ```
        ```bash
        bunx shadcn@latest add @animbits/buttons-shine
        ```
    **Step 1: Add the utility**

    ```tsx title="lib/utils.ts"
    import { clsx, type ClassValue } from "clsx"
    import { twMerge } from "tailwind-merge"

    export function cn(...inputs: ClassValue[]) {
      return twMerge(clsx(inputs))
    }
    ```

    **Step 2: Copy the component**

    ```tsx title="components/animations/buttons/shine.tsx"
"use client";
import { motion, type HTMLMotionProps } from "motion/react";
interface ShineButtonProps extends Omit<HTMLMotionProps<"button">, "animate"> {
  children: React.ReactNode;
  direction?: "left" | "right";
}
export function ShineButton({
  children,
  direction = "right",
  className,
  ...props
}: ShineButtonProps) {
  return (
    <motion.button
      className={`relative overflow-hidden ${className || ""}`}
      whileHover="hover"
      initial="initial"
      {...props}
    >
      {children}
      <motion.div
        className="absolute inset-0 w-full h-full pointer-events-none"
        style={{
          background:
            "linear-gradient(90deg, transparent, rgba(255,255,255,0.3), transparent)",
        }}
        variants={{
          initial: {
            x: direction === "right" ? "-100%" : "100%",
          },
          hover: {
            x: direction === "right" ? "100%" : "-100%",
          },
        }}
        transition={{ duration: 0.6, ease: "easeInOut" }}
      />
    </motion.button>
  );
}

```

## Usage

```tsx
import { ShineButton } from "@/components/animations/buttons/shine"

<ShineButton className="inline-flex h-11 items-center gap-2 rounded-lg bg-blue-600 px-6 text-sm font-semibold text-white">
  Hover Me
</ShineButton>
```

## Props

| `direction` | `"left" \| "right"` | `"right"` | Shine sweep direction |
| `children` | `React.ReactNode` | Required | Button content |

## Examples

```tsx
// Premium CTA
<ShineButton className="inline-flex h-11 items-center gap-2 rounded-lg bg-gradient-to-r from-purple-600 to-pink-600 px-6 text-sm font-semibold text-white">
  Upgrade Now
</ShineButton>

// Dark button
<ShineButton className="inline-flex h-11 items-center gap-2 rounded-lg bg-gray-900 px-6 text-sm font-semibold text-white">
  Dark Shine
</ShineButton>
```

## Use cases

`ShineButton` positions a `motion.div` overlay with the CSS background `linear-gradient(90deg, transparent, rgba(255,255,255,0.3), transparent)`. On mount, `initial="initial"` places the overlay at `x: "-100%"` (for `direction="right"`). When the parent's `whileHover="hover"` fires, the overlay translates to `x: "100%"` over 0.6 seconds with `easeInOut`. The shine sweeps the full button width from left to right (or right to left for `direction="left"`). Reach for it when:

- **Premium upgrade and upsell CTAs.** A "Upgrade to Pro" button on a gradient fill feels more crafted with a shine sweep than a plain color-shift on hover.
- **Product launch announcement buttons.** A "What's new" or "See release notes" button with a shine sweep signals novelty.
- **Dark-themed dashboards.** Buttons on dark backgrounds (`bg-neutral-900`, `bg-zinc-800`) show the white shine gradient most clearly.
- **One-per-section primary actions.** The shine is eye-catching; a single shining CTA per visible section draws attention without competing with other elements.

Because the overlay is `absolute inset-0 pointer-events-none`, it does not intercept clicks or affect the button's layout.

## When to use / when not to use

**Use `ShineButton` when:**

- The button has a dark or saturated fill where a white-ish gradient overlay is clearly visible.
- You want hover feedback that feels luxurious rather than mechanical.
- The button's context benefits from implying light/sheen (e-commerce "Add to cart", SaaS "Start trial").

**Reach for a different button when:**

- The button is on a light background. A `rgba(255,255,255,0.3)` shine on a white button is imperceptible. Use [Lift Button](/docs/animations/buttons/lift) or [Glow Button](/docs/animations/buttons/glow) for light surfaces.
- You need click feedback rather than hover feedback. The shine only activates on `whileHover` and has no `whileTap` behavior. Combine with [Press Button](/docs/animations/buttons/press) by passing `whileTap={{ scale: 0.97 }}` as a prop if tap confirmation is also needed.
- The button's text content includes light-colored icons or labels that would disappear under the passing shine for a moment. Check that your label remains readable during the 0.6-second sweep.
- You want to animate a border rather than the button surface itself. Use [Border Gradient Button](/docs/animations/buttons/border-gradient) for an animated perimeter effect instead.

## Accessibility notes

`ShineButton` renders a `motion.button` that contains the shine overlay as an `absolute`-positioned `motion.div`. The overlay is `pointer-events-none` and holds no content.

- **The shine div is invisible to screen readers.** It has no role, no text, and no accessible name. Assistive technology sees only the button and its children.
- **Keyboard hover.** Motion's `whileHover` fires on `focus` in some versions of Motion when the element is focused via keyboard. Test whether the shine triggers on tab focus in your Motion version. If it does, this is acceptable; if it causes distraction, wrap in a `useState` to only enable `whileHover` on mouse hover.
- **Focus ring visibility.** The button enforces `overflow-hidden` via class concatenation. Ensure your CSS focus ring uses `outline` (which draws outside the border-box and is not clipped by `overflow-hidden`) rather than `box-shadow` (which is clipped).
- **Reduced motion.** The 0.6-second sweep is directional motion that can be distracting. To disable the shine for users who prefer reduced motion:

```tsx
"use client"
import { useReducedMotion } from "motion/react"
import { ShineButton } from "@/components/animations/buttons/shine"

function AccessibleShine({ children }: { children: React.ReactNode }) {
  const reduced = useReducedMotion()
  // Render a plain motion.button with no shine overlay by passing a static class.
  // We set whileHover to an empty object to suppress the shine animation
  // by overriding the parent's whileHover="hover" variant trigger.
  return (
    <ShineButton
      direction={reduced ? undefined : "right"}
      style={reduced ? { pointerEvents: "auto" } : undefined}
      className="inline-flex h-11 items-center rounded-lg bg-blue-600 px-6 text-sm font-semibold text-white focus-visible:ring-2 focus-visible:ring-blue-400 focus-visible:ring-offset-2"
    >
      {children}
    </ShineButton>
  )
}
```

## Performance considerations

- **`translateX` animation is compositor-safe.** The shine overlay moves via `x` (a transform), so the transition runs on the compositor thread with no layout recalculation. This is the most efficient part of the component.
- **The overlay is `absolute` and `pointer-events-none`.** It does not participate in layout and does not cause repaints of sibling elements.
- **No ongoing animation.** The shine fires once on hover enter and stops at `x: "100%"`. It resets to `x: "-100%"` only when `whileHover` ends. Between hovers there are no animation frames scheduled.
- **`overflow-hidden` forces a new stacking context.** The clipping boundary is created by the `overflow-hidden` class on the button. This is a single composited layer and does not cause an excessive number of layers.
- **Avoid rendering many `ShineButton` components simultaneously.** If many buttons are hovered at once (e.g., in a card grid where the grid itself triggers hover on all children), multiple gradient overlays will sweep at the same time. This is visually noisy and wastes compositor resources; use one `ShineButton` per card at most.

# slide-in.mdx

Source: https://github.com/garvit1000/animbits/blob/main/content/docs/animations/buttons/slide-in.mdx

title: Slide In Button
description: Button with slide-in entrance animation from any direction.

import { Preview, PreviewGrid } from '@/components/preview';
import { SlideInButton } from '@/registry/new-york/animations/buttons/slide-in';

## Overview

The `SlideInButton` creates a slide-in entrance animation from any direction (left, right, up, down), perfect for sequential reveals.

## Preview

  background="grid"
  code={`import { SlideInButton } from "@/components/animations/buttons/slide-in"

<SlideInButton direction="left" className="inline-flex h-11 items-center gap-2 rounded-lg bg-blue-600 px-6 text-sm font-semibold text-white">
  Hover Me
</SlideInButton>`}
  <SlideInButton direction="left" className="inline-flex h-11 items-center gap-2 rounded-lg bg-blue-600 px-6 text-sm font-semibold text-white">
    Hover Me
  </SlideInButton>

## Installation

        ```bash
        npx shadcn@latest add @animbits/buttons-slide-in
        ```
        ```bash
        pnpm dlx shadcn@latest add @animbits/buttons-slide-in
        ```
        ```bash
        yarn dlx shadcn@latest add @animbits/buttons-slide-in
        ```
        ```bash
        bunx shadcn@latest add @animbits/buttons-slide-in
        ```
    ```tsx title="components/animations/buttons/slide-in.tsx"
"use client";
import { motion, type HTMLMotionProps } from "motion/react";
import {
  slideInVariants,
  createDelayedTransition,
} from "@/lib/animation-presets";
interface SlideInButtonProps
  extends Omit<HTMLMotionProps<"button">, "animate"> {
  children: React.ReactNode;
  delay?: number;
  duration?: number;
  direction?: "left" | "right" | "up" | "down";
}
export function SlideInButton({
  children,
  delay = 0,
  duration = 0.3,
  direction = "left",
  ...props
}: SlideInButtonProps) {
  const customVariants = {
    hidden: {
      opacity: 0,
      x: direction === "left" ? -20 : direction === "right" ? 20 : 0,
      y: direction === "up" ? -20 : direction === "down" ? 20 : 0,
    },
    visible: {
      opacity: 1,
      x: 0,
      y: 0,
    },
  };
  return (
    <motion.button
      variants={customVariants}
      initial="hidden"
      animate="visible"
      transition={createDelayedTransition(delay, duration)}
      {...props}
    >
      {children}
    </motion.button>
  );
}

```

## Usage

```tsx
import { SlideInButton } from "@/components/animations/buttons/slide-in"

<SlideInButton 
  direction="left"
  className="inline-flex h-11 items-center gap-2 rounded-lg bg-blue-600 px-6 text-sm font-semibold text-white"
>
  Slides In
</SlideInButton>
```

### Staggered

```tsx

  <SlideInButton direction="left" delay={0.1}>Second</SlideInButton>
  <SlideInButton direction="left" delay={0.2}>Third</SlideInButton>
</div>
```

## Props

| `direction` | `"left" \| "right" \| "up" \| "down"` | `"left"` | Slide direction |
| `delay` | `number` | `0` | Delay before animation (seconds) |
| `duration` | `number` | `0.3` | Animation duration (seconds) |
| `children` | `React.ReactNode` | Required | Button content |

## Use cases

`SlideInButton` builds a custom variant pair where `hidden` sets `opacity: 0` plus a 20-pixel offset in the chosen direction (`x: -20` for `left`, `x: 20` for `right`, `y: -20` for `up`, `y: 20` for `down`) and `visible` resets both to `opacity: 1, x: 0, y: 0`. The animation fires on mount via `initial="hidden"` and `animate="visible"`, using `createDelayedTransition(delay, duration)` which produces an `easeOut` transition. Reach for it when:

- **Sequenced toolbar reveals.** A row of action buttons that slide in from the left with `delay={0}`, `delay={0.1}`, `delay={0.2}` communicates that the toolbar has just become available.
- **Dialog and sheet footer buttons.** Confirmation and cancel buttons that slide up from the bottom (`direction="down"`) reinforce the vertical nature of a bottom sheet entering from below.
- **Page-level CTA sections.** A hero or section CTA that slides in from the left on mount provides a sense of arrival distinct from a plain [Fade In Button](/docs/animations/buttons/fade-in).
- **Notification action buttons.** "Undo" or "Dismiss" buttons that appear after an action can slide in from the right to draw attention without a dramatic pop.
- **Sidebar navigation items.** Navigation buttons that appear after a sidebar opens can stagger in from the left to reinforce the left-to-right reading direction.

The 20-pixel offset is small enough not to disturb the layout visually, but large enough to communicate direction clearly.

## When to use / when not to use

**Use `SlideInButton` when:**

- You want a mount-time entrance animation that includes both opacity and directional movement.
- The `direction` aligns with the conceptual origin of the content: a bottom sheet's actions should use `direction="down"`, left-rail navigation should use `direction="left"`.
- You're staggering multiple buttons with different `delay` values to create a sequence.

**Reach for a different button when:**

- You only need a fade without directional motion. [Fade In Button](/docs/animations/buttons/fade-in) animates only `opacity`, which is lighter and less distracting in dense layouts.
- You need a hover or click interaction. `SlideInButton` has no `whileHover` or `whileTap` state; it is entrance-only. Combine with [Press Button](/docs/animations/buttons/press) via `whileTap={{ scale: 0.96 }}` passed as a prop, or use a completely different button for interactive states.
- The button re-mounts frequently (conditionally shown/hidden). Every unmount and remount replays the slide-in from the beginning. If toggling visibility is the pattern, keep the component mounted and use `animate` to toggle between `hidden` and `visible` externally, or prefer [Fade In Button](/docs/animations/buttons/fade-in) whose opacity-only animation is less disruptive on repeated toggling.
- The slide direction conflicts with your layout's reading direction (e.g., a right-to-left locale where `direction="left"` feels backward). Pass `direction="right"` when entering from the leading edge in RTL layouts.

## Accessibility notes

`SlideInButton` renders a `motion.button`, so it participates in the normal tab order and is keyboard-accessible.

- **Content is in the DOM immediately.** Screen readers see the button as soon as it mounts, even while `opacity` is 0 and the element is offset by 20px. There is no visibility delay for assistive technology.
- **The `x`/`y` offset is a `transform`, not a position change.** The button's layout box stays in its normal document position throughout the animation. Nothing shifts or reflows.
- **Focus during animation.** If the user tabs to the button while it is mid-animation, it receives focus and activates normally. The transform and opacity do not affect interactivity.
- **Reduced motion.** The directional slide adds spatial motion on top of the opacity fade. Users with vestibular sensitivities may find it uncomfortable. Collapse the animation to a plain fade or skip it entirely:

```tsx
"use client"
import { useReducedMotion } from "motion/react"
import { SlideInButton } from "@/components/animations/buttons/slide-in"
import { FadeInButton } from "@/components/animations/buttons/fade-in"

function AccessibleSlideIn({ children }: { children: React.ReactNode }) {
  const reduced = useReducedMotion()
  // Use the simpler opacity-only FadeInButton when motion is reduced.
  if (reduced) {
    return (
      <FadeInButton
        duration={0.3}
        className="inline-flex h-11 items-center rounded-lg bg-blue-600 px-6 text-sm font-semibold text-white"
      >
        {children}
      </FadeInButton>
    )
  }
  return (
    <SlideInButton
      direction="left"
      duration={0.3}
      className="inline-flex h-11 items-center rounded-lg bg-blue-600 px-6 text-sm font-semibold text-white"
    >
      {children}
    </SlideInButton>
  )
}
```

## Performance considerations

- **Both `opacity` and `x`/`y` are compositor-safe.** Motion maps `x` and `y` to `transform: translateX/Y(...)`. Opacity is also handled by the compositor. Neither triggers layout recalculation or paint during the transition.
- **Single-fire animation.** Like [Fade In Button](/docs/animations/buttons/fade-in), the animation plays once on mount. After it completes, no animation frames are scheduled and the element rests at `opacity: 1, transform: none`.
- **`createDelayedTransition` uses a CSS animation delay.** The `delay` prop is passed to Motion's transition config, not a `setTimeout`. There are no extra React renders during the delay period.
- **Staggering cost.** Rendering 10 `SlideInButton` instances with increasing `delay` values is safe; the total animation duration across all instances is `0 + (n-1) * delay + duration`. All animations run concurrently on the compositor and the stagger is encoded in the delay offsets, not in sequential scheduling.
- **Remount replays.** Because `animate="visible"` is always set, unmounting and remounting the component replays the animation from scratch. If you're conditionally showing a toolbar, avoid toggling its parent's mount/unmount at high frequency.

    **Step 1: Add the utility**

    ```tsx title="lib/utils.ts"
    import { clsx, type ClassValue } from "clsx"
    import { twMerge } from "tailwind-merge"

    export function cn(...inputs: ClassValue[]) {
      return twMerge(clsx(inputs))
    }
    ```

    **Step 2: Copy the component**

    ```tsx title="components/animations/cards/background-zoom.tsx"
"use client";
import * as React from "react";
import { motion, HTMLMotionProps } from "motion/react";
import { cn } from "@/lib/utils";
export interface CardBackgroundZoomProps
  extends Omit<HTMLMotionProps<"div">, "children"> {
  backgroundImage: string;
  children: React.ReactNode;
  scale?: number;
  duration?: number;
}
export function CardBackgroundZoom({
  backgroundImage,
  children,
  className,
  scale = 1.1,
  duration = 0.6,
  ...props
}: CardBackgroundZoomProps) {
  return (
    <motion.div
      className={cn("relative overflow-hidden", className)}
      whileHover="hover"
      initial="initial"
      {...props}
    >
      <motion.div
        className="absolute inset-0 bg-cover bg-center"
        style={{ backgroundImage: `url(${backgroundImage})` }}
        variants={{
          initial: { scale: 1 },
          hover: { scale },
        }}
        transition={{ duration, ease: "easeOut" }}
      />
      <div className="relative z-10">{children}</div>
    </motion.div>
  );
}

```

## Usage

```tsx
import { CardBackgroundZoom } from "@/components/animations/cards/background-zoom"

<CardBackgroundZoom backgroundImage="/image.jpg">
  <h3>Card Title</h3>
  <p>Content</p>
</CardBackgroundZoom>
```

## Props

| `backgroundImage` | `string` | Required | Background image URL |
| `scale` | `number` | `1.1` | Zoom scale factor |
| `duration` | `number` | `0.6` | Animation duration in seconds |
| `className` | `string` | `undefined` | Additional CSS classes |

## Use cases

`CardBackgroundZoom` is the right pick when the card itself IS a photograph and text lives on top of it. The outer `motion.div` stays perfectly still while an absolutely-positioned inner `div` carrying the `backgroundImage` scales from `1` to the `scale` value (default `1.1`) on hover. Because the outer container has `overflow-hidden`, the zoom is clipped and the layout never shifts.

Common scenarios:

- **Travel and destination cards.** A mountain photo zooms in subtly while a title overlay stays anchored, drawing the eye without moving surrounding content.
- **Blog article hero images.** Tease depth on a featured post without resizing the card container.
- **Portfolio case-study cards.** Zoom into a screenshot or render while the project title remains readable.
- **Real-estate listings.** Property photography benefits from the zoomed-in sense of detail on hover.
- **Editorial magazine layouts.** Sections that pair a full-bleed image with a short headline.

## When to use / when not to use

**Use `CardBackgroundZoom` when:**

- The image is the primary content of the card and text is overlaid (typically with a gradient scrim or semi-transparent backdrop).
- You want a contained, layout-stable hover feedback. The transform stays inside `overflow-hidden` so nothing jumps.

**Reach for a different component when:**

- The card contains structured text alongside the image (not overlaid). Use [CardHoverLift](/docs/animations/cards/hover-lift) for a whole-card lift effect instead.
- You need the card itself to physically move on hover. `CardBackgroundZoom` only zooms the background layer; the card's bounding box does not move.
- The zoom feels distracting in a dense grid. At `scale={1.05}` or below the effect becomes almost invisible; consider just using a CSS hover border instead.
- Accessibility is a strong priority and you cannot provide sufficient color contrast on the text overlay. A zooming image behind low-contrast text fails WCAG 1.4.3 at any scale.

## Accessibility notes

- **Text contrast over images.** The zoom does not change the overlay color or text position, but a photograph background never guarantees consistent contrast. Always add a gradient scrim or semi-transparent backdrop behind text:

```tsx
<CardBackgroundZoom
  backgroundImage="/landscape.jpg"
  className="relative h-64 rounded-xl flex items-end"
>
  <div className="absolute inset-0 bg-gradient-to-t from-black/70 to-transparent" />
  <div className="relative z-20 p-6">
    <h3 className="text-white text-xl font-bold">Destination Title</h3>
  </div>
</CardBackgroundZoom>
```

- **Respect `prefers-reduced-motion`.** The zoom is a `whileHover` transform; with reduced motion enabled, stop it from scaling at all:

```tsx
"use client"
import { useReducedMotion } from "motion/react"
import { CardBackgroundZoom } from "@/components/animations/cards/background-zoom"

function AccessibleHeroCard() {
  const reduced = useReducedMotion()
  return (
    <CardBackgroundZoom
      backgroundImage="/landscape.jpg"
      scale={reduced ? 1 : 1.1}
      className="h-64 rounded-xl flex items-end p-6"
    >
      <h3 className="text-white text-xl font-bold">Featured Story</h3>
    </CardBackgroundZoom>
  )
}
```

- **Decorative images.** If the background image is purely decorative and the card's meaning is in the text overlay, no `alt` text is needed because the image is a CSS `backgroundImage`, not an `<img>` element. Ensure the text content is sufficient on its own.
- **Keyboard users.** The component responds to `whileHover` which does not fire on keyboard focus. If the card is a link or button, add a matching `:focus-visible` ring so keyboard users can identify it.

## Performance considerations

- **Compositor-only transform.** The inner background `div` animates only `scale`, which is a transform. No layout, no paint. The animation runs on the GPU compositor and does not block the main thread.
- **`overflow-hidden` clips without triggering layout.** The outer container uses `overflow: hidden` to clip the scaled background. This does trigger a stacking context but not a layout recalculation on each frame.
- **Large, unoptimized images dominate cost.** The `backgroundImage` prop accepts any URL. Serving a 4 MB full-resolution photo kills perceived performance regardless of how cheap the animation is. Use a CDN that resizes and serves WebP at the card's rendered dimensions (e.g., `?w=600&h=400&fit=crop`).
- **Avoid stacking many zooming cards above the fold.** Each card creates a composited layer. Ten cards on the initial viewport means ten GPU layers. Keep the number reasonable or use `content-visibility: auto` on off-screen rows.

    ```tsx title="components/animations/cards/fade-in.tsx"
import { motion, HTMLMotionProps } from "motion/react";
import { cn } from "@/lib/utils";
export interface CardFadeInProps extends HTMLMotionProps<"div"> {
  duration?: number;
  delay?: number;
}
export function CardFadeIn({
  children,
  className,
  duration = 0.5,
  delay = 0,
  ...props
}: CardFadeInProps) {
  return (
    <motion.div
      initial={{ opacity: 0 }}
      animate={{ opacity: 1 }}
      transition={{ duration, delay }}
      className={cn(className)}
      {...props}
    >
      {children}
    </motion.div>
  );
}

```

## Usage

```tsx
import { CardFadeIn } from "@/components/animations/cards/fade-in"

<CardFadeIn className="p-6 bg-white rounded-lg border">
  <h3>Card Title</h3>
  <p>Card content</p>
</CardFadeIn>
```

## Props

| `duration` | `number` | `0.5` | Animation duration in seconds |
| `delay` | `number` | `0` | Delay before animation starts |
| `className` | `string` | `undefined` | Additional CSS classes |

## Use cases

`CardFadeIn` runs a one-shot entrance animation: `opacity` goes from `0` to `1` over `duration` seconds (default `0.5`), optionally after a `delay`. The animation fires when the component mounts, not when it scrolls into view. That distinction matters for placement decisions.

Reach for it when:

- **Cards rendered on page load.** Team member grids, pricing tiers, or dashboard widgets that are already in the DOM when the user first arrives benefit from a staggered fade-in that eases the visual load.
- **Route transitions.** Fade in a card-based content panel after navigation so the new content appears smoothly without position shifts.
- **Modal or drawer content.** Items inside a panel that opens can fade in right after the panel itself opens, thanks to the `delay` prop.
- **Skeleton-to-content handoff.** Replace a skeleton placeholder with a `CardFadeIn`-wrapped card so the swap dissolves in rather than snapping.

## When to use / when not to use

**Use `CardFadeIn` when:**

- The card is present in the DOM at render time and you want a simple entrance that does not depend on scroll position.
- You are staggering multiple cards with incremental `delay` values (e.g., `0`, `0.1`, `0.2`) to create a cascade effect.

**Reach for a different component when:**

- You need the animation to trigger when the card scrolls into view. `CardFadeIn` uses `animate`, not `whileInView`, so it fires immediately on mount regardless of viewport. Use [CardSlideIn](/docs/animations/cards/slide-in) or [CardScaleIn](/docs/animations/cards/scale-in) instead; both use `whileInView` via their underlying hooks.
- You want hover feedback. `CardFadeIn` only controls the mount transition. Combine it with [CardHoverLift](/docs/animations/cards/hover-lift) or [CardHoverGlow](/docs/animations/cards/hover-glow) if you need both entrance and interaction states.
- The card contains time-sensitive content where a 0.5-second delay before content appears could frustrate users, such as a real-time alert feed.

## Accessibility notes

- **Content is invisible until the animation completes.** Screen readers announce content as soon as the DOM is populated, regardless of opacity. This is the correct behavior: do not gate screen-reader access behind animation state.
- **Respect `prefers-reduced-motion`.** A fade from `opacity: 0` is generally mild, but even subtle fades can feel disorienting to some users. Honor the OS setting by skipping the fade:

```tsx
"use client"
import { useReducedMotion } from "motion/react"
import { CardFadeIn } from "@/components/animations/cards/fade-in"

function AccessibleCard({ children }: { children: React.ReactNode }) {
  const reduced = useReducedMotion()
  // Skip the fade entirely by setting duration to 0 when reduced motion is preferred.
  return (
    <CardFadeIn duration={reduced ? 0 : 0.5} className="rounded-xl border border-neutral-200 dark:border-neutral-800 p-6">
      {children}
    </CardFadeIn>
  )
}
```

- **Staggered grids and keyboard navigation.** If cards are interactive (links, buttons), users can tab to them before they fully appear visually. Ensure `outline` / `:focus-visible` styles are present so keyboard users can locate focus even at low opacity mid-animation.
- **Do not animate critical error or success messages with `CardFadeIn`.** A fade-in delay on an alert means the user has to wait to read important feedback. Use instant rendering for status messages.

## Performance considerations

- **Only `opacity` animates.** The component transitions `opacity` from `0` to `1`. Opacity changes run on the GPU compositor and do not trigger layout or paint, so the cost is negligible even for large cards with images.
- **Fires once and stops.** Unlike hover-based animations, `CardFadeIn` does not register any event listeners. After the transition completes the component is effectively static, with zero ongoing animation cost.
- **Stagger cautiously at scale.** Staggering 20+ cards with 100ms increments means the last card does not appear until 2 seconds after mount. Keep the total stagger window under about 0.8 seconds for grids larger than 6 items.
- **Combining with image loading.** If a card contains a heavy image that loads slowly, the fade may complete while the image is still blank. Consider pairing with an `onLoad` pattern to start the fade only after the image resolves.

## Customization examples

### Staggered card grid

Use incremental `delay` values to create a cascade across multiple cards:

```tsx
import { CardFadeIn } from "@/components/animations/cards/fade-in"

const items = ["Design", "Engineering", "Marketing", "Sales"]

export function TeamGrid() {
  return (
    <div className="grid grid-cols-2 gap-4">
      {items.map((role, i) => (
        <CardFadeIn
          key={role}
          delay={i * 0.1}
          duration={0.4}
          className="rounded-xl border border-neutral-200 dark:border-neutral-800 p-6 bg-white dark:bg-neutral-900"
        >
          <p className="font-semibold">{role}</p>
        </CardFadeIn>
      ))}
    </div>
  )
}
```

### Slower, more dramatic entrance

For a hero-area card where you want the content to feel cinematic:

```tsx
<CardFadeIn duration={1.2} delay={0.3} className="rounded-2xl bg-neutral-950 p-10 text-white">
  <h2 className="text-4xl font-bold">Welcome back</h2>
  <p className="text-neutral-400 mt-2">Your dashboard is ready.</p>
</CardFadeIn>
```

### Pricing card that fades in after route transition

```tsx
import { CardFadeIn } from "@/components/animations/cards/fade-in"

interface PricingCardProps {
  plan: string
  price: string
  features: string[]
  highlighted?: boolean
  delay?: number
}

export function PricingCard({ plan, price, features, highlighted = false, delay = 0 }: PricingCardProps) {

```

### Dashboard widget that fades in after data loads

```tsx
"use client"
import { useState, useEffect } from "react"
import { CardFadeIn } from "@/components/animations/cards/fade-in"

export function RevenueWidget() {
  const [loaded, setLoaded] = useState(false)
  const [value, setValue] = useState<string | null>(null)

  useEffect(() => {
    fetchRevenue().then((v) => {
      setValue(v)
      setLoaded(true)
    })
  }, [])

  if (!loaded) {
    return <div className="h-32 animate-pulse rounded-xl bg-neutral-100 dark:bg-neutral-800" />
  }

  return (
    <CardFadeIn
      duration={0.4}
      className="rounded-xl border border-neutral-200 dark:border-neutral-800 bg-white dark:bg-neutral-900 p-6"
    >
      <p className="text-sm text-neutral-500 dark:text-neutral-400">Revenue this month</p>
      <p className="text-3xl font-bold mt-1">{value}</p>
    </CardFadeIn>
  )
}
```

title: Flip Card
description: Card that flips on hover.

import { Preview, PreviewGrid } from '@/components/preview';

## Overview

The `CardFlip` creates a 3D flip effect on hover, perfect for revealing additional content.

## Installation

        ```bash
        npx shadcn@latest add @animbits/cards-flip
        ```
        ```bash
        pnpm dlx shadcn@latest add @animbits/cards-flip
        ```
        ```bash
        yarn dlx shadcn@latest add @animbits/cards-flip
        ```
        ```bash
        bunx shadcn@latest add @animbits/cards-flip
        ```
    **Step 1: Add the utility**

    ```tsx title="lib/utils.ts"
    import { clsx, type ClassValue } from "clsx"
    import { twMerge } from "tailwind-merge"

    export function cn(...inputs: ClassValue[]) {
      return twMerge(clsx(inputs))
    }
    ```

    **Step 2: Copy the component**

    ```tsx title="components/animations/cards/flip.tsx"
"use client";
import * as React from "react";
import { motion, HTMLMotionProps } from "motion/react";
import { cn } from "@/lib/utils";
export interface CardFlipProps extends HTMLMotionProps<"div"> {
  duration?: number;
  axis?: "x" | "y";
}
export function CardFlip({
  children,
  className,
  duration = 0.6,
  axis = "y",
  ...props
}: CardFlipProps) {
  return (
    <motion.div
      whileHover={{
        rotateY: axis === "y" ? 180 : 0,
        rotateX: axis === "x" ? 180 : 0,
      }}
      transition={{ duration }}
      style={{ transformStyle: "preserve-3d" }}
      className={cn("cursor-pointer", className)}
      {...props}
    >
      {children}
    </motion.div>
  );
}

```

## Usage

```tsx
import { CardFlip } from "@/components/animations/cards/flip"

<CardFlip className="p-6 bg-white rounded-lg border">
  <h3>Card Title</h3>
  <p>Hover to flip!</p>
</CardFlip>
```

## Props

| `duration` | `number` | `0.6` | Animation duration in seconds |
| `axis` | `"x" \| "y"` | `"y"` | Flip axis |
| `className` | `string` | `undefined` | Additional CSS classes |

## Use cases

`CardFlip` applies `rotateY: 180` (or `rotateX: 180` when `axis="x"`) on `whileHover` via `transformStyle: "preserve-3d"`. The entire card contents rotate; this component does not manage a separate front and back face. It is the caller's responsibility to place front-face and back-face children and apply `backface-visibility: hidden` to each.

Use it when:

- **Product cards with front/back details.** Front shows photo and price; back reveals specs, sizing, or a CTA button.
- **Flashcard or quiz UIs.** Term on the front, definition on the back.
- **Team member cards.** Photo and name on the front, bio and social links on the back.
- **Feature reveal.** An icon tile that flips to show a short explainer paragraph.

## When to use / when not to use

**Use `CardFlip` when:**

- The hover surface is large enough that users will naturally hover over it (at least 120px x 120px).
- The back-face content adds genuine value, not just decorative text that could appear in a tooltip.

**Reach for a different component when:**

- You only want a subtle hover response without hiding content. Use [CardHoverLift](/docs/animations/cards/hover-lift) or [CardHoverGlow](/docs/animations/cards/hover-glow) instead.
- The card is in a dense grid where accidental hover triggers make the flip feel twitchy. Tighter grids work better with [CardHoverLift](/docs/animations/cards/hover-lift).
- You are building for touch-primary devices. `whileHover` does not reliably fire on touch screens; back-face content becomes inaccessible. Provide a tap-to-toggle fallback using `useState`.
- Content hierarchy is important and back-face items need to be always reachable. See the accessibility section below for keyboard and screen-reader concerns.

## Accessibility notes

**This is one of the most accessibility-sensitive animations in this library.** Address all of the following before shipping.

- **3D rotation can cause vestibular discomfort.** Flipping a card 180 degrees is a significant spatial transformation. Users with vestibular disorders, migraines, or motion sensitivity may experience nausea or disorientation. Always respect `prefers-reduced-motion` by reducing or eliminating the rotation:

```tsx
"use client"
import { useReducedMotion } from "motion/react"
import { CardFlip } from "@/components/animations/cards/flip"

function AccessibleFlipCard({ front, back }: { front: React.ReactNode; back: React.ReactNode }) {
  const reduced = useReducedMotion()
  // With reduced motion, use a near-instant fade instead of a full 3D flip.
  return (
    <CardFlip
      duration={reduced ? 0.01 : 0.6}
      className="relative h-64 w-48 rounded-xl"
    >
      <div className="absolute inset-0 backface-hidden">{front}</div>
      <div className="absolute inset-0 backface-hidden rotate-y-180">{back}</div>
    </CardFlip>
  )
}
```

- **Back-face content must remain reachable.** Because the flip is hover-only and `whileHover` does not fire on keyboard focus by default, any interactive elements on the back face (buttons, links) are unreachable by keyboard. Add a matching `whileFocus` or use a `useState`-driven toggle that responds to both hover and focus.
- **Screen readers do not perceive the visual flip.** Both front and back children are in the DOM simultaneously. Without additional management, a screen reader will read both faces. Use `aria-hidden` on the non-active face and toggle it with state.
- **Do not convey meaning through rotation alone.** If the back face contains the only CTA or price, that information must also be accessible to users who cannot hover or use a mouse.

## Performance considerations

- **3D transforms run on the compositor.** `rotateX` and `rotateY` are transforms; they do not trigger layout or paint. The flip itself is GPU-accelerated.
- **`transformStyle: preserve-3d` creates a stacking context.** Every `CardFlip` instance establishes a new stacking context and composited layer. Dozens of flip cards on one page add GPU memory overhead. For long lists, consider rendering flip behavior only on the currently hovered card.
- **`whileHover` polls continuously during hover.** Motion tracks the hover state and re-evaluates variants on each relevant pointer event. This is lightweight but worth noting for extremely large DOM trees.
- **Avoid animating heavy children.** If the back face contains large images or complex layouts, the flip will stutter on low-end hardware because compositing the rotated face is more expensive when the painted content is large.

## Customization examples

### X-axis flip (vertical flip)

```tsx
import { CardFlip } from "@/components/animations/cards/flip"

    style={{ backfaceVisibility: "hidden" }}

    <p className="font-semibold">Front face</p>
  </div>
  <div
    className="absolute inset-0 rounded-xl bg-neutral-900 dark:bg-white flex items-center justify-center"
    style={{ backfaceVisibility: "hidden", transform: "rotateX(180deg)" }}
  >
    <p className="font-semibold text-white dark:text-neutral-900">Back face</p>

```


## Real-world examples

### Team member card with bio on back

```tsx
"use client"
import { CardFlip } from "@/components/animations/cards/flip"

interface TeamCardProps {
  name: string
  role: string
  avatar: string
  bio: string
  twitter: string
}

export function TeamCard({ name, role, avatar, bio, twitter }: TeamCardProps) {
  return (
    <CardFlip
      axis="y"
      duration={0.6}
      className="relative h-72 w-56 rounded-2xl"
      style={{ perspective: 1000 }}
    >
      {/* Front */}
      <div
        className="absolute inset-0 rounded-2xl overflow-hidden border border-neutral-200 dark:border-neutral-800 bg-white dark:bg-neutral-900 flex flex-col items-center justify-center gap-3 p-6"
        style={{ backfaceVisibility: "hidden" }}
      >
        <img src={avatar} alt={name} className="w-20 h-20 rounded-full object-cover" />
        <div className="text-center">
          <p className="font-bold">{name}</p>
          <p className="text-sm text-neutral-500 dark:text-neutral-400">{role}</p>
        </div>
      </div>

      {/* Back */}
      <div
        className="absolute inset-0 rounded-2xl border border-neutral-200 dark:border-neutral-800 bg-neutral-50 dark:bg-neutral-800 flex flex-col items-center justify-center gap-4 p-6"
        style={{ backfaceVisibility: "hidden", transform: "rotateY(180deg)" }}
      >
        <p className="text-sm text-center text-neutral-600 dark:text-neutral-300">{bio}</p>
        <a
          href={`https://twitter.com/${twitter}`}
          className="text-sm font-semibold text-blue-500 hover:underline"
          aria-label={`${name} on Twitter`}
        >
          @{twitter}
        </a>
      </div>
    </CardFlip>
  )
}
```

### Flashcard for a quiz app

```tsx
"use client"
import { useState } from "react"
import { motion } from "motion/react"

// Using raw motion here for a click-controlled flip, which is more accessible than hover-only.
export function Flashcard({ term, definition }: { term: string; definition: string }) {
  const [flipped, setFlipped] = useState(false)

  return (
    <button
      onClick={() => setFlipped((f) => !f)}
      className="relative h-48 w-80 cursor-pointer [perspective:1000px] focus-visible:ring-2 focus-visible:ring-neutral-900 dark:focus-visible:ring-white rounded-2xl"
      aria-label={flipped ? `Definition: ${definition}` : `Term: ${term}`}
    >
      <motion.div
        animate={{ rotateY: flipped ? 180 : 0 }}
        transition={{ duration: 0.5 }}
        style={{ transformStyle: "preserve-3d" }}
        className="relative w-full h-full"
      >
        <div
          className="absolute inset-0 rounded-2xl bg-white dark:bg-neutral-900 border border-neutral-200 dark:border-neutral-800 flex items-center justify-center p-6"
          style={{ backfaceVisibility: "hidden" }}
        >
          <p className="text-xl font-bold text-center">{term}</p>
        </div>
        <div
          className="absolute inset-0 rounded-2xl bg-neutral-900 dark:bg-white flex items-center justify-center p-6"
          style={{ backfaceVisibility: "hidden", transform: "rotateY(180deg)" }}
        >
          <p className="text-sm text-center text-white dark:text-neutral-900">{definition}</p>
        </div>
      </motion.div>
    </button>
  )
}
```

        ```bash
        bunx shadcn@latest add @animbits/cards-grayscale
        ```
    **Step 1: Add the utility**

    ```tsx title="lib/utils.ts"
    import { clsx, type ClassValue } from "clsx"
    import { twMerge } from "tailwind-merge"

    export function cn(...inputs: ClassValue[]) {
      return twMerge(clsx(inputs))
    }
    ```

    **Step 2: Copy the component**

    ```tsx title="components/animations/cards/grayscale.tsx"
"use client";
import * as React from "react";
import * as motion from "framer-motion/client";
import type { HTMLMotionProps } from "motion/react";
import { cn } from "@/lib/utils";
export interface CardGrayscaleProps
  extends Omit<HTMLMotionProps<"div">, "children"> {
  children: React.ReactNode;
  duration?: number;
}
export function CardGrayscale({
  children,
  className,
  duration = 0.5,
  ...props
}: CardGrayscaleProps) {
  const [isHovered, setIsHovered] = React.useState(false);
  return (
    <motion.div
      className={cn("relative overflow-hidden", className)}
      onHoverStart={() => setIsHovered(true)}
      onHoverEnd={() => setIsHovered(false)}
      animate={{
        filter: isHovered ? "grayscale(0%)" : "grayscale(100%)",
      }}
      transition={{ duration }}
      {...props}
    >
      {children}
    </motion.div>
  );
}

```

## Usage

```tsx
import { CardGrayscale } from "@/components/animations/cards/grayscale"

<CardGrayscale className="rounded-lg overflow-hidden">
  <img src="/photo.jpg" alt="Photo" className="w-full h-full object-cover" />
</CardGrayscale>
```

## Props

| `duration` | `number` | `0.5` | Animation duration in seconds |
| `className` | `string` | `undefined` | Additional CSS classes |

## Use cases

`CardGrayscale` manages a `isHovered` boolean with `onHoverStart`/`onHoverEnd` and animates the CSS `filter` between `grayscale(100%)` (resting state) and `grayscale(0%)` (hovered). The transition takes `duration` seconds (default `0.5`). The wrapper has `relative overflow-hidden` baked in.

Use it when:

- **Photography portfolios.** All thumbnails start muted; hovering one saturates it, drawing attention without competing colors.
- **Editorial image galleries.** News, magazine, or blog image grids where you want a calm default state that springs to life on interaction.
- **Team member photos.** A classic design pattern that conveys "hover to see who this person is."
- **Partner/client logo grids.** Logos shown in grayscale by default, full color on hover, keeping the grid visually balanced.
- **Before/after product showcases.** Wrap only the image portion while keeping the surrounding card layout in full color.

## When to use / when not to use

**Use `CardGrayscale` when:**

- The content inside the wrapper is primarily an image or video that benefits visually from desaturation at rest.
- You want a low-motion, filter-only hover effect without any geometry change.

**Reach for a different component when:**

- The card content is mostly text or UI chrome without strong color. Grayscale has no visible effect on black-and-white content.
- You want a physical hover response like lift or glow. Combine `CardGrayscale` with [CardHoverLift](/docs/animations/cards/hover-lift) by wrapping one inside the other, or use `CardHoverGlow` alone if the image coloring is secondary.
- You need the full-color version visible by default and want to desaturate on hover. The component always starts at `grayscale(100%)` and cannot be inverted without forking the source.
- The images are already low-contrast or monochromatic. The effect will be imperceptible.

## Accessibility notes

- **CSS `filter` animates on the GPU compositor.** It does not affect DOM structure, tab order, or the accessibility tree. Screen readers are unaffected by the grayscale state.
- **Do not rely on color alone to convey meaning.** WCAG 1.4.1 prohibits using color as the only visual means of conveying information. If the only way to distinguish an "active" card from an "inactive" one is the presence of color vs. grayscale, add a secondary indicator (e.g., a border, label, or icon).
- **Respect `prefers-reduced-motion`.** The `filter` transition is subtle but still motion. Users who prefer reduced motion should see an instant switch rather than a 0.5-second dissolve:

```tsx
"use client"
import { useReducedMotion } from "motion/react"
import { CardGrayscale } from "@/components/animations/cards/grayscale"

function AccessibleGrayscaleCard({ src, alt }: { src: string; alt: string }) {
  const reduced = useReducedMotion()
  return (
    <CardGrayscale
      duration={reduced ? 0 : 0.5}
      className="rounded-xl overflow-hidden w-64"
    >
      <img src={src} alt={alt} className="w-full h-48 object-cover" />
    </CardGrayscale>
  )
}
```

- **Keyboard access.** `onHoverStart`/`onHoverEnd` do not fire on keyboard focus. If the card is interactive (a link, a button), add matching `onFocus`/`onBlur` behavior so keyboard users also see the color state.

## Performance considerations

- **CSS `filter` is GPU-composited on modern browsers.** The transition between `grayscale(100%)` and `grayscale(0%)` runs off the main thread on Chrome, Firefox, and Safari. It does not trigger layout or paint.
- **Filter creates a stacking context.** Applying a CSS filter promotes the element to its own composited layer. In a grid of many thumbnails, this adds GPU memory. For image grids with 50+ items, consider only applying the filter to the visible viewport (e.g., with `content-visibility`).
- **Two state updates per hover cycle.** The component calls `setIsHovered` on each `onHoverStart` and `onHoverEnd`. These are cheap React state updates, but avoid nesting `CardGrayscale` inside rapidly re-rendering parents.
- **`framer-motion/client` import.** The source uses `import * as motion from "framer-motion/client"`, which enables RSC-compatible rendering. No client bundle overhead beyond the motion library itself.

    **Step 1: Copy the hook**
    
    ```tsx title="lib/hooks/use-hover-glow.ts"
    import { type MotionProps, type Easing } from "motion/react";

    export interface UseHoverGlowOptions {
      /**
       * Glow color (CSS color value)
       * @default "rgba(59, 130, 246, 0.5)" - Blue glow
       */
      glowColor?: string;

      /**
       * Glow blur radius (in pixels)
       * @default 20
       */
      glowBlur?: number;

      /**
       * Glow spread (in pixels)
       * @default 5
       */
      glowSpread?: number;

      /**
       * Animation duration (in seconds)
       * @default 0.3
       */
      duration?: number;

      /**
       * Animation easing
       * @default "easeOut"
       */
      ease?: Easing | Easing[];

      /**
       * Scale on hover (1 = no scale)
       * @default 1.02
       */
      scale?: number;

      /**
       * Whether to add inner glow
       * @default false
       */
      innerGlow?: boolean;
    }

    export function useHoverGlow(options: UseHoverGlowOptions = {}): MotionProps {
      const {
        glowColor = "rgba(59, 130, 246, 0.5)",
        glowBlur = 20,
        glowSpread = 5,
        duration = 0.3,
        ease = "easeOut",
        scale = 1.02,
        innerGlow = false,
      } = options;

      const baseShadow = "0 2px 8px rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.1)";
      const glowShadow = `0 0 ${glowBlur}px ${glowSpread}px ${glowColor}`;
      const innerGlowShadow = innerGlow
        ? `inset 0 0 ${glowBlur / 2}px ${glowColor}`
        : "";

      const hoverShadow = innerGlow
        ? `${baseShadow}, ${glowShadow}, ${innerGlowShadow}`
        : `${baseShadow}, ${glowShadow}`;

      return {
        initial: {
          scale: 1,
          boxShadow: baseShadow,
        },
        whileHover: {
          scale,
          boxShadow: hoverShadow,
        },
        transition: {
          duration,
          ease,
        },
      };
    }
    ```

    **Step 2: Copy the utility function (if not already present)**
    
    ```tsx title="lib/utils.ts"
    import { type ClassValue, clsx } from "clsx"
    import { twMerge } from "tailwind-merge"

    export function cn(...inputs: ClassValue[]) {

    }
    ```

    **Step 3: Copy the component**
    
    ```tsx title="components/animations/cards/hover-glow.tsx"
"use client";
import * as React from "react";
import { motion, HTMLMotionProps } from "motion/react";
import { cn } from "@/lib/utils";
import { useHoverGlow } from "@/lib/use-hover-glow";
export interface CardHoverGlowProps extends HTMLMotionProps<"div"> {
  glowColor?: string;
  glowSpread?: number;
  duration?: number;
}
export function CardHoverGlow({
  children,
  className,
  glowColor = "rgba(59, 130, 246, 0.5)",
  glowSpread = 20,
  duration = 0.3,
  ...props
}: CardHoverGlowProps) {
  const glowProps = useHoverGlow({
    glowColor,
    glowBlur: glowSpread,
    duration,
  });
  return (
    <motion.div
      {...glowProps}
      className={cn("cursor-pointer", className)}
      {...props}
    >
      {children}
    </motion.div>
  );
}

```

## Props

| `glowColor` | `string` | `"rgba(59, 130, 246, 0.5)"` | Glow color (rgba or hex) |
| `glowSpread` | `number` | `20` | Glow spread in pixels |
| `duration` | `number` | `0.3` | Animation duration in seconds |
| `className` | `string` | `undefined` | Additional CSS classes |

## Use cases

`CardHoverGlow` delegates to the `useHoverGlow` hook, which computes `boxShadow` strings for initial and hover states and also scales the card to `1.02` by default. At rest the card shows `0 2px 8px rgba(0,0,0,0.1)`. On hover it adds `0 0 ${glowSpread}px ${glowSpread/4}px ${glowColor}` on top. The `glowSpread` prop (default `20`) maps to the hook's `glowBlur` parameter.

Use it when:

- **Pricing tiers.** Highlight the recommended plan with a brand-colored glow while the other tiers use no glow or a neutral shadow.
- **Feature cards on a dark background.** A colored glow on a dark surface reads immediately as interactive and premium.
- **Call-to-action cards.** Single-card CTAs that need to stand out from surrounding content.
- **Integration or plugin galleries.** Each tile glows in a color that matches the integration's brand color.
- **Dashboard widgets.** A subtle blue glow on the active or selected stat card.

## When to use / when not to use

**Use `CardHoverGlow` when:**

- The page background is dark or neutral so the glow reads clearly. On a white background, `rgba(59, 130, 246, 0.5)` at `20px` spread can be almost invisible.
- You want both a glow AND a slight scale (`1.02` by default from `useHoverGlow`). If you want glow without any scale, you will need to customize the hook directly.

**Reach for a different component when:**

- You want a lift (vertical translation) rather than a glow. Use [CardHoverLift](/docs/animations/cards/hover-lift) instead.
- The card is small (under 80px wide) and a 20px spread glow will dominate the element visually. Reduce `glowSpread` to `8` or `10`.
- You need the inner glow variant. The `useHoverGlow` hook supports `innerGlow: true` but `CardHoverGlow` does not expose that prop; use the hook directly.
- Dense grids where simultaneous glows on neighboring cards compete visually. Consider [CardHoverLift](/docs/animations/cards/hover-lift) for grids and reserve glow for isolated or hero cards.

## Accessibility notes

- **`boxShadow` is purely decorative.** Shadow changes are invisible to assistive technology. The glow does not convey state or meaning that must be communicated another way.
- **Scale of `1.02` is small but still motion.** Respect `prefers-reduced-motion` by disabling the scale and reducing the glow transition to instant:

```tsx
"use client"
import { useReducedMotion } from "motion/react"
import { CardHoverGlow } from "@/components/animations/cards/hover-glow"

function AccessibleGlowCard({ children }: { children: React.ReactNode }) {
  const reduced = useReducedMotion()
  return (
    <CardHoverGlow
      duration={reduced ? 0 : 0.3}
      glowColor="rgba(59, 130, 246, 0.5)"
      glowSpread={reduced ? 0 : 20}
      className="rounded-xl border border-neutral-200 dark:border-neutral-800 bg-white dark:bg-neutral-900 p-6"
    >
      {children}
    </CardHoverGlow>
  )
}
```

- **Do not use glow color to indicate required or error state.** A red glow on hover is a nice effect but fails as an error indicator because it only appears on hover. Error states must be persistently visible and perceivable without color alone.
- **Focus visibility.** `CardHoverGlow` adds `cursor-pointer`. Ensure the card has proper `:focus-visible` styling, especially if it wraps an anchor or button, since `whileHover` does not fire on keyboard focus.

## Performance considerations

- **`boxShadow` animates off the main thread in modern browsers.** Chrome and Firefox can composite box-shadow changes without layout or paint when the element is already composited. However, complex multi-layer shadows (the hook combines a base shadow and a glow shadow) can be slower to composite on low-end devices.
- **Scale of `1.02` adds a composited layer.** The `whileHover: { scale }` triggers compositing. This is appropriate for isolated cards but expensive for large grids. In a 30-card grid, every `CardHoverGlow` creates its own composited layer even when not hovered, because motion reserves the layer during initial render.
- **`duration: 0.3` is fast by default.** This reads as snappy. Increasing it to `0.6` or more makes the glow feel sluggish and can cause the glow to still be fading out when the user moves to the next card.
- **Avoid `glowSpread` values above `60`.** Very large spreads produce wide blurs that force the browser to composite a larger area, increasing GPU memory use.

```tsx
    >
      <img src={image} alt={title} className="w-full h-44 object-cover" />
      <div className="p-5 flex flex-col gap-2 flex-1">
        <span className="text-xs font-semibold uppercase tracking-wider text-purple-500">{category}</span>
        <h3 className="font-bold leading-snug">{title}</h3>
        <p className="text-xs text-neutral-400 mt-auto">{readTime} min read</p>
      </div>
    </CardHoverGlow>
  )
}
```

## Overview

The `CardHoverLift` creates a subtle lift effect on hover, making cards feel interactive and responsive. Perfect for product cards, blog posts, and interactive elements.

## Installation

        ```bash
        npx shadcn@latest add @animbits/cards-hover-lift
        ```
        ```bash
        pnpm dlx shadcn@latest add @animbits/cards-hover-lift
        ```
        ```bash
        yarn dlx shadcn@latest add @animbits/cards-hover-lift
        ```
        ```bash
        bunx shadcn@latest add @animbits/cards-hover-lift
        ```
    **Step 1: Copy the hook**
    
    ```tsx title="lib/hooks/use-hover-lift.ts"
    import { type MotionProps, type Easing } from "motion/react";

    export interface UseHoverLiftOptions {
      /**
       * Distance to lift the element on hover (in pixels)
       * @default 8
       */
      liftDistance?: number;

      /**
       * Whether to add shadow on hover
       * @default true
       */
      addShadow?: boolean;

      /**
       * Shadow intensity (0-1)
       * @default 0.3
       */
      shadowIntensity?: number;

      /**
       * Animation duration (in seconds)
       * @default 0.2
       */
      duration?: number;

      /**
       * Animation easing
       * @default "easeOut"
       */
      ease?: Easing | Easing[];

      /**
       * Scale on hover (1 = no scale)
       * @default 1
       */
      scale?: number;
    }

    export function useHoverLift(options: UseHoverLiftOptions = {}): MotionProps {
      const {
        liftDistance = 8,
        addShadow = true,
        shadowIntensity = 0.3,
        duration = 0.2,
        ease = "easeOut",
        scale = 1,
      } = options;

      const shadowBlur = liftDistance * 2;
      const shadowSpread = Math.round(liftDistance / 4);

      return {
        initial: {
          y: 0,
          scale: 1,
          boxShadow: addShadow
            ? `0 2px 4px rgba(0, 0, 0, ${shadowIntensity * 0.3})`
            : undefined,
        },
        whileHover: {
          y: -liftDistance,
          scale,
          boxShadow: addShadow
            ? `0 ${shadowBlur}px ${shadowBlur + shadowSpread}px rgba(0, 0, 0, ${shadowIntensity})`
            : undefined,
        },
        transition: {
          duration,
          ease,
        },
      };
    }
    ```

    **Step 2: Copy the utility function (if not already present)**
    
    ```tsx title="lib/utils.ts"
    import { type ClassValue, clsx } from "clsx"
    import { twMerge } from "tailwind-merge"

    export function cn(...inputs: ClassValue[]) {
      return twMerge(clsx(inputs))
    }
    ```

    **Step 3: Copy the component**
    
    ```tsx title="components/animations/cards/hover-lift.tsx"
"use client";
import * as React from "react";
import { motion, HTMLMotionProps } from "motion/react";
import { cn } from "@/lib/utils";
import { useHoverLift } from "@/lib/use-hover-lift";
export interface CardHoverLiftProps extends HTMLMotionProps<"div"> {
  liftDistance?: number;
  duration?: number;
  addShadow?: boolean;
}
export function CardHoverLift({
  children,
  className,
  liftDistance = 8,
  duration = 0.2,
  addShadow = true,
  ...props
}: CardHoverLiftProps) {
  const liftProps = useHoverLift({
    liftDistance,
    duration,
    addShadow,
  });
  return (
    <motion.div
      {...liftProps}
      className={cn("cursor-pointer", className)}
      {...props}
    >
      {children}
    </motion.div>
  );
}

```

## Props

| `liftDistance` | `number` | `8` | Lift distance in pixels |
| `duration` | `number` | `0.2` | Animation duration in seconds |
| `addShadow` | `boolean` | `true` | Whether to add shadow on lift |
| `className` | `string` | `undefined` | Additional CSS classes |

## Use cases

`CardHoverLift` delegates to `useHoverLift`, which translates the card `y: -liftDistance` (default `8px`) on hover and deepens the `boxShadow` proportionally (shadow blur = `liftDistance * 2`, spread = `liftDistance / 4`). The `scale` prop in the hook defaults to `1`, so no scale is applied unless you call the hook directly. The animation runs over `0.2s easeOut`, which feels immediate but not jarring.

Use it when:

- **E-commerce product grids.** Every card in a grid lifts independently on hover, making it feel clickable without a disruptive animation.
- **Blog post listings.** Horizontal or vertical card stacks where you want hover feedback without color change or glow.
- **Service or feature tiles.** A row of tiles on a landing page where each one lifts to draw attention.
- **Dashboard panels.** Clickable stat cards or recent-activity rows that need to signal interactivity.
- **App navigation cards.** Large tap-target cards linking to sub-sections.

## When to use / when not to use

**Use `CardHoverLift` when:**

- Cards are interactive (links, buttons, navigable items) and you want a physical "pick up" affordance.
- The layout is stable and you can afford an `8px` upward shift without overlapping adjacent content. `z-index` management may be required in tight grids.

**Reach for a different component when:**

- You want a glow or color effect rather than a physical movement. Use [CardHoverGlow](/docs/animations/cards/hover-glow) instead.
- Cards are very small (under 60px tall) and an 8px lift is proportionally too dramatic. Reduce `liftDistance` to `4` or use `addShadow={false}` with only a shadow change.
- The cards are inside a container with `overflow: hidden` at a height that clips the lifted card. Lift clipping looks broken; switch to [CardHoverGlow](/docs/animations/cards/hover-glow) or remove the clip.
- The card is purely informational (non-interactive). Applying a hover lift implies clickability, which is misleading for non-interactive content.

## Accessibility notes

- **`y` translation is a transform.** It does not affect the accessibility tree, tab order, or focus outline position. The browser moves the painted card but the hit area and focus ring may remain at the original position in some browsers. Test with keyboard navigation.
- **Cursor set to `pointer`.** The component applies `cursor-pointer`. This is correct when the card is interactive; remove it with `className="cursor-default"` if the lift is purely cosmetic.
- **Respect `prefers-reduced-motion`.** The 8px upward translate is a positional shift. Some users find positional motion uncomfortable even at small distances:

```tsx
"use client"
import { useReducedMotion } from "motion/react"
import { CardHoverLift } from "@/components/animations/cards/hover-lift"

function AccessibleLiftCard({ children }: { children: React.ReactNode }) {
  const reduced = useReducedMotion()
  return (
    <CardHoverLift
      liftDistance={reduced ? 0 : 8}
      duration={reduced ? 0 : 0.2}
      addShadow={!reduced}
      className="rounded-xl border border-neutral-200 dark:border-neutral-800 bg-white dark:bg-neutral-900 p-6"
    >
      {children}
    </CardHoverLift>
  )
}
```

- **Do not rely on the lift to signal the only interactive affordance.** Combine it with a visible focus ring and underline or color change on the card's text link so keyboard users get the same signal without hover.

## Performance considerations

- **`y` translation and `boxShadow` are both GPU-composited.** The `y` translate runs as a transform; `boxShadow` changes can also be composited in Chrome and Firefox. Neither triggers layout.
- **`duration: 0.2` is intentionally fast.** A card that lifts in 200ms and returns equally quickly produces no noticeable lag when moving through a grid. Increasing duration to `0.4+` makes the return animation feel slow and sticky.
- **Shadow recalculation happens once per hover enter/leave.** The shadow is computed inside `useHoverLift` at hook call time, not on each frame, so there is no per-frame JavaScript cost.
- **`z-index` for overlapping neighbors.** When a card in a tight grid lifts 8px, it may render underneath a neighbor's shadow if stacking context is not managed. Add `className="relative z-10"` inside a `hover:z-20` group if you see layering issues.

## Overview

The `CardParallaxTilt` creates an advanced 3D tilt effect with shadow separation for a premium feel.

## Preview

  </CardParallaxTilt>

## Installation

        ```bash
        npx shadcn@latest add @animbits/cards-parallax-tilt
        ```
        ```bash
        pnpm dlx shadcn@latest add @animbits/cards-parallax-tilt
        ```
        ```bash
        yarn dlx shadcn@latest add @animbits/cards-parallax-tilt
        ```
        ```bash
        bunx shadcn@latest add @animbits/cards-parallax-tilt
        ```
    **Step 1: Copy the hook**

    ```tsx title="lib/hooks/use-parallax-tilt.ts"
    import * as React from "react"
    import { useMotionValue, useSpring, useTransform } from "motion/react"

    export interface UseParallaxTiltOptions {
      maxTilt?: number
      duration?: number
      shadowIntensity?: number
      stiffness?: number
      damping?: number
    }

    export function useParallaxTilt(options: UseParallaxTiltOptions = {}) {
      const {
        maxTilt = 15,
        duration = 0.3,
        shadowIntensity = 0.3,
        stiffness = 300,
        damping = 30,
      } = options

      const ref = React.useRef<HTMLElement>(null)
      const x = useMotionValue(0)
      const y = useMotionValue(0)

      const mouseXSpring = useSpring(x, { stiffness, damping })
      const mouseYSpring = useSpring(y, { stiffness, damping })

      const rotateX = useTransform(mouseYSpring, [-0.5, 0.5], [maxTilt, -maxTilt])
      const rotateY = useTransform(mouseXSpring, [-0.5, 0.5], [-maxTilt, maxTilt])

      const shadowX = useTransform(mouseXSpring, [-0.5, 0.5], [-20, 20])
      const shadowY = useTransform(mouseYSpring, [-0.5, 0.5], [-20, 20])

      const handleMouseMove = (e: React.MouseEvent<HTMLElement>) => {
        if (!ref.current) return

        const rect = ref.current.getBoundingClientRect()
        const width = rect.width
        const height = rect.height
        const mouseX = e.clientX - rect.left
        const mouseY = e.clientY - rect.top
        const xPct = mouseX / width - 0.5
        const yPct = mouseY / height - 0.5
        x.set(xPct)
        y.set(yPct)
      }

      const handleMouseLeave = () => {
        x.set(0)
        y.set(0)
      }

      const tiltProps = {
        style: {
          rotateX,
          rotateY,
          transformStyle: "preserve-3d" as const,
          boxShadow: useTransform(
            [shadowX, shadowY],
            ([x, y]) => `${x}px ${y}px 30px rgba(0, 0, 0, ${shadowIntensity})`
          ),
        },
        onMouseMove: handleMouseMove,
        onMouseLeave: handleMouseLeave,
        transition: { duration },
      }

      return { tiltProps, ref }
    }
    ```

    **Step 2: Copy the utility**

    ```tsx title="lib/utils.ts"
    import { type ClassValue, clsx } from "clsx"
    import { twMerge } from "tailwind-merge"

    export function cn(...inputs: ClassValue[]) {
      return twMerge(clsx(inputs))
    }
    ```

    **Step 3: Copy the component**

    ```tsx title="components/animations/cards/parallax-tilt.tsx"
"use client";
import * as React from "react";
import { motion, HTMLMotionProps } from "motion/react";
import { cn } from "@/lib/utils";
import {
  useParallaxTilt,
  type UseParallaxTiltOptions,
} from "@/lib/use-parallax-tilt";
export interface CardParallaxTiltProps
  extends Omit<HTMLMotionProps<"div">, "ref">,
    UseParallaxTiltOptions {}
export function CardParallaxTilt({
  children,
  className,
  maxTilt,
  duration,
  shadowIntensity,
  stiffness,
  damping,
  ...props
}: CardParallaxTiltProps) {
  const { tiltProps, ref } = useParallaxTilt({
    maxTilt,
    duration,
    shadowIntensity,
    stiffness,
    damping,
  });
  return (
    <motion.div
      ref={ref as any}
      {...tiltProps}
      className={cn("cursor-pointer", className)}
      {...props}
    >
      {children}
    </motion.div>
  );
}

```

## Usage

```tsx
import { CardParallaxTilt } from "@/components/animations/cards/parallax-tilt"

<CardParallaxTilt className="p-6 bg-white rounded-lg border">
  <h3>Card Title</h3>
  <p>Interactive 3D card</p>
</CardParallaxTilt>
```

## Props

| `maxTilt` | `number` | `15` | Maximum tilt angle in degrees |
| `shadowIntensity` | `number` | `0.3` | Shadow intensity (0 to 1) |
| `duration` | `number` | `0.3` | Animation duration in seconds |
| `stiffness` | `number` | `300` | Spring stiffness for tilt smoothing |
| `damping` | `number` | `30` | Spring damping for tilt smoothing |
| `className` | `string` | `undefined` | Additional CSS classes |

## Use cases

`CardParallaxTilt` is the most mechanically complex card in this library. The `useParallaxTilt` hook computes normalized cursor position (`xPct`, `yPct` in the range -0.5 to 0.5) on every `mousemove` event, feeds those values into `useMotionValue` instances, smooths them with `useSpring` (stiffness `300`, damping `30` by default), and pipes the spring output through `useTransform` to produce `rotateX` and `rotateY` (bounded by `maxTilt`, default `15 degrees`). A separate `boxShadow` is also derived from the cursor position via `useTransform`, creating a directional shadow that makes the card look physically lit from the cursor direction.

Use it when:

- **Premium plan or product cards.** The directional shadow and 3D tilt signal quality and invite interaction.
- **Hero feature showcases.** A single large card (320px or wider) that you want users to engage with before clicking.
- **Game or entertainment UI.** Character cards, pack reveals, achievement cards.
- **Portfolio project showcases.** Large image tiles where depth adds perceived craft.
- **Onboarding or tutorial cards.** Inviting the user to explore the card before proceeding.

## When to use / when not to use

**Use `CardParallaxTilt` when:**

- The card is a focal point, not one of twenty items in a grid. This effect is best reserved for cards that deserve individual attention.
- You are targeting a desktop audience. The effect requires `mousemove` and does not work on touch surfaces.

**Reach for a different component when:**

- You need a tilt effect but want simpler implementation without spring physics. Use [CardTilt](/docs/animations/cards/tilt) which uses direct `animate` calls rather than motion values and springs.
- The card is in a tight grid where 15-degree tilts will overlap neighbors or clip inside containers. Reduce `maxTilt` to `5` or use [CardHoverLift](/docs/animations/cards/hover-lift) for grids.
- Touch is the primary interaction model. Neither tilt component works on touch. Provide a non-interactive version as the mobile fallback.
- Vestibular sensitivity is a concern in your audience. A card tilting to 15 degrees as the user moves their mouse continuously is one of the most motion-intensive effects in this library. See the accessibility section.

## Accessibility notes

**`CardParallaxTilt` produces continuous 3D motion tied to mouse position.** This is the most likely component in this library to cause vestibular discomfort. Take the following precautions seriously.

- **Users with vestibular disorders, migraines, or motion sensitivity can be harmed by continuous parallax motion.** Always respect `prefers-reduced-motion` and eliminate the tilt entirely when it is enabled:

```tsx
"use client"
import { useReducedMotion } from "motion/react"
import { CardParallaxTilt } from "@/components/animations/cards/parallax-tilt"
import { CardHoverLift } from "@/components/animations/cards/hover-lift"

function AccessibleParallaxCard({ children }: { children: React.ReactNode }) {
  const reduced = useReducedMotion()

  // Replace the parallax tilt with a simple lift when reduced motion is preferred.
  if (reduced) {
    return (
      <CardHoverLift className="rounded-2xl border border-neutral-200 dark:border-neutral-800 bg-white dark:bg-neutral-900 p-6">
        {children}
      </CardHoverLift>
    )
  }

  return (
    <CardParallaxTilt maxTilt={15} className="rounded-2xl border border-neutral-200 dark:border-neutral-800 bg-white dark:bg-neutral-900 p-6">
      {children}
    </CardParallaxTilt>
  )
}
```

- **`transformStyle: preserve-3d` and `backface-visibility`.** Nested content rotates with the card in 3D space. Text inside the card tilts, which may be harder to read for some users. Keep card content concise.
- **Keyboard focus.** The tilt is entirely mouse-driven. Keyboard users receive no tilt; ensure the card has a visible `:focus-visible` ring so it remains discoverable.
- **Screen readers.** The rotation and shadow changes are purely visual and do not affect the accessibility tree.

## Performance considerations

- **`mousemove` fires on every frame during cursor movement.** The hook updates two `MotionValue` instances (`x` and `y`) on each event. Motion values update without re-rendering the React component, but the handler itself runs on the main thread. On slow devices, dense mouse movement can create measurable CPU cost.
- **Spring physics run as a subscription to motion values.** `useSpring` attaches an animation loop that evaluates spring state on every animation frame until the spring settles. This is off the main thread in modern browsers but still consumes GPU time.
- **`useTransform` for `boxShadow`.** Shadow transforms involve string interpolation (`${x}px ${y}px 30px ...`), which runs on the main thread unlike pure numeric transforms. For very high frame rates, consider simplifying the shadow or disabling it with `shadowIntensity={0}`.
- **Limit to a few cards per page.** One or two `CardParallaxTilt` instances are fine. Twelve simultaneous tilt cards each with active spring animations and shadow transforms will visibly strain less powerful hardware.
- **`stiffness` and `damping` tuning.** Defaults of `300`/`30` produce a fast, snappy spring. Lower stiffness (e.g., `150`) and higher damping (e.g., `20`) give a looser, slower return, which is less demanding on the animation loop.

## Customization examples

### Tighter tilt for a card in a grid

# scale-in.mdx

Source: https://github.com/garvit1000/animbits/blob/main/content/docs/animations/cards/scale-in.mdx

title: Scale In Card
description: Card that scales in when entering viewport.

import { Preview, PreviewGrid } from '@/components/preview';
import { CardScaleIn } from '@/registry/new-york/animations/cards/scale-in';

## Overview

The `CardScaleIn` scales up from a smaller size when entering the viewport, creating a zoom-in effect.

## Preview

      <h3 className="text-lg font-semibold mb-2">Consulting</h3>
