  gradient
</SvgTextDraw>
```

> **Note:** This component uses SVG path drawing animation. Only lowercase letters (a-z) and spaces are currently supported. The text will be automatically converted to lowercase.

## Use cases

`SvgTextDraw` renders each lowercase letter as a `<motion.path>` inside an `<svg>` with a fixed `letterWidth` of 50 units per character. The `pathLength` of each path is animated from `0` to `1` with a 0.5 s `easeInOut` duration (multiplied by `speed`). Each letter is delayed by `delay + index * 0.15 * speed` seconds, so a 5-letter word at default speed takes about `0 + 4 * 0.15 + 0.5 = 1.1 s` to complete. The SVG contains a `<title>` element with the original string. Reach for it when:

- **Signature or handwriting aesthetic.** A product name or short phrase drawn stroke by stroke mimics handwriting and is well suited to personal brand sites, creative portfolios, or craft-focused products.
- **Onboarding welcome screen.** "hello" or a user's first name drawn as an animated greeting sets a warm, personal tone.
- **Logo animation.** A wordmark that draws itself on page load creates a memorable first impression for a short brand name.
- **Decorative section dividers.** A short decorative word drawn across a section break can replace a static rule or illustration.

The component inherits `stroke="currentColor"` from the SVG, so it adopts the parent text color automatically.

## When to use / when not to use

**Use svg-text-draw when:**

- The text is short: 3 to 8 characters at a reasonable speed complete in 1 to 2 seconds. Longer strings take proportionally longer to draw and can feel like an indefinite wait.
- The drawn, outline aesthetic is intentional. This is not a replacement for normal text; it is a decorative or brand-driven effect.
- You are working exclusively with lowercase `a-z` characters and spaces. Numbers, uppercase, punctuation, and most diacritics are not in the `letterPaths` dictionary and will be silently dropped.

**Reach for something else when:**

- **The text contains uppercase, numbers, or punctuation.** The component will skip unknown characters silently. If you need animated text with mixed character sets, use [Slide Up](/docs/animations/text/slide-up), [Blur In](/docs/animations/text/blur-in), or [Fade In](/docs/animations/text/fade-in) on a normal `<p>` or heading.
- **Long strings or full sentences.** A 10-word sentence produces 50+ paths. The total draw time at default speed is about `4.5 * 0.15 + 0.5 = well over 5 s` for a 30-character string. This is too slow for most user-facing text.
- **Body copy or any text that must be immediately readable.** The stroke-draw effect is invisible during animation; users cannot read partially drawn letters. Functional text must be readable on arrival.
- **You need responsive text sizing via `font-size`.** This component outputs an SVG scaled by its height class, not by font-size. Use the `h-*` utility to control size and ensure the SVG scales with the viewport.

## Accessibility notes

The SVG contains a `<title>` element that holds the original `children` string. Most screen readers will announce the `<title>` of an SVG if it is the first child, but support varies. Reinforce accessibility with `aria-label` on the `<svg>` and `role="img"`:

```tsx
<SvgTextDraw
  aria-label="hello world"
  role="img"
  className="h-12"
>
  hello world
</SvgTextDraw>
```

The `<motion.svg>` component forwards arbitrary props, so `aria-label` and `role` pass through to the DOM element.

**Reduced motion.** The component animates `pathLength` from 0 to 1 for each letter. For users who prefer reduced motion, skip the draw and render the final stroke immediately:

```tsx
"use client"
import { useReducedMotion } from "motion/react"
import { SvgTextDraw } from "@/components/animations/text/svg-text-draw"

function AccessibleSvgDraw({ children, ...props }: { children: string; [key: string]: unknown }) {
  const reduced = useReducedMotion()
  // When motion is reduced, pass speed=999 so transitions are near-instant
  return <SvgTextDraw speed={reduced ? 0.01 : 1} {...props}>{children}</SvgTextDraw>
}
```

**Color contrast.** The SVG uses `stroke="currentColor"` with `fill="none"`, so the strokes must have sufficient contrast against the background. Outlined strokes at `strokeWidth={3}` (the default) on a white background with a black stroke pass contrast comfortably. If you use low-contrast colors (e.g., light gray stroke on white), check WCAG 1.4.3.

## Performance considerations

- **One `<motion.path>` per character.** A 10-character string creates 10 independently animating paths. Each path animates `pathLength` and `opacity`, both handled by motion. `pathLength` maps to `stroke-dasharray`/`stroke-dashoffset`, which is a paint operation and cannot be fully composited. This is acceptable for short strings but expensive for long ones.
- **Fixed `letterWidth = 50`.** The SVG `viewBox` is `0 0 (text.length * 50) 60`. Long strings produce wide SVGs that browsers must paint at full width. Use `overflow: hidden` or a wrapping container with `max-w-*` if needed.
- **Single-shot.** Each path animates once on mount via its own `transition.delay`. After completion there is no ongoing cost.
- **`speed` multiplier.** `speed` scales all durations: `calc(0.5)` produces path duration `0.5 * speed`. Setting `speed={2}` halves both duration and per-character delay, completing the draw twice as fast but with shorter strokes per frame.

## Props

| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| `children` | `React.ReactNode` | - | The text content to highlight. |
| `className` | `string` | - | Additional CSS classes. |
| `delay` | `number` | `0` | Delay before animation starts (in seconds). |
| `duration` | `number` | `0.6` | Duration of the animation (in seconds). |
| `color` | `string` | `"#fde047"` | The color of the marker underline. |

## Features

- **Simple marker underline**: Clean 8px underline that animates from left to right
- **Smooth animation**: Custom easing for professional motion
- **Fully customizable**: Adjust color, duration, and delay
- **Minimal design**: No glow, shimmer, or background effects - just clean highlighting

## Use cases

`TextHighlight` renders a `<span>` containing the `children` text and an absolutely positioned `<motion.span>` acting as an 8 px rounded underline bar. The bar animates `scaleX` from `0` to `1` with `transformOrigin: "left"` using a custom spring-like ease `[0.16, 1, 0.3, 1]`. The color defaults to `#fde047` (Tailwind `yellow-300`). The bar is `bottom-0` inside a `pb-1` padded wrapper, so it sits just below the text baseline. Reach for it when:

- **Marketing copy keyword emphasis.** Highlight 1 to 3 keywords in a hero tagline or features section to draw the eye to the most important claim.
- **Tutorials and docs callouts.** Draw attention to a term being introduced in a step-by-step guide or onboarding walkthrough.
- **Testimonials.** Highlight the most impactful phrase in a customer quote to anchor the reader's eye.
- **Blog article pull-quotes.** Underline a short memorable phrase in a featured excerpt.
- **Animated section headings.** A highlight that sweeps in as a section enters the viewport adds a subtle editorial flourish.

Multiple `TextHighlight` instances in the same sentence can be staggered using the `delay` prop to produce a sequential "marker sweep" effect.

## When to use / when not to use

**Use text-highlight when:**

- The highlighted word or phrase is genuinely the most important in its context. Overusing it dilutes the effect.
- The text is inline within a sentence or heading, not a standalone block.
- You want a color accent that complements (not replaces) the text color. The bar sits below the text; the text color itself is unchanged.

**Reach for something else when:**

- **Long phrases or multiple lines.** The `scaleX` animation on a multi-line span will only draw a bar under the last line because `bottom: 0` is relative to the last line box. For multi-line highlights, apply one `TextHighlight` per line or use a background-highlight approach.
- **Critical information that must be highlighted for accessibility.** Color underlines are a visual-only cue. If the highlight is intended to convey "important" or "error" meaning, supplement with a semantic element (`<strong>`, `<em>`, `aria-label`).
- **You need a background fill behind the text (like a real marker highlighter).** This component uses an underline bar, not a background fill. For a full-width background fill that sweeps behind the text, you would need a custom implementation.
- **Navigation or interactive contexts.** Do not use `TextHighlight` on links or buttons, as the animated underline conflicts with the conventional hover underline affordance.

## Accessibility notes

The highlight is a purely visual decoration. The `<motion.span>` underline bar has no semantic meaning and is not announced by screen readers. The text content inside `TextHighlight` is read normally.

**Do not rely on the highlight to convey meaning alone.** If the highlight signals importance, pair it with a semantic element:

```tsx
<strong>
  <TextHighlight color="#fbbf24">critical update</TextHighlight>
</strong>
```

**Reduced motion.** The `scaleX` animation sweeps the bar horizontally. For users who have opted out of motion, render the bar in its final state immediately:

```tsx
"use client"
import { useReducedMotion } from "motion/react"
import { TextHighlight } from "@/components/animations/text/text-highlight"

function AccessibleHighlight({ children, color, ...props }: React.ComponentProps<typeof TextHighlight>) {
  const reduced = useReducedMotion()
  return (
    <TextHighlight
      color={color}
      duration={reduced ? 0 : 0.6}
      {...props}
    >
      {children}
    </TextHighlight>
  )
}
```

**Color contrast.** The `color` prop sets the bar's `backgroundColor`. The bar is 8 px tall below the text; it is a supporting decoration, not the text itself. However, ensure the bar color does not clash with the background to the point of invisibility. The default `#fde047` on a white background is visible but does not meet contrast requirements as a text color: this is acceptable because the bar is not text and carries no meaning independently.

## Performance considerations

- **Single `scaleX` animation.** The bar animates only `scaleX`, which is a CSS transform composited on the GPU. There is no paint cost after the initial render. This is the most performant animation in the text animation collection.
- **One extra DOM node per highlight.** Each `TextHighlight` instance adds two `<span>` elements (the wrapper and the bar). For a paragraph with 5 highlighted keywords, this is 10 extra nodes, which is negligible.
- **Single-shot.** The animation fires once on mount and does not loop. After it completes there is no ongoing cost.
- **Inline layout.** The wrapper `<span>` is `inline-block` with `pb-1`. This adds 4 px of bottom padding that slightly increases line height on the highlighted words. If you need tight line spacing, adjust with a negative margin or reduce `pb`.

# typewriter.mdx

Source: https://github.com/garvit1000/animbits/blob/main/content/docs/animations/text/typewriter.mdx

title: Typewriter Text
description: Text that types out character by character with optional cursor.

import { Preview, PreviewGrid } from '@/components/preview';
import { TextTypewriter } from '@/registry/new-york/animations/text/typewriter';

## Overview

The `TextTypewriter` creates a classic typewriter effect with optional blinking cursor.

## Preview

  background="default"
  code={`import { TextTypewriter } from "@/components/animations/text/typewriter"

<TextTypewriter className="text-2xl font-bold">
  Hello, I'm a typewriter effect!
</TextTypewriter>`}
  <TextTypewriter className="text-2xl font-bold">Hello, I'm a typewriter effect!</TextTypewriter>

## Installation

        ```bash
        npx shadcn@latest add @animbits/text-typewriter
        ```
        ```bash
        pnpm dlx shadcn@latest add @animbits/text-typewriter
        ```
        ```bash
        yarn dlx shadcn@latest add @animbits/text-typewriter
        ```
        ```bash
        bunx shadcn@latest add @animbits/text-typewriter
        ```
    **Step 1: Add the utility**

    ```tsx title="lib/utils.ts"
    import { clsx, type ClassValue } from "clsx"
    import { twMerge } from "tailwind-merge"

    export function cn(...inputs: ClassValue[]) {
      return twMerge(clsx(inputs))
    }
    ```

    **Step 2: Copy the component**

    ```tsx title="components/animations/text/typewriter.tsx"
"use client";
import * as React from "react";
import { motion, HTMLMotionProps } from "motion/react";
import { cn } from "@/lib/utils";
export interface TextTypewriterProps
  extends Omit<HTMLMotionProps<"p">, "children"> {
  children: string;
  delay?: number;
  speed?: number;
  cursor?: boolean;
  cursorChar?: string;
}
export function TextTypewriter({
  children,
  className,
  delay = 0,
  speed = 30,
  cursor = true,
  cursorChar = "|",
  ...props
}: TextTypewriterProps) {
  const [displayedText, setDisplayedText] = React.useState("");
  const [currentIndex, setCurrentIndex] = React.useState(0);
  const [isComplete, setIsComplete] = React.useState(false);
  React.useEffect(() => {
    if (currentIndex === 0) {
      const startTimeout = setTimeout(() => {
        setCurrentIndex(1);
      }, delay * 1000);
      return () => clearTimeout(startTimeout);
    }
    if (currentIndex <= children.length) {
      const timeout = setTimeout(() => {
        setDisplayedText(children.slice(0, currentIndex));
        setCurrentIndex(currentIndex + 1);
      }, 1000 / speed);
      return () => clearTimeout(timeout);
    } else {
      setIsComplete(true);
    }
  }, [currentIndex, children, delay, speed]);
  return (
    <motion.p className={cn(className)} {...props}>
      {displayedText}
      {cursor && !isComplete && (
        <motion.span
          animate={{ opacity: [1, 0] }}
          transition={{
            duration: 0.5,
            repeat: Infinity,
            repeatType: "reverse",
          }}
          className="inline-block"
        >
          {cursorChar}
        </motion.span>
      )}
    </motion.p>
  );
}

```

## Usage

```tsx
import { TextTypewriter } from "@/components/animations/text/typewriter"

<TextTypewriter>Hello World</TextTypewriter>
```

## Examples

### Different Speeds

<PreviewGrid cols={2}>
  <Preview background="dots" code={`<TextTypewriter speed={20}>Slow typing</TextTypewriter>`}>
    <TextTypewriter speed={20}>Slow typing effect</TextTypewriter>
  
  <Preview background="dots" code={`<TextTypewriter speed={50}>Fast typing</TextTypewriter>`}>
    <TextTypewriter speed={50}>Fast typing effect</TextTypewriter>
</PreviewGrid>

### Without Cursor

<Preview background="default" code={`<TextTypewriter cursor={false}>No cursor</TextTypewriter>`}>
  <TextTypewriter cursor={false} className="text-lg">Typing without a cursor</TextTypewriter>

## Props

| `children` | `string` | Required | Text to animate |
| `delay` | `number` | `0` | Delay before animation starts (seconds) |
| `speed` | `number` | `30` | Typing speed (characters per second) |
| `cursor` | `boolean` | `true` | Show blinking cursor |
| `cursorChar` | `string` | `"\|"` | Cursor character |

## Use cases

`TextTypewriter` types one character every `1000 / speed` milliseconds (default `speed=30` gives one character every ~33 ms). It uses `setDisplayedText` to progressively slice `children.slice(0, currentIndex)`, incrementing `currentIndex` via nested `setTimeout` calls. A blinking cursor (`opacity: [1, 0]` on a 0.5 s `reverse` repeat) is shown while incomplete and hidden when `isComplete` is true. Reach for it when:

- **Terminal or CLI aesthetic.** A command-line style interface where output "types out" is the most natural fit.
- **Chat or AI response simulation.** A message that appears to be written in real time creates engagement in chat UI demos and AI-powered interfaces.
- **Onboarding prompts.** A question or instruction that types out step-by-step draws the user's attention and implies interactivity.
- **Animated placeholder text.** A short "What do you want to build?" inside a search or prompt input that types itself as a hint.

The blinking cursor closely mimics a real terminal cursor, making the effect credible in developer-tool and CLI contexts.

## When to use / when not to use

**Use typewriter when:**

- The content is short (under 60 characters) and the reveal time is acceptable. At `speed=30`, a 50-character string completes in about 1.7 s.
- The user is expected to wait for the text to finish before acting, or the text is decorative.

**Reach for something else when:**

- **Essential information.** The typewriter effect actively delays reading. Error messages, status alerts, confirmations, and labels that users need to act on should be fully visible immediately. Use [Fade In](/docs/animations/text/fade-in) or static text.
- **Long text.** A 200-character paragraph at `speed=30` takes nearly 7 seconds to complete. Users will not wait. Increase `speed` significantly or skip the animation.
- **Frequently changing text.** Each `children` change resets `displayedText` and `currentIndex` to 0, replaying the full animation. If text updates on a short interval, the typewriter restarts every time and never settles.
- **You need the text to remain accessible during animation.** The partially typed text is the only thing in the DOM during the effect; incomplete characters are absent. For SEO or screen reader completeness, see the accessibility notes below.
- **Pages with multiple typewriters.** More than one simultaneously typing element is hard to follow. Sequence them with `delay` or pick only the most important one.

## Accessibility notes

The component renders only the typed characters so far in the DOM. Screen readers will either read partial text as the component types (if in a live region) or announce nothing until they encounter the element (which may read partial content). Both outcomes are suboptimal.

**Recommended pattern:** Add `aria-label` with the full final text so assistive technology announces the complete string immediately, regardless of animation state:

```tsx
<TextTypewriter
  aria-label="Hello, I'm a typewriter effect!"
  className="text-2xl font-bold"
>
  Hello, I'm a typewriter effect!
</TextTypewriter>
```

**Avoid `aria-live` around a typewriter.** An `aria-live="polite"` or `aria-live="assertive"` region will announce every character addition as a separate update, creating extremely chatty screen reader output. Use `aria-label` on the element itself and keep it outside live regions.

**Cursor accessibility.** The blinking cursor `<motion.span>` is a decorative character (`|`). It has no semantic role. Ensure it does not interfere with text selection or copying.

**Reduced motion.** The typewriter types characters over time, which is a sustained animation. For users who prefer reduced motion, skip straight to the final state:

```tsx
"use client"
import { useReducedMotion } from "motion/react"
import { TextTypewriter } from "@/components/animations/text/typewriter"

function AccessibleTypewriter({ children, ...props }: { children: string; [key: string]: unknown }) {
  const reduced = useReducedMotion()
  if (reduced) return <p {...props}>{children}</p>
  return <TextTypewriter {...props}>{children}</TextTypewriter>
}
```

## Performance considerations

- **Chained `setTimeout` calls.** The component drives itself via `useEffect` + `setTimeout`, incrementing one character per call at `1000 / speed` ms. This is one timer at a time, not a `setInterval`, so cleanup is clean and no timers pile up. However, each timer fires a React state update and re-render.
- **Re-render frequency.** At `speed=30`, the component re-renders ~30 times per second during typing. This is equivalent to a slow `requestAnimationFrame` loop. Keep the component tree under `TextTypewriter` simple to minimize reconciliation cost.
- **Cursor animation.** The cursor blink uses `motion.span` with `opacity: [1, 0]` on `repeat: Infinity`. After typing completes (`isComplete=true`), the cursor unmounts, ending the loop. No cleanup needed.
- **String length.** Total typing duration is `delay * 1000 + children.length * (1000 / speed)` ms. For very long strings, consider whether the user experience of waiting justifies the animation.

### Fast typing for a live label

```

# word-carousel.mdx

Source: https://github.com/garvit1000/animbits/blob/main/content/docs/animations/text/word-carousel.mdx

title: Word Carousel Text
description: Text that cycles through an array of words.

import { Preview } from '@/components/preview';

## Overview

The `TextWordCarousel` cycles through an array of words with smooth transitions.

        ```bash
        pnpm dlx shadcn@latest add @animbits/text-word-carousel
        ```
        ```bash

        ```bash
        bunx shadcn@latest add @animbits/text-word-carousel

    **Step 1: Copy the hook**

    ```tsx title="lib/hooks/use-word-carousel.ts"
    import * as React from "react"

    export interface UseWordCarouselOptions {
      words: string[]
      interval?: number
    }

    export function useWordCarousel(options: UseWordCarouselOptions) {
      const { words, interval = 2 } = options
      const [currentIndex, setCurrentIndex] = React.useState(0)

      React.useEffect(() => {
        const timer = setInterval(() => {
          setCurrentIndex((prev) => (prev + 1) % words.length)
        }, interval * 1000)

        return () => clearInterval(timer)
      }, [words.length, interval])

      return {
        currentWord: words[currentIndex],
        currentIndex,
        key: currentIndex,
      }
    }
    ```

    **Step 2: Copy the utility**

    ```tsx title="lib/utils.ts"
    import { type ClassValue, clsx } from "clsx"
    import { twMerge } from "tailwind-merge"

    export function cn(...inputs: ClassValue[]) {
      return twMerge(clsx(inputs))
    }
    ```

    **Step 3: Copy the component**

    ```tsx title="components/animations/text/word-carousel.tsx"
"use client";
import * as React from "react";
import { motion, AnimatePresence, HTMLMotionProps } from "motion/react";
import { cn } from "@/lib/utils";
import {
  useWordCarousel,
  type UseWordCarouselOptions,
} from "@/lib/use-word-carousel";
export interface TextWordCarouselProps
  extends Omit<HTMLMotionProps<"span">, "children">,
    UseWordCarouselOptions {
  duration?: number;
}
export function TextWordCarousel({
  words,
  interval,
  className,
  duration = 0.3,
  ...props
}: TextWordCarouselProps) {
  const { currentWord, key } = useWordCarousel({ words, interval });
  return (
    <span className={cn("inline-block relative", className)}>
      <AnimatePresence mode="wait">
        <motion.span
          key={key}
          initial={{ opacity: 0, y: 20 }}
          animate={{ opacity: 1, y: 0 }}
          exit={{ opacity: 0, y: -20 }}
          transition={{ duration }}
          className="inline-block"
          {...props}
        >
          {currentWord}
        </motion.span>
      </AnimatePresence>
    </span>
  );
}

```

## Props

| `words` | `string[]` | Required | Array of words to cycle through |
| `interval` | `number` | `2` | Time between words (seconds) |
| `duration` | `number` | `0.3` | Transition duration (seconds) |

## Use cases

`TextWordCarousel` cycles words using the `useWordCarousel` hook, which runs `setInterval` at `interval * 1000` ms (default `interval=2` seconds). The hook returns `{ currentWord, currentIndex, key }`. The component wraps the current word in `<AnimatePresence mode="wait">` so the outgoing word exits (`opacity: 0, y: -20`) before the incoming word enters (`opacity: 0, y: 20` to `opacity: 1, y: 0`), each with a `duration` of 0.3 s. Reach for it when:

- **Hero tagline with multiple value propositions.** Inline within a heading: "Build [Fast / Modern / Beautiful] websites" cycles through adjectives without changing the surrounding copy.
- **Tech stack showcase.** "Built with [React / Next.js / TypeScript]" in a footer or about section.
- **Dynamic benefit statement.** "Save time on [deployments / reviews / testing]" cycles through pain points addressed.
- **Rotating testimonial attribution.** A name or company cycling below a quote.

Unlike [DiaText](/docs/animations/text/dia-text), `TextWordCarousel` uses a plain `y` slide without the multi-color gradient trace, making it a simpler, less visually assertive choice.

## When to use / when not to use

**Use word-carousel when:**

- The visual treatment should be subtle. The default 0.3 s slide with no color change is appropriate when the surrounding heading already has strong typography.
- You want consistent, reliable cycling with a clean API: pass `words`, optionally set `interval` and `duration`, done.
- The words in your array are similar in length. Width changes between words can shift surrounding text unless you apply a fixed width to the carousel span.

**Reach for something else when:**

- **You want a dramatic visual trace on each word change.** Use [DiaText](/docs/animations/text/dia-text), which adds a multi-color gradient sweep during entry.
- **You need the word change to pause after the last word.** Both `TextWordCarousel` and `DiaText` loop indefinitely. There is no `loop={false}` prop.
- **More than 4 to 5 words in the array.** Users typically see only 2 to 3 words before losing interest; longer lists cycle out-of-sight content. Keep the list short enough that users notice the pattern within the first two rotations.
- **The text must be screen-reader friendly per-word.** The cycling text is announced continuously as words change, which can be disruptive for screen reader users. See accessibility notes below.
- **You need a specific easing or spring on the transition.** The component hardcodes the exit/enter with `duration` and default easing. For a spring-based word change, use [DiaText](/docs/animations/text/dia-text) which uses `stiffness: 300, damping: 30`.

## Accessibility notes

The cycling animation is inside a plain `<span>`. Screen readers may announce each word as it rotates, which is disruptive mid-sentence. To prevent this, mark the cycling span as `aria-hidden` and provide a static `aria-label` on the parent element:

```tsx
<h1 aria-label="Build Fast websites">
  Build{" "}
  <span aria-hidden="true">
    <TextWordCarousel words={["Fast", "Modern", "Beautiful"]} className="text-blue-500" />
  </span>{" "}
  websites
</h1>
```

If the cycling content genuinely communicates different meaning to all users (not just visual flair), use `aria-live="polite"` on a companion visually-hidden element that mirrors the current word, and keep the visual carousel `aria-hidden`:

```tsx
"use client"
import { useState } from "react"
import { TextWordCarousel } from "@/components/animations/text/word-carousel"

// This pattern announces words on change without over-announcing.
// Maintain currentWord in state via the hook if exposing it is needed.
```

**Reduced motion.** The component animates `y` (translate) and `opacity` on each word change, indefinitely. Wrap to disable cycling under reduced motion:

```tsx
"use client"
import { useReducedMotion } from "motion/react"
import { TextWordCarousel } from "@/components/animations/text/word-carousel"

function AccessibleCarousel({ words, ...props }: { words: string[] }) {
  const reduced = useReducedMotion()
  if (reduced) return <span {...props}>{words[0]}</span>
  return <TextWordCarousel words={words} {...props} />
}
```

## Performance considerations

- **`setInterval` runs indefinitely.** The interval is cleared on unmount via the effect cleanup. If the component mounts off-screen and stays mounted, it keeps cycling. Pair with an `IntersectionObserver` or a conditional mount if the carousel is below the fold for extended periods.
- **`AnimatePresence mode="wait"`.** The `wait` mode ensures the exit animation completes before the enter animation starts. At `duration=0.3`, each full transition (exit + enter) takes 0.6 s. During this window, both the exiting and entering `<motion.span>` are in the DOM briefly. At `interval=2 s`, this is well within tolerance.
- **No width stabilization by default.** The `<span>` wrapping the carousel does not fix its width to the widest word. If words differ in length, surrounding text will reflow on each change. Add `min-w-[Xch]` or `w-[Xch]` to the `className` to prevent layout shift:

```tsx
<TextWordCarousel
  words={["Fast", "Modern", "Beautiful"]}
  className="inline-block min-w-[9ch] text-center text-blue-500"
/>
```

# bounce.mdx

Source: https://github.com/garvit1000/animbits/blob/main/content/docs/hooks/bounce.mdx

title: useBounce
description: Bouncing animation for playful, attention-grabbing interactions.

import { Callout } from 'fumadocs-ui/components/callout';

## Overview

The `useBounce` hook creates a bouncing animation effect. Use it continuously for attention-grabbing elements or on hover for interactive feedback. Perfect for playful UIs, celebrations, and notifications.

<Callout type="info">
  **Playful interactions:** Bounce animations add personality and energy to your interface.
</Callout>

## Installation

        ```bash
        npx shadcn@latest add @animbits/hooks-use-bounce
        ```
        ```bash
        pnpm dlx shadcn@latest add @animbits/hooks-use-bounce
        ```
        ```bash
        yarn dlx shadcn@latest add @animbits/hooks-use-bounce
        ```
        ```bash
        bunx shadcn@latest add @animbits/hooks-use-bounce
        ```
    ```tsx title="lib/hooks/use-bounce.ts"
import { type MotionProps, type Easing } from "motion/react";

export interface UseBounceOptions {
  bounceHeight?: number;

  duration?: number;

  ease?: Easing | Easing[];

  repeat?: number;

  delay?: number;

  onHover?: boolean;
}

export function useBounce(options: UseBounceOptions = {}): MotionProps {
  const {
    bounceHeight = -20,
    duration = 0.6,
    ease = [0.68, -0.55, 0.265, 1.55],
    repeat = Infinity,
    delay = 0,
    onHover = false,
  } = options;

  if (onHover) {
    return {
      whileHover: {
        y: [0, bounceHeight, 0],
      },
      transition: {
        duration,
        ease,
      },
    };
  }

  return {
    animate: {
      y: [0, bounceHeight, 0],
    },
    transition: {
      duration,
      ease,
      repeat,
      delay,
    },
  };
}

```

## Usage

### Bounce on Hover

```tsx
import { motion } from "motion/react"
import { useBounce } from "@/lib/hooks/use-bounce"

export function HoverBounce() {
  const bounceProps = useBounce({ onHover: true })
  
  return (
    <motion.button {...bounceProps} className="btn">
      Hover me!
    </motion.button>
  )
}
```

### Limited Bounces

```tsx
import { motion } from "motion/react"
import { useBounce } from "@/lib/hooks/use-bounce"

export function ThreeBounces() {
  const bounceProps = useBounce({ 
    repeat: 3,  // Bounce 3 times then stop
    bounceHeight: -25 
  })
  
  return (
    <motion.div {...bounceProps}>
      Bounces 3 times
    </motion.div>
  )
}
```

## API Reference

### Options

| Option | Type | Default | Description |
|--------|------|---------|-------------|
| `bounceHeight` | `number` | `-20` | Bounce height in pixels (negative = up) |
| `duration` | `number` | `0.6` | Duration for one bounce cycle |
| `ease` | `string \| number[]` | `[0.68, -0.55, 0.265, 1.55]` | Bounce easing (cubic bezier) |
| `repeat` | `number` | `Infinity` | Number of times to repeat |
| `delay` | `number` | `0` | Delay before animation starts |
| `onHover` | `boolean` | `false` | Bounce on hover instead of continuous |

## Examples

### Subtle Bounce

```tsx
const bounceProps = useBounce({
  bounceHeight: -10,
  duration: 0.5,
})
```

### Energetic Bounce

```tsx
const bounceProps = useBounce({
  bounceHeight: -50,
  duration: 0.8,
})
```

### Quick Bounce

```tsx
const bounceProps = useBounce({
  bounceHeight: -15,
  duration: 0.4,
})
```

### Hover Bounce

```tsx
const bounceProps = useBounce({
  onHover: true,
  bounceHeight: -30,
})
```

## Common Use Cases

### Success Celebration

```tsx
<motion.div {...useBounce({ repeat: 3, bounceHeight: -30 })}>
  Success!
</motion.div>
```

### Notification Badge

```tsx
<motion.span {...useBounce({ bounceHeight: -15, duration: 0.5 })}>
  New
</motion.span>
```

### Interactive Button

```tsx
<motion.button {...useBounce({ onHover: true })}>
  Click me
</motion.button>
```

### Scroll Indicator

```tsx
<motion.div {...useBounce({ bounceHeight: 10, duration: 1 })}>
  ↓ Scroll down
</motion.div>
```

## Use cases

`useBounce` is component-agnostic: the returned `MotionProps` can be spread onto any `motion.*` element.

- **Notification badges and counters.** A small badge that bounces continuously draws the eye to new unread items without requiring the user to hunt for them.
- **Scroll-down indicators.** Spread the props onto a `motion.div` wrapping an arrow icon. Use `bounceHeight: 10` (positive, so it moves downward) to point the user toward more content.
- **Hover-activated icon buttons.** Pass `onHover: true` to a `motion.button` wrapping a social icon or action button. The bounce starts only on pointer entry, keeping the idle state clean.
- **Success or completion feedback.** After a form submits, mount a checkmark inside a `motion.div` with `repeat: 3` so it bounces three times and stops, signaling completion without looping forever.
- **Playful empty states.** A bouncing illustration in an empty-state screen adds personality without being permanently distracting.

## When to use / when not to use

**Use `useBounce` when:**

- You need the effect on a custom element that is not covered by a prebuilt component, such as a `motion.span` inside a heading or a `motion.li` in a custom list.
- You want to compose bouncing with another hook, for example combining it with `usePress` so an icon button bounces on hover and shrinks on click.
- You need fine control over `bounceHeight`, `repeat`, or `ease` that the prebuilt component does not expose.

**Reach for the prebuilt component when:**

- You just need a standard button or badge with a bounce and do not need to customize the host element or compose effects.

**Avoid `useBounce` when:**

- The element is large (a card or a section). A full-card bounce is disorienting; prefer [useHoverLift](/docs/hooks/hover-lift) for card-level hover feedback.
- Multiple elements bounce simultaneously. Stagger the `delay` option or switch to a one-time `repeat: 1` to avoid overwhelming the user.
- The bounce carries critical information by itself, such as "there are new items." Always pair it with a text label or badge count so non-animated experiences remain informative.

## Accessibility notes

The bounce animation animates the `y` transform, which is composited and does not affect the DOM structure or ARIA tree. However, perpetual motion can be distracting or cause vestibular discomfort.

Respect the user's reduced-motion preference by returning empty props when the OS setting is active:

```tsx
"use client"
import { motion } from "motion/react"
import { useReducedMotion } from "motion/react"
import { useBounce } from "@/lib/use-bounce"

export function NotificationBadge({ count }: { count: number }) {
  const reduced = useReducedMotion()
  const bounceProps = useBounce({ bounceHeight: -12, duration: 0.5 })

  return (
    <motion.span
      {...(reduced ? {} : bounceProps)}
      className="inline-flex h-5 w-5 items-center justify-center rounded-full bg-red-500 text-xs font-bold text-white"
    >
      {count}
    </motion.span>
  )
}
```

Additional guidance:

- When `onHover: true` is used on a `motion.button`, the bounce is triggered only by pointer interaction and does not run continuously, which is friendlier for motion-sensitive users.
- Do not rely on the bounce animation alone to convey meaning. Pair it with visible text or an icon so keyboard-only and screen reader users receive the same information.
- If the element wraps interactive content, ensure focus styles remain visible. Framer Motion's `whileHover` and `animate` do not remove focus outlines, but verify your CSS does not suppress them.

## Performance considerations

- `useBounce` animates only the `y` transform via the `animate` or `whileHover` props. Transforms run on the compositor thread and do not trigger layout or paint, so the animation stays at 60fps even on modest hardware.
- With the default `repeat: Infinity`, the animation keeps the compositor awake indefinitely. Conditionally render the element when the bounce is no longer needed, or use `repeat: 3` for a finite number of bounces, so the compositor thread is freed after the last cycle.
- When dozens of elements on a single page use `repeat: Infinity`, each schedules its own frame. Limit continuous bouncing to one or two focal elements per view.
- The custom cubic-bezier easing `[0.68, -0.55, 0.265, 1.55]` produces the overshoot that makes the bounce feel springy. It is evaluated in JavaScript by Framer Motion but has negligible CPU cost.

# fade-in.mdx

Source: https://github.com/garvit1000/animbits/blob/main/content/docs/hooks/fade-in.mdx

title: useFadeIn
description: Smooth fade-in entrance animation for elegant content reveals.

import { Callout } from 'fumadocs-ui/components/callout';

## Overview

The `useFadeIn` hook creates a smooth fade-in entrance animation. One of the most versatile and subtle animations, perfect for page loads, modal entrances, content reveals, and progressive disclosure.

<Callout type="info">
  **Subtle and elegant:** Fade-in is the most universally accepted animation, working well in any context.
</Callout>

## Installation

        ```bash
        npx shadcn@latest add @animbits/hooks-use-fade-in
        ```
        ```bash
        pnpm dlx shadcn@latest add @animbits/hooks-use-fade-in
        ```
        ```bash
        yarn dlx shadcn@latest add @animbits/hooks-use-fade-in
        ```
        ```bash
        bunx shadcn@latest add @animbits/hooks-use-fade-in
        ```
    Copy and paste the hook code into your project:

    ```tsx title="lib/hooks/use-fade-in.ts"
import { type MotionProps, type Easing } from "motion/react";

export interface UseFadeInOptions {
  duration?: number;

  delay?: number;

  from?: number;

  to?: number;

  ease?: Easing | Easing[];

  viewport?: "once" | "always";
}

export function useFadeIn(options: UseFadeInOptions = {}): MotionProps {
  const {
    duration = 0.5,
    delay = 0,
    from = 0,
    to = 1,
    ease = "easeOut",
    viewport = "once",
  } = options;

  return {
    initial: {
      opacity: from,
    },
    whileInView: {
      opacity: to,
    },
    viewport: {
      once: viewport === "once",
    },
    transition: {
      duration,
      delay,
      ease,
    },
  };
}

```

### Returns

Returns `MotionProps` object containing:
- `initial` - Initial opacity state (0)
- `whileInView` - Target opacity state (1)
- `viewport` - Viewport animation config
- `transition` - Animation transition config

## Composing with Other Hooks

Combine fade with other animations:

```tsx
import { useFadeIn } from "@/lib/hooks/use-fade-in"
import { useSlideIn } from "@/lib/hooks/use-slide-in"

// Fade + Slide
const fade = useFadeIn({ duration: 0.6 })
const slide = useSlideIn({ direction: "left", distance: 30 })

const combined = {
  initial: {
    ...fade.initial,
    ...slide.initial,
  },
  whileInView: {
    ...fade.whileInView,
    ...slide.whileInView,
  },
  transition: fade.transition,
}

<motion.div {...combined}>Fade + Slide</motion.div>
```

## Use cases

`useFadeIn` returns `MotionProps` with `initial`, `whileInView`, `viewport`, and `transition` fields. Spread them on any `motion.*` element and the element fades in as it enters the viewport.

- **Hero sections and above-the-fold headings.** A `motion.section` or `motion.h1` with `useFadeIn({ duration: 0.8 })` announces content without jarring the user on page load.
- **Image galleries.** Each `motion.img` can receive `useFadeIn({ delay: index * 0.08 })` to stagger the reveal as the user scrolls down a grid.
- **Feature sections in a landing page.** Apply the hook to alternating `motion.article` or `motion.div` columns with `direction`-specific stagger delays.
- **Modal overlays.** Mount a `motion.div` backdrop with `useFadeIn({ duration: 0.2, viewport: "always" })` so the overlay fades in every time the modal opens, not just the first time.
- **Lazy-loaded content panels.** Sections that fetch data on scroll can fade in their content once it resolves, hiding the empty skeleton state transition.

## When to use / when not to use

**Use `useFadeIn` directly when:**

- The element you want to animate is not a standard prebuilt component, for example a `motion.aside` sidebar or a custom `motion.figure`.
- You want to combine the fade with another hook such as [useSlideIn](/docs/hooks/slide-in): merge the two `MotionProps` objects by spreading `initial` and `whileInView` from both.
- You need `viewport: "always"` so the element fades in every time it enters the viewport, not just the first.

**Avoid `useFadeIn` when:**

- The wait would be over 2 seconds. A slow fade delays content visibility and can frustrate users on slow connections.
- You are fading in text that is part of the primary content hierarchy. Screen readers render all text regardless of opacity, but sighted users may be confused if important text is invisible for a perceptible moment.
- You need a combined entrance with translation. Use [useSlideIn](/docs/hooks/slide-in) instead, which handles both opacity and translate together, or compose both hooks manually.

## Accessibility notes

`useFadeIn` uses `whileInView` and animates only `opacity`. The element exists in the DOM from mount and is accessible to screen readers even while invisible. However, there are still considerations:

Honor the user's reduced-motion preference by returning plain props with no animation:

```tsx
"use client"
import { motion } from "motion/react"
import { useReducedMotion } from "motion/react"
import { useFadeIn } from "@/lib/use-fade-in"

export function FeatureCard({ title, body }: { title: string; body: string }) {
  const reduced = useReducedMotion()
  const fadeProps = useFadeIn({ duration: 0.6 })

  return (
    <motion.div
      {...(reduced ? {} : fadeProps)}
      className="rounded-xl border border-neutral-200 p-6 dark:border-neutral-800"
    >
      <h3 className="font-semibold">{title}</h3>
      <p className="mt-2 text-sm text-neutral-500">{body}</p>
    </motion.div>
  )
}
```

Additional guidance:

- Do not fade in interactive elements such as buttons or links unless they become fully opaque before the user can reach them via keyboard Tab navigation. If they can be focused while still semi-transparent, add `pointer-events: none` during the animation.
- The default `from: 0` means the element starts fully transparent. Any content inside is still in the DOM, so `Ctrl+F` in-browser search and screen readers can still find it.
- Avoid `viewport: "always"` on sections that contain forms or other interactive controls. Reflowing the opacity on every scroll can momentarily hide UI state.

## Performance considerations

- `useFadeIn` animates only `opacity`, which is a compositor property. No layout or paint is triggered, and the animation runs off the main thread.
- The hook uses `whileInView`, which relies on an `IntersectionObserver` under the hood in Framer Motion. This is far cheaper than a scroll event listener and does not block the main thread.
- With `viewport: "once"` (the default), the observer disconnects after the first intersection, eliminating any ongoing cost.
- Stagger patterns calling `useFadeIn` inside a `.map()` create one `IntersectionObserver` per element. For very large lists (50 or more items) consider batching with Framer Motion's `staggerChildren` inside a `variants` object instead.
- `opacity` transitions do not affect `will-change`. You do not need to add `will-change: opacity` manually; Framer Motion handles compositing hints internally.

# hover-glow.mdx

Source: https://github.com/garvit1000/animbits/blob/main/content/docs/hooks/hover-glow.mdx

title: useHoverGlow
description: Add a glowing shadow effect on hover to any element.

import { Callout } from 'fumadocs-ui/components/callout';

## Overview

The `useHoverGlow` hook adds a colored glow effect (via box-shadow) when hovering over an element. Perfect for creating attention-grabbing interactive elements.

## Installation

        ```bash
        npx shadcn@latest add @animbits/hooks-use-hover-glow
        ```
        ```bash
        pnpm dlx shadcn@latest add @animbits/hooks-use-hover-glow
        ```
        ```bash
        yarn dlx shadcn@latest add @animbits/hooks-use-hover-glow
        ```
        ```bash
        bunx shadcn@latest add @animbits/hooks-use-hover-glow
        ```
    Copy the hook into your project:

    ```tsx title="lib/hooks/use-hover-glow.ts"
import { type MotionProps, type Easing } from "motion/react";

export interface UseHoverGlowOptions {
  glowColor?: string;

  glowBlur?: number;

  glowSpread?: number;

  duration?: number;

  ease?: Easing | Easing[];

  scale?: number;

  innerGlow?: boolean;
}

export function useHoverGlow(options: UseHoverGlowOptions = {}): MotionProps {
  const {
    glowColor = "rgba(59, 130, 246, 0.5)",
    glowBlur = 20,
    glowSpread = 5,
    duration = 0.3,
    ease = "easeOut",
    scale = 1.02,
    innerGlow = false,
  } = options;

  const baseShadow = "0 2px 8px rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.1)";
  const glowShadow = `0 0 ${glowBlur}px ${glowSpread}px ${glowColor}`;
  const innerGlowShadow = innerGlow
    ? `inset 0 0 ${glowBlur / 2}px ${glowColor}`
    : "";

  const hoverShadow = innerGlow
    ? `${baseShadow}, ${glowShadow}, ${innerGlowShadow}`
    : `${baseShadow}, ${glowShadow}`;

  return {
    initial: {
      scale: 1,
      boxShadow: baseShadow,
    },
    whileHover: {
      scale,
      boxShadow: hoverShadow,
    },
    transition: {
      duration,
      ease,
    },
  };
}

```

## Usage

### Basic Example

```tsx
import { motion } from "motion/react"
import { useHoverGlow } from "@/lib/hooks/use-hover-glow"

export function GlowButton() {
  const glowProps = useHoverGlow()
  
  return (
    <motion.button 
      {...glowProps}
      className="inline-flex h-11 items-center gap-2 rounded-lg bg-blue-600 px-6 text-sm font-semibold text-white"
    >
      Hover for glow
    </motion.button>
  )
}
```

### Custom Colors

```tsx
import { motion } from "motion/react"
import { useHoverGlow } from "@/lib/hooks/use-hover-glow"

export function ColoredGlows() {
  const blueGlow = useHoverGlow({ 
    glowColor: "rgba(59, 130, 246, 0.6)" 
  })
  
  const purpleGlow = useHoverGlow({ 
    glowColor: "rgba(168, 85, 247, 0.6)" 
  })
  
  const greenGlow = useHoverGlow({ 
    glowColor: "rgba(34, 197, 94, 0.6)" 
  })
  
  return (
    <div className="flex gap-4">
      <motion.button {...blueGlow}>Blue</motion.button>
      <motion.button {...purpleGlow}>Purple</motion.button>
      <motion.button {...greenGlow}>Green</motion.button>
    </div>
  )
}
```

## API Reference

### Options

| Option | Type | Default | Description |
|--------|------|---------|-------------|
| `glowColor` | `string` | `"rgba(59, 130, 246, 0.5)"` | CSS color for the glow |
| `glowSize` | `number` | `20` | Glow spread in pixels |
| `duration` | `number` | `0.3` | Animation duration in seconds |
| `ease` | `string \| number[]` | `"easeOut"` | Animation easing |

  glowSize: 40,
})
```

### Subtle Glow

```

### Combine with Lift

```tsx

## Use cases

`useHoverGlow` returns `MotionProps` with `initial`, `whileHover`, and `transition` fields. On idle, it sets a faint base shadow (`0 2px 8px rgba(0,0,0,0.1)`) and `scale: 1`. On hover, it transitions to the colored glow shadow and `scale` (default `1.02`).

- **CTA buttons.** A blue glow around a primary action button gives it a "lit" quality that draws the eye without relying solely on color. Pass `glowColor: "rgba(59, 130, 246, 0.6)"` to match a blue brand.
- **Product cards in an e-commerce grid.** A subtle glow on a card signals interactivity when the card itself has no obvious click affordance beyond the image.
- **Dark-mode dashboards and analytics widgets.** A colored glow reads particularly well against dark backgrounds, where box-shadows on light themes would be invisible.
- **Feature highlight tiles.** Each tile can receive a different `glowColor` corresponding to its category color, creating visual grouping through hover state.
- **Icon buttons in toolbars.** Keep `glowBlur: 10` and `glowSpread: 2` small for tight toolbar buttons so the glow stays contained within the button's hit area.

## When to use / when not to use

**Use `useHoverGlow` directly when:**

- The element is a custom component that does not have a prebuilt AnimBits wrapper.
- You want to compose the glow with [useHoverLift](/docs/hooks/hover-lift) or [usePress](/docs/hooks/press) by merging their `whileHover` objects.
- You need `innerGlow: true` for a UI where the element should appear to glow from within (useful for neon-style dark UI).

**Avoid `useHoverGlow` when:**

- The element is purely text without a visible bounding box. A glow on an inline `<span>` without padding or border-radius looks broken because the box-shadow follows the text line.
- The background is already heavily colored. A blue glow on a blue card is invisible; adjust `glowColor` or switch to [useHoverLift](/docs/hooks/hover-lift) to rely on shadow depth instead.
- The user's pointer never hovers the element, such as on a touch-only device. The glow only triggers via `whileHover`, so touch users see no feedback at all. Pair with [usePress](/docs/hooks/press) for the tap state.

## Accessibility notes

`useHoverGlow` animates `scale` and `boxShadow`. Neither affects the element's position in the DOM or ARIA properties. However:

- The glow is purely visual and must not be the sole indicator of hover state for users who cannot perceive color or shadow. Ensure the element also has a CSS `:focus-visible` outline.
- Respect `prefers-reduced-motion`. The scale change in `whileHover` (default `1.02`) is minor but still motion. Return empty props when the preference is set:

```tsx
"use client"
import { motion } from "motion/react"
import { useReducedMotion } from "motion/react"
import { useHoverGlow } from "@/lib/use-hover-glow"

export function GlowCard({ children }: { children: React.ReactNode }) {
  const reduced = useReducedMotion()
  const glowProps = useHoverGlow({ glowColor: "rgba(168, 85, 247, 0.5)" })

  return (
    <motion.div
      {...(reduced ? {} : glowProps)}
      className="rounded-xl border border-neutral-200 p-6 focus-visible:outline focus-visible:outline-2 focus-visible:outline-offset-2 focus-visible:outline-purple-500"
    >
      {children}
    </motion.div>
  )
}
```

- When `innerGlow: true` is set, the hook adds an inset box-shadow. Confirm that the inner glow does not obscure text or interactive controls inside the element.

## Performance considerations

- `useHoverGlow` animates `scale` and `boxShadow`. Scale is a transform and runs on the compositor. `boxShadow`, however, is not a transform: animating it triggers a repaint on each frame. For most elements this is imperceptible, but avoid animating `boxShadow` on elements that repaint a large area (full-width banners, hero images).
- The `duration` default is `0.3s` with `"easeOut"`. This is short enough that any repaint cost from `boxShadow` is limited to a few frames at most.
- The `initial` state sets a base `boxShadow`. This means the element always has a shadow in the DOM, which may affect layout in some flex/grid containers if `overflow: hidden` is not set. Check that the base shadow does not cause unexpected clipping.
- Memoize the returned props if the parent component re-renders often, because `useHoverGlow` reconstructs its return object on every call.

### Warm amber glow for a feature card

```tsx

export function FeatureCard({ icon, title }: { icon: React.ReactNode; title: string }) {

    glowColor: "rgba(251, 146, 60, 0.5)",
    glowBlur: 24,
    glowSpread: 4,
    scale: 1.01,
    duration: 0.25,
  })

  return (
    <motion.div {...glowProps} className="rounded-2xl border border-neutral-100 bg-white p-6 dark:border-neutral-800 dark:bg-neutral-900">
      <div className="mb-3 text-orange-400">{icon}</div>
      <h3 className="font-semibold">{title}</h3>
    </motion.div>
  )
}
```

### Neon inner glow for a dark-mode button

```tsx

# hover-lift.mdx

Source: https://github.com/garvit1000/animbits/blob/main/content/docs/hooks/hover-lift.mdx

title: useHoverLift
description: Component-agnostic hover lift animation hook that adds elevation and shadow effects on hover.

import { Callout } from 'fumadocs-ui/components/callout';

## Overview

The `useHoverLift` hook returns Framer Motion props that add a lift effect with optional shadow when hovering over an element. It works with any HTML element via `motion` components.

<Callout type="info">
  **Component-agnostic:** This hook works with buttons, cards, divs, articles, or any other element. Not locked into specific use cases.
</Callout>

## Installation

        ```bash
        npx shadcn@latest add @animbits/hooks-use-hover-lift
        ```
        ```bash
        pnpm dlx shadcn@latest add @animbits/hooks-use-hover-lift
        ```
        ```bash
        yarn dlx shadcn@latest add @animbits/hooks-use-hover-lift
        ```
        ```bash
        bunx shadcn@latest add @animbits/hooks-use-hover-lift
        ```
    Copy and paste the hook code into your project:

    ```tsx title="lib/hooks/use-hover-lift.ts"
import { type MotionProps, type Easing } from "motion/react";

export interface UseHoverLiftOptions {
  liftDistance?: number;

  addShadow?: boolean;

  shadowIntensity?: number;

  duration?: number;

  ease?: Easing | Easing[];

  scale?: number;
}

export function useHoverLift(options: UseHoverLiftOptions = {}): MotionProps {
  const {
    liftDistance = 8,
    addShadow = true,
    shadowIntensity = 0.3,
    duration = 0.2,
    ease = "easeOut",
    scale = 1,
  } = options;

  const shadowBlur = liftDistance * 2;
  const shadowSpread = Math.round(liftDistance / 4);

  return {
    initial: {
      y: 0,
      scale: 1,
      boxShadow: addShadow
        ? `0 2px 4px rgba(0, 0, 0, ${shadowIntensity * 0.3})`
        : undefined,
    },
    whileHover: {
      y: -liftDistance,
      scale,
      boxShadow: addShadow
        ? `0 ${shadowBlur}px ${shadowBlur + shadowSpread}px rgba(0, 0, 0, ${shadowIntensity})`
        : undefined,
    },
    transition: {
      duration,
      ease,
    },
  };
}

```

      className="p-6 bg-white rounded-lg border"
    >

      <p>This card lifts on hover</p>
    </motion.div>
  )
}
```

### Returns

- `initial` - Initial animation state
- `whileHover` - Hover animation state
- `transition` - Animation transition config

  duration: 0.15,

```

### Dramatic Lift

```

## Composing with Other Hooks

Combine with other animation hooks for complex effects:

```tsx
import { useHoverLift } from "@/lib/hooks/use-hover-lift"
import { useHoverGlow } from "@/lib/hooks/use-hover-glow"

export function FancyCard() {
  const lift = useHoverLift({ liftDistance: 12 })
  const glow = useHoverGlow({ glowColor: "rgba(59, 130, 246, 0.5)" })
  
  // Merge the animations
  const combined = {
    ...lift,
    whileHover: {
      ...lift.whileHover,
      ...glow.whileHover,
    },
  }
  
  return (
    <motion.div {...combined} className="card">
      Lift + Glow effect!
    </motion.div>
  )
}
```

## Use cases

`useHoverLift` returns `MotionProps` with `initial`, `whileHover`, and `transition` fields. The `initial` state sets `y: 0` and a faint base shadow. On hover, the element moves up by `liftDistance` pixels (default `8`) and the shadow deepens proportionally: `shadowBlur` is `liftDistance * 2` and `shadowSpread` is `Math.round(liftDistance / 4)`.

- **Content cards and article teasers.** A card grid where each card lifts slightly on hover communicates "this is clickable" without adding a separate hover color change that may conflict with the card's background.
- **Product tiles in a shop.** Combine `liftDistance: 12` and `scale: 1.02` on a `motion.article` wrapping a product image and price to give a tactile "pick it up" feel.
- **Nav bar links with pill backgrounds.** A link inside a pill-shaped `motion.a` with `liftDistance: 4` and `addShadow: false` creates a subtle floating cue without a distracting shadow.
- **Gallery images.** Use `liftDistance: 16` and `scale: 1.04` on `motion.img` in an image grid for a lightbox-preview affordance.
- **Dashboard stat cards.** A minimal lift (`liftDistance: 4`, `shadowIntensity: 0.15`) keeps the dashboard calm while still making each card feel interactive.

## When to use / when not to use

**Use `useHoverLift` directly when:**

- You need the lift effect on a custom element, such as a `motion.article`, `motion.a`, or a third-party card component wrapped in `motion()`.
- You want to compose lift with another hook, for example merging the `whileHover` from `useHoverLift` and [useHoverGlow](/docs/hooks/hover-glow) to achieve both lift and a colored shadow in a single `motion.*` element.
- You need `addShadow: false` because the element already has a box-shadow from CSS that you want to keep.

**Reach for a prebuilt component when:**

- You are building a standard button and do not need to customize the host element. The [HoverLift button](/docs/animations/buttons/lift) wraps `useHoverLift` with sensible defaults and a ready-to-use markup structure.
- You are building a standard hoverable card. The [HoverLift card](/docs/animations/cards/hover-lift) component is pre-styled.

**Avoid `useHoverLift` when:**

- The element is inside a container with `overflow: hidden` and the shadow would be clipped. Either set `addShadow: false` or ensure the container has enough padding.
- The element is very large (full-width or full-height). A `liftDistance` of 8px on a 100vw element creates a jarring shift; reduce `liftDistance` to 2 to 4px or disable the effect entirely for large viewports.

## Accessibility notes

`useHoverLift` uses `whileHover`, which is pointer-driven. Keyboard users who focus the element but do not hover it will not see the lift. This is acceptable as long as the element has a visible `:focus-visible` outline that provides equivalent feedback.

Respect `prefers-reduced-motion` by returning empty props when the OS preference is set. The `y` translation is the part most likely to cause discomfort:

```tsx
"use client"
import { motion } from "motion/react"
import { useReducedMotion } from "motion/react"
import { useHoverLift } from "@/lib/use-hover-lift"

export function ProjectCard({ title, description }: { title: string; description: string }) {
  const reduced = useReducedMotion()
  const liftProps = useHoverLift({ liftDistance: 8, shadowIntensity: 0.25 })

  return (
    <motion.div
      {...(reduced ? {} : liftProps)}
      className="cursor-pointer rounded-xl border border-neutral-200 p-6 focus-visible:outline focus-visible:outline-2 focus-visible:outline-blue-500 dark:border-neutral-800"
    >
      <h3 className="font-semibold">{title}</h3>
      <p className="mt-2 text-sm text-neutral-500">{description}</p>
    </motion.div>
  )
}
```

Additional guidance:

- Ensure that interactive elements inside the card (links, buttons) remain focusable in their natural tab order. `useHoverLift` does not alter `tabIndex` or ARIA properties.
- Do not use the lift alone to indicate that an element is clickable. Pair it with an appropriate ARIA role or a semantic element (`<button>`, `<a>`).

## Performance considerations

- `useHoverLift` animates `y` (a transform) and `scale` (a transform). Both run on the compositor. No layout is triggered.
- The `boxShadow` animation in `whileHover` causes a repaint on each frame. For most card-sized elements, this cost is negligible. Avoid using `addShadow: true` on full-width or very large elements.
- The `duration` default is `0.2s`. Short transitions minimize the total number of repaint frames for `boxShadow`.
- The hook returns a new object reference on every render. If the parent component re-renders frequently (for example, it subscribes to a real-time data stream), memoize the options object passed to `useHoverLift` with `useMemo` to avoid unnecessary recalculation.

# magnetic.mdx

Source: https://github.com/garvit1000/animbits/blob/main/content/docs/hooks/magnetic.mdx

title: useMagnetic
description: Magnetic cursor follow effect that makes elements smoothly follow the mouse with spring physics.

import { Callout } from 'fumadocs-ui/components/callout';

## Overview

The `useMagnetic` hook creates a magnetic attraction effect where elements smoothly follow the cursor on hover using spring physics. Perfect for creating engaging, interactive UI elements.

<Callout type="info">
  **Spring-based animation:** Uses Framer Motion's spring physics for natural, fluid movement.
</Callout>

## Installation

        ```bash
        npx shadcn@latest add @animbits/hooks-use-magnetic
        ```
        ```bash
        pnpm dlx shadcn@latest add @animbits/hooks-use-magnetic
        ```
        ```bash
        yarn dlx shadcn@latest add @animbits/hooks-use-magnetic
        ```
        ```bash
        bunx shadcn@latest add @animbits/hooks-use-magnetic
        ```
    Copy and paste the hook code into your project:

    ```tsx title="lib/hooks/use-magnetic.ts"
import * as React from "react";
import { useMotionValue, useSpring } from "motion/react";

export interface UseMagneticOptions {
  strength?: number;
  stiffness?: number;
  damping?: number;
}

export function useMagnetic(options: UseMagneticOptions = {}) {
  const { strength = 30, stiffness = 150, damping = 15 } = options;

  const ref = React.useRef<HTMLElement>(null);
  const x = useMotionValue(0);
  const y = useMotionValue(0);

  const springConfig = { damping, stiffness };
  const springX = useSpring(x, springConfig);
  const springY = useSpring(y, springConfig);

  const handleMouseMove = (e: React.MouseEvent<HTMLElement>) => {
    if (!ref.current) return;

    const rect = ref.current.getBoundingClientRect();
    const centerX = rect.left + rect.width / 2;
    const centerY = rect.top + rect.height / 2;

    const distanceX = e.clientX - centerX;
    const distanceY = e.clientY - centerY;

    x.set(distanceX * (strength / 100));
    y.set(distanceY * (strength / 100));
  };

  const handleMouseLeave = () => {
    x.set(0);
    y.set(0);
  };

  const magneticProps = {
    style: { x: springX, y: springY },
    onMouseMove: handleMouseMove,
    onMouseLeave: handleMouseLeave,
  };

  return { magneticProps, ref };
}

```

## Usage

### Basic Example

```tsx
import { motion } from "motion/react"
import { useMagnetic } from "@/lib/hooks/use-magnetic"

export function MagneticButton() {
  const { magneticProps, ref } = useMagnetic()
  
  return (
    <motion.button 
      ref={ref}
      {...magneticProps}
      className="inline-flex h-11 items-center gap-2 rounded-lg bg-blue-600 px-6 text-sm font-semibold text-white"
    >
      Hover me - I follow your cursor!
    </motion.button>
  )
}
```

### With Custom Strength

```tsx

export function StrongMagnet() {
  const { magneticProps, ref } = useMagnetic({
    strength: 50, // Stronger attraction
    stiffness: 200,
    damping: 20,
  })
  
  return (
    <motion.div 
      ref={ref}
      {...magneticProps}
      className="card"
    >
      <h3>Strong Magnetic Card</h3>
      <p>Follows cursor more aggressively</p>
    </motion.div>
  )
}
```

          <HeartIcon />
        </motion.div>
      )
    }
    ```
  <Tab value="Link">

## Combining with Other Effects

Combine magnetic effect with other animations:

```tsx
import { useMagnetic } from "@/lib/hooks/use-magnetic"
import { useHoverLift } from "@/lib/hooks/use-hover-lift"

export function MagneticLiftButton() {
  const { magneticProps, ref } = useMagnetic()
  const liftProps = useHoverLift()
  
  return (
    <motion.button

      {...magneticProps}
      {...liftProps}
      className="fancy-button"

    </motion.button>
  )
}
```

## Use cases

`useMagnetic` returns `{ magneticProps, ref }`. The `magneticProps` object contains a `style` with spring-driven `x` and `y` MotionValues, plus `onMouseMove` and `onMouseLeave` event handlers. Attach `ref` to the element so the hook can read its bounding rect.

- **Hero CTA buttons.** A primary action button that follows the cursor by a few pixels feels alive and invites a click more than a static button.
- **Social media icon links in a footer or profile page.** Small icons with `strength: 40` and `stiffness: 200` respond snappily to precise cursor movement.
- **Navigation pill links.** A subtle `strength: 20` on nav links creates a soft floating effect without moving the link far enough to confuse the user about its position.
- **Logo mark in a header.** A logo that gently shifts toward the cursor adds personality to an otherwise static header without interfering with the nav layout.
- **Floating action buttons.** An FAB with `strength: 35` and `damping: 12` gives a satisfying pull-toward-you feel before the user clicks.

## When to use / when not to use

**Use `useMagnetic` directly when:**

- You need the magnetic effect on a custom element, such as a `motion.a` or a styled icon wrapper, that is not covered by a prebuilt component.
- You want to compose the magnetic translation with another hook: because `magneticProps.style` sets `x` and `y` as MotionValues, you can pass those values into `useTransform` for derived effects.

**Avoid `useMagnetic` when:**

- The element is inside a scrollable container. The hook uses `getBoundingClientRect()` to compute the center; inside a scrolled container the `rect.left` and `rect.top` values are correct, but rapid scroll while hovering can cause visible jumps.
- Multiple adjacent elements each have the magnetic effect and their movement radius overlaps. Users hovering the gap between two magnetic elements can trigger both, making both elements shift unpredictably.
- The surface is touch-only. The `onMouseMove` handler never fires on a touch device, so the element appears completely static. Pair with [usePress](/docs/hooks/press) for touch feedback.
- The element is a form input or a text area. Mouse-following translation on an input moves the entire field, making it hard to click a specific character position.

## Accessibility notes

`useMagnetic` attaches `onMouseMove` and `onMouseLeave` event handlers that animate `x` and `y` via MotionValues. These are pointer-driven and have no effect on keyboard navigation.

- The magnetic effect is decorative. Do not use it to signal interactivity for keyboard users. Rely on semantic HTML (`<button>`, `<a>`) and visible `:focus-visible` styles for keyboard affordance.
- Respect `prefers-reduced-motion`. The spring-based motion can cause vestibular discomfort, especially with high `strength` values. When the preference is set, return static props with no movement:

```tsx
"use client"
import { motion } from "motion/react"
import { useReducedMotion } from "motion/react"
import { useMagnetic } from "@/lib/use-magnetic"

export function MagneticCTA({ label }: { label: string }) {
  const reduced = useReducedMotion()
  const { magneticProps, ref } = useMagnetic({ strength: 30 })

  return (
    <motion.button
      ref={ref}
      {...(reduced ? {} : magneticProps)}
      className="rounded-xl bg-blue-600 px-8 py-3 text-sm font-semibold text-white focus-visible:outline focus-visible:outline-2 focus-visible:outline-offset-2 focus-visible:outline-blue-500"
    >
      {label}
    </motion.button>
  )
}
```

- Because the element translates away from its original position, ensure that its hover hitbox remains consistent. Framer Motion keeps the layout anchor at the original position, so the painted element may appear to drift outside its clickable area at large `strength` values (above 50). Keep `strength` at or below 40 for buttons that need precise clicking.

## Performance considerations

- `useMagnetic` drives `x` and `y` via `useMotionValue` and `useSpring`. Both are MotionValues that bypass React renders entirely. The spring interpolation is performed in Framer Motion's internal rAF loop and only updates the DOM via direct style writes. No component re-render occurs on mouse move.
- `onMouseMove` fires on every pointer move event. Framer Motion's MotionValue batches updates in its animation frame loop, so even rapid cursor movement does not schedule extra frames.
- Each `useMagnetic` call creates two springs. On pages with many magnetic elements, the total number of active springs grows linearly. Keep the number of simultaneously visible magnetic elements low (single digits) to avoid saturating the animation frame budget.
- When the element unmounts, Framer Motion automatically cancels the springs and removes the listeners. No manual cleanup is needed.

# parallax-tilt.mdx

Source: https://github.com/garvit1000/animbits/blob/main/content/docs/hooks/parallax-tilt.mdx

title: useParallaxTilt
description: 3D parallax tilt effect that creates depth and dimension based on mouse position.

import { Callout } from 'fumadocs-ui/components/callout';

## Overview

The `useParallaxTilt` hook creates a stunning 3D tilt effect where elements rotate based on mouse position, complete with dynamic shadows for enhanced depth perception.

<Callout type="info">
  **3D Transform:** Uses CSS 3D transforms with `preserve-3d` for realistic depth effects.
</Callout>

## Installation

        ```bash
        npx shadcn@latest add @animbits/hooks-use-parallax-tilt
        ```
        ```bash
        pnpm dlx shadcn@latest add @animbits/hooks-use-parallax-tilt
        ```
        ```bash
        yarn dlx shadcn@latest add @animbits/hooks-use-parallax-tilt
        ```
        ```bash
        bunx shadcn@latest add @animbits/hooks-use-parallax-tilt
        ```
    ```tsx title="lib/hooks/use-parallax-tilt.ts"
import * as React from "react";
import { useMotionValue, useSpring, useTransform } from "motion/react";

export interface UseParallaxTiltOptions {
  maxTilt?: number;
  duration?: number;
  shadowIntensity?: number;
  stiffness?: number;
  damping?: number;
}

export function useParallaxTilt(options: UseParallaxTiltOptions = {}) {
  const {
    maxTilt = 15,
    duration = 0.3,
    shadowIntensity = 0.3,
    stiffness = 300,
    damping = 30,
  } = options;

  const ref = React.useRef<HTMLElement>(null);
  const x = useMotionValue(0);
  const y = useMotionValue(0);

  const mouseXSpring = useSpring(x, { stiffness, damping });
  const mouseYSpring = useSpring(y, { stiffness, damping });

  const rotateX = useTransform(mouseYSpring, [-0.5, 0.5], [maxTilt, -maxTilt]);
  const rotateY = useTransform(mouseXSpring, [-0.5, 0.5], [-maxTilt, maxTilt]);

  const shadowX = useTransform(mouseXSpring, [-0.5, 0.5], [-20, 20]);
  const shadowY = useTransform(mouseYSpring, [-0.5, 0.5], [-20, 20]);

  const handleMouseMove = (e: React.MouseEvent<HTMLElement>) => {
    if (!ref.current) return;

    const rect = ref.current.getBoundingClientRect();
    const width = rect.width;
    const height = rect.height;
    const mouseX = e.clientX - rect.left;
    const mouseY = e.clientY - rect.top;
    const xPct = mouseX / width - 0.5;
    const yPct = mouseY / height - 0.5;
    x.set(xPct);
    y.set(yPct);
  };

  const handleMouseLeave = () => {
    x.set(0);
    y.set(0);
  };

  const tiltProps = {
    style: {
      rotateX,
      rotateY,
      transformStyle: "preserve-3d" as const,
      boxShadow: useTransform(
        [shadowX, shadowY],
        ([x, y]) => `${x}px ${y}px 30px rgba(0, 0, 0, ${shadowIntensity})`,
      ),
    },
    onMouseMove: handleMouseMove,
    onMouseLeave: handleMouseLeave,
    transition: { duration },
  };

  return { tiltProps, ref };
}

```

## Advanced: Layered 3D Effect

Create depth with nested elements:

```tsx
import { motion } from "motion/react"
import { useParallaxTilt } from "@/lib/hooks/use-parallax-tilt"

export function LayeredCard() {
  const { tiltProps, ref } = useParallaxTilt()
  
  return (
    <motion.div 
      ref={ref}
      {...tiltProps}
      className="card"
    >
      {/* Background layer */}
      <div style={{ transform: "translateZ(-20px)" }}>
        Background
      </div>
      
      {/* Middle layer */}
      <div style={{ transform: "translateZ(0px)" }}>
        Content
      </div>
      
      {/* Front layer */}
      <div style={{ transform: "translateZ(40px)" }}>
        Floating Element
      </div>
    </motion.div>
  )
}
```

## Use cases

`useParallaxTilt` returns `{ tiltProps, ref }`. The `tiltProps` object contains a `style` with spring-driven `rotateX`, `rotateY`, `transformStyle: "preserve-3d"`, and a derived `boxShadow` MotionValue, plus `onMouseMove` and `onMouseLeave` handlers. Attach `ref` to the element so the hook can compute the relative cursor position as a fraction of element width and height.

- **Product showcase cards.** A pricing card or feature card that tilts as the cursor sweeps across it creates a sense of depth and 3D presence on an otherwise flat page.
- **Profile or team member cards.** A headshot card with `maxTilt: 10` and `shadowIntensity: 0.2` gives a subtle layered look without being distracting.
- **Portfolio project thumbnails.** Gallery images and project screenshots with a modest tilt feel like physical cards on a table.
- **Landing page hero illustrations.** Wrapping a hero image or SVG illustration in a `motion.div` with `useParallaxTilt` makes it respond to cursor movement across the entire above-the-fold area.
- **Interactive pricing tiers.** Each pricing column can tilt independently as the user moves the cursor across the page, drawing attention to the tier the cursor is nearest.

## When to use / when not to use

**Use `useParallaxTilt` directly when:**

- You need the 3D tilt on a custom element not covered by a prebuilt component.
- You want to place child elements at different `translateZ` depths using `transformStyle: "preserve-3d"` to create a true parallax depth illusion inside the tilting container.
- You need fine control over `stiffness` (default `300`) and `damping` (default `30`) to tune the spring feel.

**Avoid `useParallaxTilt` when:**

- The page is primarily a touch interface. `onMouseMove` never fires on touch, so the effect is invisible to mobile users. Disable it conditionally:

```tsx
const isTouchDevice = typeof window !== "undefined" && window.matchMedia("(hover: none)").matches
const { tiltProps, ref } = useParallaxTilt()
```

- The element contains a `<video>` or `<canvas>`. Applying `rotateX` and `rotateY` to a video can trigger a re-decode cycle in some browsers, causing a flicker.
- The element is inside a scrollable container with `overflow: hidden`. The `getBoundingClientRect` call in `onMouseMove` returns coordinates relative to the viewport, not the scroll container, which can produce incorrect tilt directions during scroll.
- The user's `prefers-reduced-motion` preference is set. 3D rotation is among the most vestibuler-discomfort-causing animation types.

## Accessibility notes

`useParallaxTilt` applies `rotateX` and `rotateY` transforms driven by pointer movement. The effect is purely cosmetic.

- The 3D rotation does not change the element's position in the tab order or its ARIA semantics.
- Respect `prefers-reduced-motion`. 3D tilting is one of the animation types most likely to trigger vestibular discomfort. Return an empty object when the preference is set:

```tsx
"use client"
import { motion } from "motion/react"
import { useReducedMotion } from "motion/react"
import { useParallaxTilt } from "@/lib/use-parallax-tilt"

export function TiltCard({ children }: { children: React.ReactNode }) {
  const reduced = useReducedMotion()
  const { tiltProps, ref } = useParallaxTilt({ maxTilt: 12, shadowIntensity: 0.25 })

  return (
    <motion.div
      ref={ref}
      {...(reduced ? {} : tiltProps)}
      className="rounded-2xl border border-neutral-200 bg-white p-6 focus-visible:outline focus-visible:outline-2 focus-visible:outline-blue-500"
    >
      {children}
    </motion.div>
  )
}
```

- On a keyboard-only workflow, the element is never in a `mousemove` interaction, so sighted keyboard users see no tilt. Ensure the card conveys its interactive state through focus styling rather than the tilt alone.
- If the tilt contains interactive children (buttons, links), confirm they remain reachable after the tilt is applied. Framer Motion applies transforms via `style` and does not alter hit-testing bounds, so click targets remain at their painted position.

## Performance considerations

- `useParallaxTilt` maintains four MotionValues (`x`, `y`, `mouseXSpring`, `mouseYSpring`) and three derived MotionValues (`rotateX`, `rotateY`, `boxShadow`). All updates flow through Framer Motion's rAF loop and do not trigger React renders.
- `rotateX` and `rotateY` are transforms, which run on the compositor. However, the derived `boxShadow` MotionValue causes a repaint on each frame when the cursor is moving. For card-sized elements this is typically one or two layers and not perceptible. For large hero elements, consider setting `shadowIntensity: 0` to disable the shadow.
- `onMouseMove` fires on every pointer event. The hook normalizes the cursor position to a fraction (`-0.5` to `0.5`) and calls `x.set()` and `y.set()`. The spring then interpolates to the new target over the next several frames. This means one `set` call per frame at most, regardless of how fast the cursor moves.
- The `transformStyle: "preserve-3d"` style creates a stacking context. Descendants with absolute positioning that extend outside the element's bounds may be clipped by the 3D rendering layer. Test child overflow before deploying.

## Customization examples

### Subtle tilt for a team member card

```tsx
import { motion } from "motion/react"
import { useParallaxTilt } from "@/lib/use-parallax-tilt"

export function PersonCard({ name, title, avatar }: { name: string; title: string; avatar: string }) {
  const { tiltProps, ref } = useParallaxTilt({
    maxTilt: 8,
    shadowIntensity: 0.15,
    stiffness: 250,
    damping: 28,
  })

  return (
    <motion.div ref={ref} {...tiltProps} className="w-56 overflow-hidden rounded-2xl border border-neutral-100 bg-white">
      <img src={avatar} alt={name} className="aspect-square w-full object-cover" />
      <div className="p-4">
        <p className="font-semibold">{name}</p>
        <p className="text-xs text-neutral-400">{title}</p>
      </div>
    </motion.div>
  )
}
```
